guides.title: Adding painted panel lines
guides.summary: Paint extra dark panel lines with a fine pale edge, plus small markings, to make plain armour or vehicles look more detailed.
body: Find a reference for where extra panels and markings would sit, such as a larger or more detailed version of the same design. Lines that join up look more believable and give natural borders for a two-tone scheme.
Paint each new panel line as a thin, near-black line with a fine brush and well thinned paint.
Run a fine pale line along one side of each dark line, on the side facing the light. The pair reads as a cut groove, not a drawn line.

For real grooves, cut them before priming. Mark the line lightly with a hobby knife, deepen it with a fine saw that matches the existing lines, brush a little thin plastic glue in to melt the fuzz, then sand lightly.

Add a few small markings, numbers or warning stripes. Small, thin markings make a big machine look bigger; too many looks busy. Use an opaque paint, and paint the pale colour first, as dark covers pale more easily than the reverse.
For straight, matching lines, use a rivet or bolt as a guide and pull the line from it with the brush tip, using the same guide on the other side. Turn the model between strokes.
If a line wobbles, tidy it with the panel colour once dry rather than trying to fix it wet. Then shade and edge highlight the new markings like the rest of the surface.

guides.title: Airbrush handling basics
guides.summary: Spray in short bursts at the right distance and pressure, and turn the model rather than the airbrush, for thin even coats.
body: Before anything else, learn to strip the airbrush and put it back together; you will need to for cleaning and faults. Tighten parts by hand, not with tools, and never clean it with a wire brush. Wear a mask with filters, and test spray on paper or a spare part before the model every time.

For most work, thin paint about half and half with airbrush thinner. Put the thinner in the cup first, then the paint, so neat paint never reaches the needle. Close detail needs much thinner paint, around one part paint to ten of thinner.

Push the trigger down for air, draw it back for paint, and let it spring forward again. Start the air before the paint and stop the paint before the air, which avoids spits. Practise with air only, then water on card, then paint. Work in short bursts so each pass dries fast and stays thin.

Distance sets the spray size. About a fist's width away suits priming and base coats. Come in to about three fingers' width for highlights, and an inch or less for fine work with only the tiniest trigger movement.

Most work sits between 20 and 30 psi; start around 25. Match paint to pressure. Thick paint at low pressure speckles; thin paint at high pressure close in blows out into spidery lines. Do not turn the pressure up to force thick paint through; thin it. For close work use thin paint and low pressure.
Keep the airbrush steady and rotate the model beneath it instead. Tipping the airbrush can spill paint from the cup.
When spraying several colours, do the top or the smaller area first and angle the spray away from finished parts. Near a finished area, stop short and finish by brush.

Start with priming and big base coats, where slips do not show. Light colours over black take many coats, so prime white or grey for bright schemes. Mix only a little paint per stage, as a full cup tempts you to over-spray, and practise often on spare models.

guides.title: Highlighting with an airbrush
guides.summary: Spray each lighter tone into a smaller area where light hits, keep the shadows, then sharpen the brightest spots by brush.
body: Mix a dark shadow, a mid tone and a light tone of the colour before you start. Label them, or keep leftovers in small lidded jars, so a whole army matches. For rich shadows, darken the base with a deeper version of the colour or a grey rather than pure black.

Spray the shadow tone over everything in thin coats until it is solid, getting it right into the recesses, which are hard to reach later. Paint thinned to the feel of milk at about 20 to 25 psi suits this.

Spray the mid tone from above, towards the centre of panels and the upper surfaces, leaving a ring of the dark tone near edges and recesses. Make it a step lighter than you think you need, and stop earlier than feels natural. On busy shapes such as muscled creatures, start wide and get more selective with each step.

Spray the light tone, such as a warm off-white, into an even smaller area on the top surfaces only; too much washes the model out. Thin it more, drop to about 15 psi and work close. For tiny highlights, aim, hold still and pulse very short bursts. A fine nozzle helps.

The common mistake is spraying each tone until the one below vanishes. If you lose the shadows, spray the shadow mix back in from below. If the mid tone is lost, a thin glaze of the main colour over everything brings it back.

To pick out ridges and texture, spray a lighter mix from one low angle; only the faces pointing at the airbrush catch paint. For crisp panel highlights, hold a straight-edged card against a raised edge and spray along it so paint stays off the recess beside it.

A pure airbrushed gradient can look too even and flat. Once other colours are blocked in, push the brightest spots further by brush, add a paler touch on the highest points and a few sharp reflections, and blend with thin glazes.

Where overspray would spoil nearby areas, or with no airbrush, do the same by brush, layering each lighter tone into the middle of the panel, or dab it on with a damp make-up sponge in thin layers of normal brush paint.

guides.title: Masking with an airbrush
guides.summary: Cover finished areas with tape, putty or liquid mask, then spray thin dry coats so the new colour stops in a clean line.
body: Where you can, paint parts separately before gluing; it is far easier than masking. Otherwise spray the lighter or smaller colour area first, since a dark colour covers overspray more easily and a small area is easier to mask. Let it dry fully. A light gloss varnish over it helps masks lift cleanly without pulling paint.

Lay low-tack masking tape on flat parts in small strips, right up to where the new colour should stop, and burnish the edges down with a fingernail. For a crisp edge, lay it over a panel line and trim it along the line with a sharp knife.

On curves and awkward spots where tape lifts, press in a low-tack reusable putty, never children's modelling clay, which leaves oily marks. Cut strips for a straight edge, or shape wavy lines and seal every edge with the side of a brush, as gaps let spray through. Do not leave putty on overnight; it slowly sags.

Liquid mask suits small odd shapes and inset parts. It ruins good brushes, so use a sponge or an old brush rubbed with soap and wash it at once. Lay it on with some body, as thin mask tears, and test it on a hidden spot, as it can lift paint. Peel it soon after spraying, rolling it onto a toothpick; stuck bits cling to the mask already on it.

Spray thin, slightly dry coats at low pressure, close in and aimed at the open area, and let each dry before the next. Wet coats creep under the mask. Cover the rest of the model with putty or cling film if overspray is a worry, and mask again for each further colour.

For stripes, tape both sides of a band and spray between them. For a glowing circle, spray a bright centre, press a cut tape disc over it and spray darker tones around it. Through a stencil, spray white first and then the bright colour. Low-tack stencils give slightly soft edges on uneven surfaces.

Once dry, peel tape slowly back on itself at a low angle. Dark marks along the edge may only be tape residue; try a damp sponge. Tidy small bleeds by brush rather than spraying again. A dark brown reads as shading or wear on any colour, or hide it under chipping.
Allow plenty of time. Masking a whole squad can take well over an hour, and small fragile parts can snap off.

guides.title: Airbrush glazing and tinting
guides.summary: Mist very thin ink, wash or glaze through the airbrush in light passes for smooth transitions, colour depth and glows.
body: Thin far more than usual: about one part paint or ink to six to twelve parts thinner and water, plus a drop of matt medium; on paper it should only stain. One-coat contrast-style paints need about two to four parts thinner, and most ready washes spray as they are. A glaze from opaque paint, about three parts paint to one each of glaze medium, thinner and water, should look like whole milk.
Use a fine needle and lower pressure, start the air first and barely rock the trigger back so very little colour comes out. Spidering comes from too much paint at once more than from pressure.

Do not spray wet on wet. Make a light pass, blow plain air over it or move to the next model, and come back once dry. Two to four passes give the colour. Colours look different wet and dry, red especially, so judge only when dry and under more than one light.

Over a zenithal or pre-shaded undercoat, spray lighter transparent colours first, such as yellow, then darker ones, from above first and then lightly on the sides. Put little colour in the black areas: a glaze cannot brighten black, and too much there flattens the model. Spray a darker version of the same hue into the shadows so they read as coloured, not grey.

A filter of one or two light passes over the whole area pulls rough layers together, adds saturation and knocks highlights back, so push your last highlight a step brighter beforehand. A warm yellow from above and a cool purple from below unify a quick paint job. A faint earthy green low down grounds a figure.

Mist from below or at a steep angle into the shadows to add depth, with a touch of black for the darkest spots. A different faint colour from each side, or a different wash colour per model, adds variety across an army.

To smooth brushwork, block the tones in by brush, then mist thin glazes over the joins. Pale greys and whites glaze in seconds this way. It works best on medium to large surfaces. Thin airbrushed glazes can leave a sheen, so matt varnish afterwards.
For a glow, brush the source white first, then mist colour over it and just around it. Repeat for a stronger effect. Overspray travels further than you expect, so shield nearby areas.

guides.title: Airbrush trigger control
guides.summary: Air on before paint and paint off before air, with your finger set back on the trigger to meter tiny amounts.
body: On a dual action airbrush, pressing the trigger down gives air only and pulling it back opens the needle for paint. The further back, the more paint. A single action airbrush cannot meter paint separately, so it is a poor choice for models.

Hold it like a pen and rest the pad of your index finger on top of the trigger, a little back from the front edge. A finger perched at the front tends to snatch the trigger and dump paint. Bracing your thumb under the trigger area gives a fixed stop for tiny, repeatable pulls.

Starting: press down for air first, then ease back for paint. Starting with air blows out debris. Stopping: push forward to stop the paint, then release the air, which clears the tip. Stopping both at once leaves a droplet on the needle that spits onto the model next time.
While learning, set the trigger limiter, a collar or dial at the back, so the trigger cannot pull back too far and flood the model. Remove it only once your control is good.

Practise on paper first: grids of dots from different distances, lines with no blob at either end, tracing drawn circles, and fades from solid colour to nothing. It feels dull, but it makes the first models far easier.

For priming and base coats, hold about 10 to 15 cm away, press fully down and pull well back for plenty of paint. Build colour over several coats. Between coats, press down without pulling back to blow plain air over the model and dry it.
For small highlights or glows, move close, keep the air on and give the trigger short light taps, pulling back only a fraction.
Keep the pressure steady and let the trigger change the flow. Use less paint than you think, and build smooth gradients from many light passes back and forth.

guides.title: Airbrushing cloaks and cloth
guides.summary: Spray smooth shadows and highlights onto big cloth areas over a pre-shade, then sharpen the contrast by brush.
body: Large flat cloth such as a cloak is hard to blend by brush, as every stopped stroke leaves a break. An airbrush gives smooth transitions from the start. Paint the cloak as a separate piece if the kit allows, or mask the parts already finished.

Pre-shade first: black or a dark grey overall, then white or off-white sprayed from the direction of the light so only the upward-facing folds catch it. Check the light and shadow placement now and correct it before adding colour or detail.
Thin the cloth colour, about two parts thinner to one part paint, and spray light layers so the pre-shade shows through as shadow and highlight.

Spray a darker mix, or a complementary colour such as purple on green, into the shadows at a low, steep angle so it lands only on the shadowed sides of the folds. Spraying dark over light is easier and less speckled than light over dark. Then spray the highlight again to tidy overspray.

For seams and panels, lay flexible masking tape along the seam and spray light on one side and shadow on the other. For a woven or rough texture, use slightly thicker paint and feather the trigger until the spray spatters into a fine grain; test on card first.
If paint goes on too wet, leave it alone. Spraying more air or using a hair dryer on wet paint pushes it into ridges.
Switch to a brush with fairly thin paint to push the contrast further. Brushwork over spraying is slow to blend, so decide early which tool does which step.
Finish with short fine lines on the brightest spots to suggest woven fabric catching the light. Push them further for thick wool. Stitching is plain brushwork and just needs patience.

guides.title: Airbrushed metal gradients
guides.summary: Spray a mid steel all over, a dark tone from below and bright silver from above for fast shaded metal.
body: Over a black primer, spray a mid steel metallic across the whole model in smooth coats. Metallics with a fine flake spray best and avoid a glittery look.
Spray a thin dark blue-black, around #1c2230, from underneath so the lower surfaces fall into shadow. Several passes of very thin black give a more even shade than a wash.
Then spray bright silver from above, anywhere from straight down to about 45 degrees, so the upper surfaces catch the light.
The same order works for gold: a darker gold base, a brighter gold from above, then the dark gold mixed about half and half with a dark brown ink sprayed from below.
Tip leftover shadow mix onto the palette and brush it into spots the airbrush cannot reach cleanly.
There is no need for an all-over wash, as the lower recesses are already in shadow. Run a dark oil or enamel wash only into upper panel lines that the silver brightened.
For scorched exhausts and barrels, spray a slightly thicker black right on the tips.
Finish with a few brush edge highlights on the top edges if you want more sparkle.

guides.title: One wash over the whole model
guides.summary: Wash a base-coated model all over for quick shading and a unified tone, then layer the raised areas back up.
body: Plan which areas share a wash, for example cloth, leather, bone and metal under a dark brown. Base coat all of them first, largest area first, tidying edges as each colour goes on. Metal can be drybrushed at this stage and washed with the rest.

With a large brush and a palette for control, run the wash over the whole model so it settles in every recess, keeping it thin on flat panels. Let it flow and settle rather than brushing it about like paint. Hold the model at one angle while it settles; tipping it about sends the wash several ways.

Then use a damp brush to move it: thin it where you want it lighter, such as small badges, and add more on pouches and straps. Dry the brush and lift pools, especially on lower edges and parts that stick out.

Pick the wash to suit the model. A warm brown ties earthy colours together and warms gold; a black wash suits clean silver and pulls mismatched touch-ups together, and a touch of red in it makes shadows read brown rather than dead grey. A warm flesh one-coat paint over skin, gold, yellow and red shades them all at once.

A wash over a neutral base also shifts its colour. Sepia over white gives cream; brown over a mid grey gives a drab green. Over a bone primer, a white one-coat paint mixed one to one with medium gives soft, light all-over shading. Test on a spare part first.

Let it dry naturally, about 45 minutes. Blowing on a wash pushes it around and leaves tide marks. Then paint and wash areas that need a different wash, such as skin or gold, with a small brush. Colours that must stay bright, like clean white markings or pale horns, go on last or are skipped by the wash.

An all-over wash suits textured areas like fur or chainmail and busy, studded armour. On big smooth panels or bright colours such as yellow it leaves tide marks and dulls the flats, so shade only the recesses there.

Once dry, layer each main colour back over the raised areas, always leaving some of the darker tone in creases and recesses, and touch up any silver the wash dulled. One clear step brighter is enough for the table.

guides.title: Highlighting blocky, angular shapes
guides.summary: Treat each flat face of a hard, angular model as its own light level and push the difference between faces.
body: Robots, vehicles and blocky armour are flat planes and corners, not curves. Light changes at each corner, not gradually.
Decide where the light comes from. Faces turned to it go clearly lighter; faces turned away go clearly darker.
Exaggerate the step between neighbouring faces more than feels natural. Bold, clean steps read well at a distance.
On big flat faces, a gradient from one corner to the opposite one gives a polished, crystal-like sheen.
Finish the corners with crisp edge highlights. Illustrations and box art are useful references for which faces are light and dark.

guides.title: Applying one-coat contrast paints
guides.summary: Get an even coat of one-coat contrast or speed paint by working one panel at a time so it does not pool or go streaky.
body: Prime white, bone or light grey, or drybrush a light colour first. The paint is see-through, so what is underneath sets how bright it ends up. It shines on fur, scales, mail, faces and yellow, and vertical faces come out cleaner than flat tops. Big smooth panels tend to go blotchy, so use opaque paint and painted highlights there.

Shake the pot well; a small ball bearing in the pot helps. Keep pots closed and stuck down or in a holder, as they tip easily and thicken when open. Pour some onto a palette and load the brush full but not dripping. Test the strength on a hidden spot; if unsure, mix half and half with clear medium and plan two coats.
Do lighter colours first and blacks and browns last, as a dark colour covers a light slip but not the reverse. Paint undersides first so you do not tip the model later while other areas are wet.

Work one panel at a time. Put a little extra at the top, flow it across the whole panel to a natural edge and slightly over it, then move on. End strokes where you want it darkest; on a blade, one stroke down each flat face. Keep the model the same way up while it dries; tipping it sends the paint two ways and leaves crossed streaks.

While it is fully wet you can pull excess out of recesses and spread it. Once it starts to dry, leave it alone. Brushing back into half-dry paint tears its skin and leaves a fuzzy, streaky patch that another coat will not hide.

If paint pools in a recess or on a flat area, press a clean, damp brush into it to soak it up. Check low corners such as under shoulder plates. Lifting paint off raised areas the same way gives instant highlights, and if edges stay weak, or mild blotches remain, a light drybrush of a brighter colour fixes both.

It stays wet longer than normal paint and can look dry before it is, so coat one model and move to the next. Allow 30 to 45 minutes before a second coat and an hour before washing over it, or it may lift or bleed into whites. Each coat only darkens; to go lighter, add medium, not water. Seal it with thin coats of matt varnish, as it rubs off raised areas.

A slip cannot be covered by another see-through paint, and some reactivate and bleed through a different colour, so test first. Paint the spot back in the primer colour, then redo it. If a colour came out too heavy and hid detail, drybrush the light base back over and redo it in two thinner coats.

guides.title: Applying waterslide transfers
guides.summary: Gloss the area, soak and slide the transfer on, soften it into place, then seal and matt it so it looks painted on.
body: Plan where transfers go before painting, and apply them part way through, before weathering. They are see-through, so paint a light patch under any that need a bright background. Then gloss varnish the whole panel so the finish matches later, and let it cure, ideally overnight; softener can lift fresh varnish and the paint beneath it.

Cut close to the design with a sharp knife rather than scissors, keeping corners rounded. Leave very thin spiky bits joined to a little film so they do not curl. On a curve, make a small cut into the film so it can bend. Cut a spare in case one tears, and mirror creature emblems on opposite sides so both face forward.

Use clean water. Soak the transfer on damp tissue or in water for 20 to 60 seconds, until it slides on its backing. Too long and it floats off and sinks; pushed off too early, it tears. Rub-on transfers work differently: press the sticky side down firmly, wet the backing paper and slide it away.

Brush a little setting solution or water onto the model, slide the transfer off with a soft brush and nudge it into place. Keep it wet the whole time or it sticks where it lands. Press the water out with a damp cotton bud or tissue corner, without pushing it sideways.

Once it is positioned, brush on a softening solution and leave it. It will look wrinkled at first. Walk away for about fifteen minutes while it pulls down. Then gently roll out any wrinkles or trapped air with a cotton bud dampened with softener. On strong curves, repeat softening and pressing a few times. Flat areas need only the setting solution.
Let it dry fully, ideally overnight; a hair dryer held well back speeds it up. If a fold will not settle on a round shoulder, paint it over as a scratch or chip.

Seal with gloss to hide the film edge, then matt varnish the whole panel to kill the shine. A handy order is: gloss coat, transfers and pin wash together, then matt over everything, then chips and fine details. A very thin dark wash over the transfer also dulls it and ties it in.

To wear it, chip it with a toothpick or sponge the panel colour lightly over it. If a transfer is too big or the wrong colour, trim it, then paint over it in your own colour using it as a stencil, and freehand any missing part. Check old sheets for cracks or yellowing before use.

guides.title: Applying a wash
guides.summary: Place a wash with a well loaded brush, steer it into recesses and lift pools before they dry into tide marks.
body: Use a medium or larger brush with a good belly, an older synthetic one if possible. A tiny brush runs dry and leaves rings. Load only the bristles, never up to the metal collar, where wash wicks in and spoils good brushes. Keep a small brush only for fine detail and tight spots next to other colours.

There are two ways. Flood it all over and repaint the raised areas afterwards, or place it only in the recesses, which is slower but needs less tidying. Mix them: flood busy areas such as heads and chests, and be precise on large flat panels.

Shake or stir the wash first, as the pigment settles. Load from a palette so the brush is full but not dripping. Use the wash mostly straight, or brush it on neat and work a little water or medium into it on the model. That pushes it off raised areas and gives more control than thinning on the palette.

Hold the model at one angle until the wash dries; a wash that runs two ways dries in streaks. Use gravity: lay a face flat and pointing up for an even shade, or stand a part upright so the wash gathers into runs for grime. Point the edges you want darkest downwards.

Touch down, push the wash towards the spot and lift off where you want it darkest; it gathers where the brush leaves. A dot in the middle of an area darkens the centre, while a wash run up to the walls darkens the edges. Next to pale skin, start away from it and pull the wash towards the edge.

Work in small sections, such as one arm or half a cloak, and round the model so wet always meets wet. With a big brush, wash a new area, then sweep back over the last one to lift and spread any excess. Never brush into wash that has started to dry; some form a skin that peels, and that is what leaves tide marks.

Keep watching. Pools form at the bottom of folds, on parts that hang down and in tight gaps such as ribs and waists. Press a blotted brush into a pool to lift it. If wash lands where you did not want it, rinse the brush and gently scrub the spot while it is wet.

Let it dry fully before touching it: about 15 minutes for a normal coat, up to an hour for a heavy one. Keep a hair dryer well back. Two thin washes give more control than one heavy one; put the second only where it still looks light. Glossy washes suit metal and leather; matt ones suit cloth, hair and bone.

guides.title: Asking for feedback and reading critique
guides.summary: Ask a narrow question with good photos, then pick one or two points to work on and test them before changing everything.
body: Ask a narrow question. "Do the cloak highlights read from arm's length?" gets useful answers. "What do you think?" mostly gets polite praise or noise.
Show the model well: a sharp photo from the front and one from the side or back, in bright even light on a plain background. A blurry, dim photo hides exactly the things you want checked.
Say what you were aiming for, such as quick tabletop standard or a slow display piece, and how long you have been painting. People then judge it against your goal and not their own.
Look for repeats. If three people mention low contrast or messy edges, that is the thing to fix first. A single odd comment can wait.
Read comments as notes about the model, not about you. If one stings, wait a day before replying. Thank people even when you disagree.
Weigh who is talking. Someone whose work you like, or who explains why, is worth more than a one-word reply. Taste remarks about colour can be ignored if your scheme is deliberate.
Test the advice on a spare model or one small area before repainting the lot. Take before and after photos so you can see whether it actually helped.
Give feedback the same way you want it: one thing that works, one clear thing to try next, and the reason.

guides.title: Base coating
guides.summary: Lay a smooth, solid first colour with no streaks or brush marks in two or three thin coats, each left to dry fully.
body: Prime first; white makes colours brighter, black dulls them slightly. Bright colours over black can need three or four coats. Over a zenithal undercoat, a thin base coat lets some light and dark show through for free contrast.

Shake the pot well. Thin a small puddle on the palette to the feel of melted ice cream: it clings to the brush, flows to the end of the stroke and dries flat with no ridges. Too much water turns it patchy. Load enough for four or five strokes, the same amount each time, rather than dumping a blob and spreading it. Keep paint out of the metal collar.

On big areas use the largest brush you can control, with a good belly. Start with the belly and pull towards the tip, stroking outwards from the middle and along the shapes, not across them. Brushing across detail pushes paint into it and blurs it.

Another way for big or busy areas is to dampen a large soft round brush, pick up a little paint and scrub and stipple it on. It leaves the same thickness on edges and in recesses, so detail stays crisp and edges get a protective film for later drybrushing. Watch raised lips for drifts.

On faces and small detail, thin a little more and use just the brush tip. For neat plates, touch well thinned paint near the trim; it runs to the edge and stops, giving a clean border before you fill the middle.

You have only a few seconds to work each coat. Lay it, smooth it briefly and let it dry however patchy it looks. Brushing over half-dry paint drags it into a rough texture that shows through every later layer. Lift off in the middle of a smooth area, not by a recess, as paint pools where the brush leaves.

Two or three thin coats beat one thick one, which can crack or peel; yellow and white need more, and 3D prints soak paint along their layer lines and may need several extra. Recoat only where primer still shows. It is done when the colour is even, with no primer, texture or pooling in the recesses.

Paint the largest areas, or the innermost layers such as skin, first, then work outwards to cloth, armour and trim, so each colour tidies the last. Do not stop to fix every slip; tidy at the end. Block in all the main colours early to see the scheme. It will look messy for a while, and that is normal.

guides.title: Lighting a base to match the model
guides.summary: Light the base from the same direction and in the same colours as the model, so the scene holds together.
body: A common mistake is painting directional light on the model, then giving the base flat, even colour. If light hits the model from one side, or in a colour, it hits the ground too.
Drybrush the base in one direction only, from the side the light comes from. Use the highlight colours already on your palette for each side, and keep the shadow colour under and between the feet.
Work pale pigment into the lit side and dark brown or black pigment into the recesses on the shadow side. Pick out raised edges on the lit side with a thin pale glaze.

Another way: paint the ground in the light colours, give it an enamel wash for the ground's own colour, then once dry buff it back with a dry sponge. A touch of white spirit on the sponge lifts more where the light is strongest.
Tufts and stones follow the light too. Drybrush the tufts on the lit side paler and those on the shadow side a darker bone, and add a few small glints on pebbles in the highlight colour.

guides.title: Finishing touches for a base
guides.summary: Carry the ground right to the edge, paint a clean rim and blend in tufts so the base looks finished.
body: Treat the base as a slice of a larger ground. Texture, cracks and colour should run right up to the edge as if they carry on beyond it. Debris piles around objects rather than on top of them; look at real ground if unsure.

Avoid the usual rough signs. Wipe sand off the rim with a finger while the glue is wet, or scrape it later. Nudge sand that has crept up rocks back down. Spread glue flat and keep it slightly back from details, or it leaves bulges and clumps.

Paint everything on the base. Real twigs and stones look out of scale left bare, so give them at least a wash and a light drybrush. Small clutter such as skulls and helmets needs only a light primer, flat colours and one brown wash; use a thinned black wash on white items.

To tie a busy base together, give the whole base one brown wash, then a light drybrush of a pale bone over everything. Drybrush heavier at the front and lighter at the back, using the same highlight colour as the model.
Keep it restrained. Bright snow or slime should not be the brightest thing on the piece, and a scratch or two of rust or grime beats heavy weathering everywhere. Stop before it gets busy.

Pick up tufts with a hobby knife and press them into dips and against rocks rather than in the open. Mix a few tuft colours, and give them a light drybrush or a dusting of pigment so they look less clean. A little pigment on the feet ties the model to the ground.

Before painting the rim, scrape off any texture stuck to its side. Paint it last, in two thin coats, stopping at the top edge so the ground stays clean. A smooth rim looks neat in satin; a rough one hides better in matt. Never leave it bare or messy.

guides.title: Batch painting
guides.summary: Paint one colour across a small group of models before moving to the next, and keep batches small enough to finish.
body: Pick a batch you can finish in days, not months. Three to ten similar models suits most people, fewer for very detailed ones; fifteen or more tends to feel endless. Paint leaders separately. Bulk steps such as priming and the main colour can go across the whole army in one or two sittings so the colour matches; then split into small groups for the details.

Plan first. Simple models and about five colours per batch go fastest. Take one test model all the way to the finish, note each step and any mixes, and keep it or a picture on the desk. Check you have enough of each paint for the whole batch.

For a time budget, multiply minutes per model by the count, then add basing, transfers and varnish. Glue models to their bases and onto corks or handles before priming. Leave parts like shoulder pads off to paint separately. A primer close to the main colour saves a whole stage.

Do each step on every model before starting the next, largest areas first for quick visible progress. Line them up and work along the row, and down each figure from head to feet so nothing is skipped. By the last model the first is dry. After each colour, and after any break, check for missed areas.

Base coat all the colours that share a wash, then wash the whole batch at once. Keep base coats smooth; a blotchy one multiplies the fixing across every model. Put long-drying steps, such as transfers, oil washes and base texture, together so they dry overnight. Use the biggest brush that keeps a good point.
Swap which items get which colour, or vary the skin tone, across the group for variety while the scheme stays unified.

Spend extra time only where the eye goes, such as faces and a leader model. Skip detailed eyes on rank and file; a dark line in the sockets is enough. Keep strong contrast, as the models are seen from about arm's length or more. Most of an army at a good standard beats a few perfect models.

Huge batches drag on and sap motivation. Even a one minute step takes over an hour across seventy models. Run two or three small batches side by side and switch while one dries, paint a leader between batches, and set a steady target such as one unit a week. Expect a slump near the end and push through, or split the batch and finish part of it.

guides.title: Battered brass and copper
guides.summary: Stipple highlights and shades over a warm metal base for a pitted, worn brass or copper finish with broken bright edges.
body: Base coat a strong orange copper in two thin coats. It looks too bright on its own; later steps knock it back.
Overbrush a brass colour over most of it, leaving copper only in the deepest recesses.
Stipple the highlights rather than blending: dab brass with about a third silver mixed in on the upper areas, then a mostly silver mix only on the very tops. Texture is a good thing here.

Wash a brown shade heavily into the recesses and thinly over everything to kill the shine. Once dry, dab that brown onto the lower, shaded parts for texture, and run a very dark brown ink round rivets, cuts and holes.
Dull next to shiny is a contrast, just like dark next to light. Wash some areas with a thinned mid grey to flatten them and leave others bright.
For a hint of age, add a thin dark turquoise wash, or mix about four parts brown wash to one part turquoise. A water-based wash dulls metal more than an oil wash. Keep plenty of warm metal showing.
Stipple a silver-heavy mix or a few specks of bright bronze back onto the highest points, then coat it all with clear matt medium so the sheen is even.
The same approach gives quick textured gold: a dark metallic brown base, a mid gold stippled and scratched on edges facing the light, then bright gold with a little silver.

guides.title: Chipped and battle-worn blades
guides.summary: Paint chips spreading from the cutting edge, larger where blows land and finer further away, with a bright lip on each.
body: Work out where the blade takes hits: the cutting edge, the tip and any teeth. That is where damage starts.
Paint small dark chips running in from that edge, slightly random but all with the same general direction.
Make them larger at the main point of impact and smaller and finer as they spread along and away from the edge.
Add a fine light highlight on the edge-facing side of each chip, mostly on upper points and corners, so it reads as a dent.

On a metallic blade, base a dark silver and wash it dark. Then paint short silver strokes from the cutting edge inwards, as if each were a nick from a blow. Repeat a few with a bright silver and run it along the whole outer edge. It reads as both scratches and a sharpened edge.
Keep the flat of the blade mostly clean. A few chips in the right places look more convincing than an even scatter.

guides.title: Black lining
guides.summary: Paint thin dark lines where two colours or parts meet so each area reads cleanly, like inking a comic.
body: Wherever two surfaces meet in real life, a thin shadow sits in the join. Without it, colour boundaries look muddy, especially after dry brushing or airbrushing. Lining divides parts so they read; it is not the same job as shading.

Use a fine brush with a sharp tip and only a little paint on it, thinned until it flows like ink. It does not have to be pure black; a very dark brown, softer on warm colours, or a very dark version of a neighbouring colour also works. Brace your hands for steady lines.

Run the line into the gap where plates overlap, cloth meets armour or a hand grips a hilt, and around bolts and rivets. Thinned paint also defines shallow engraved lines that a wash would only stain. On belts and straps, painting the whole item black is easier than lining both sides.
A strong dark wash does the same job and is more forgiving. Touch it right into the corner without dragging it over either surface and it fades out on its own. A weak wash is not dark enough.
Do it soon after base coating, or as a last pass to clean up the border between two finished areas. If it spreads, go back with the colour next to it until only a thin, sharp line remains.
Another way is to undercoat very dark and stop each base coat just short of the join, leaving a thin dark gap. It is slower but very crisp.

It matters more the smaller the figure. On small-scale models, a fine line around each part stops skin, cloth and kit blurring together at arm's length. Keep it thin, or it looks like a cartoon outline.

You do not need to line every recess. Lining just the obvious ones gets you most of the benefit, and it hides small slips such as metallic paint in a gap. A fine waterproof ink pen is easier to steer on reachable lines.

guides.title: The black-out stage
guides.summary: After the main colour, paint every other part black so the model reads clearly and the details are easier to finish.
body: Once the main colour is done, along with any transfers and varnish on it, paint everything else black: straps, pouches, guns, under suits and metal parts.

Slightly thinned black runs into cracks and leaves neat dark lines between areas with very little effort. With a fine brush, run the same thinned black between garments and around belts where it did not reach.
Work in big chunks instead of painting around small details. Paint a whole lower leg or a glove up to the elbow black, then add back the few strips of main colour that show.

Paint guns black all over, then pick out only the raised metal parts, lining only where needed, such as around rivets. The recesses already look shaded, and a thin black wash over the metal ties it in.
This stage stops the model looking like one colour blob, shows what is left to paint and keeps unfinished areas from fooling your eye while you judge contrast.
When touching the main colour back in over a dry brushed area, mix the base and dry brush colours about half and half so the patch matches.
Some painters skip this and base coat details straight over the primer, relying on a wash later. Both work, so use whichever helps you.

guides.title: Choosing a blending method
guides.summary: Wet blending is fastest, stippling is quick and textured, and layering with glazes is slowest but most controlled.
body: Acrylic paint dries fast and hard, which works against blending. Every method is a way of working with that, and none gives a perfect blend in one pass, so expect to go back and forth. Pick one method and practise it on a spare model rather than switching between them.

A smooth change comes from translucent paint, from layers close in value, or both. If one step is a big jump, mix a midway colour and blend it in between. Choose colours that mix cleanly; colours far apart on the wheel can turn muddy in the middle.

Wet blending merges two colours while both are still wet on the model, using paint at normal or slightly thicker consistency. It is very quick but harder to place exactly. It suits skin, cloth, fire and organic shapes.

Feathering and loaded-brush blending are close relatives. Feathering drags the wet edge of a fresh coat out with a clean damp brush. A loaded brush carries two colours at once so they mix as you lay them down.
Stippling builds a blend from many small dabs, denser in one tone and sparser towards the next. It is quick, and thicker paint adds texture for worn or rough surfaces.

Layering with glazes is slower but gives the most control and the fewest accidents. It suits painted metal, faces and small precise areas, and is the most reliable place to start. Thin glazes until see-through; laying dark over light is quicker, as dark colours cover better.
Large smooth panels such as vehicle armour are hard to wet blend evenly. An airbrush, or blending only the narrow join between layers, works better.

For smooth results without spending all day, mix them: paint a few midtone layers, wet blend where they meet, then tidy with a couple of glazes. A wet palette and a fresh mix for each step keep the paint consistent; slightly thicker paint is easier to control than over-thinned.

guides.title: Blending tiny areas
guides.summary: Where there is no room for a blending stroke, paint in-between colour mixes over the join to smooth the step.
body: Glazing and feathering need space for the stroke. On small parts like fingers, straps or small plates there often is not enough.
Mix one or two colours halfway between the two layers on the palette.
Paint them over the join at normal covering consistency, each a little smaller than the one before.
Add more in-between steps until the change looks smooth from normal viewing distance. At this size, two or three steps usually read as a blend.

The same trick blends one material into another, such as a claw, horn or thorn growing out of skin. Paint a halfway mix where they meet. Then keep the skin highlights soft and the claw highlights sharp, so the two still read as different materials.
If you do want to glaze a small area, use a small brush, very thin paint and only a little on the brush. Push it towards the darker side, let it dry and repeat over a slightly smaller patch.

guides.title: Blood, gore and smears
guides.summary: Paint splatter, smears, drips and handprints with dark, see-through glossy reds, and finish wet areas with gloss.
body: Use a dark red rather than a bright one. A clear gloss red with a touch of black, around #5e0a0d, reads as real blood; bright or opaque reds look like paint, because real blood is see-through. More black makes it look older. Keep it loose and uneven; neat blood looks painted on.
For splatter, tear a small piece of sponge for a ragged edge, hold it in tweezers, blot most of the paint off and dab lightly. Build it up gradually. Press too hard and you coat the whole blade.

For finer random spatter, load a stiff brush or old toothbrush with thinned red and pull a fingertip across the bristles, tap the handle, or blow across them. Thicker paint gives bigger drops. Test on paper first, cover anything nearby, and aim from the direction the blow came from.

For smears and stains, a warm flesh-coloured wash first gives a raw base. Then thin the red a lot and glaze it on in uneven patches. Add a little dark brown where blood would be thicker or older, but not too much, as it dulls the shine.

A handprint at this scale is an upside-down L for the palm and thumb, then four short lines for fingers. Add short drips running down from marks and edges. On a blade, drag the paint along it in the direction of the swing.

Put a little more on blades and edges for fresh, pooled spots. For a hanging drop, glue a short bristle to the tip, dab thick blood paint on the end and let it gather into a teardrop. Repeat once dry.

Old blood dries matt and fresh blood is glossy. A matt deep red with gloss red over part of it looks more real than one finish; mixing a little deep red and dark wash into a glossy blood paint dulls it. For wet mouths and gums, build red ink in gloss varnish in thin layers and let each air dry.
Use less than you think and stop early. A few well placed marks look better than a model drenched in red. If a blob lands, do not spread it around finished paint; lift it off with a damp brush.

guides.title: Bone and cream armour
guides.summary: Lay a smooth cream base over a light primer, let neat shading and lining do the work, then add one highlight.
body: Prime light grey or white. Cream over black needs coat after coat and seldom ends up smooth. Paint any dark under suit roughly first; the cream can tidy it afterwards.
Base coat a cream, around #d8cdb0, in several thin coats. An airbrush makes this fast; touch up any missed crevices by brush.

For a soft gradient, glaze a slightly darker, warmer mix into the recesses and over the lower part of each panel. Another way is a thin brown or sepia wash pushed into the shadows over a few passes, then the cream layered back on the raised areas.
Line every panel line with a dark brown thinned half and half with water. That dark line against the pale colour is what gives the armour its crisp look.
Look the model over and smooth any rough joins with a glaze of the base colour.
Finish with one edge highlight of the base mixed half and half with white, on all edges or only the upper ones. Pure white edges give a sharper, brighter look.
For a worn look, sponge small dark chips along the edges after the last highlight. The pale edge around each chip makes it read as damage.

guides.title: Breaking up large plain areas
guides.summary: Add bands, markings, chips or colour shifts to big flat areas like wings, cloaks and shells so they hold interest.
body: Large plain areas such as wing membranes, cloaks, shells and big panels look dull in one colour even when well highlighted.
Paint lines, bands or patterns through them. On wings, building a cool blue up to pale ice blue against a warm main colour adds contrast. They can stand for veins, energy or natural markings.
On shells and carapace, paint thin parallel striations or blended colour markings near the edges. On big scaly creatures, pick out one band, such as the belly, in a different colour.
On armour or vehicles, small chips and marks in the highlight colour break the surface up.

A gentle colour shift across the area, such as warmer at one end and cooler at the other, also helps. Mix in a related hue, such as a dusty yellow into a green, instead of only going lighter and darker.
Texture works too. Stipple or dab a little highlight colour with a torn sponge, following the light rather than at random, then tie it together with very thin glazes over the whole area.
On a squad in one colour, paint one panel per model, such as a shoulder plate, in a contrasting colour like black, and vary which panel it is.
If the result is too strong, knock it back with thin glazes of the base colour.

guides.title: Combining airbrush and brush work
guides.summary: Use the airbrush for smooth gradients and soft blends over brushed layers, then do edges and texture by hand.
body: Each tool does a different job. The airbrush is good at smooth gradients, soft transitions and filters. The brush is better for placing light and shadow, edge highlights, texture and fine detail.
Spraying alone from the start often gives a soft, obviously sprayed look with the light in the wrong places. Sketching light and shadow by brush first keeps control.
To smooth brushed work, thin the same colours, and half mixes between them, until they are almost like water. Use a fine needle and low pressure, around 15 to 20 psi, so you can work small areas.
Spray close and light in many short passes along the edges where one layer meets the next. The aim is to soften and reinforce the brushwork, not to cover it.
Paint brushed highlights slightly larger and brighter than you want, because the mist of mid tone over their edges knocks them back. If you overdo it, repaint the highlight and try again.
It also works the other way round. On vehicles, spray the base coats for a quick, even surface, then build the panel highlights by brush with many thin glazes, each pulled a little short of the last.
A thin wash or filter sprayed over the whole area ties it together, though it shifts the colour a little.
Do the airbrush stages before the fine brush work where you can, so any overspray gets painted over. Then finish edges, textures and details by hand.

guides.title: Brush control
guides.summary: Grip, angle, light pressure, bracing and a small paint load on a good point matter as much as a steady hand.
body: Brace both hands: the hand holding the model rests on the desk, and the painting hand rests against the other hand. Hold the brush like a pen, firm but relaxed, and breathe out slowly through the finest strokes.

Hold the brush nearer the bristles for precision, further back for longer movements. Turn the model so each stroke runs the way your hand pulls best, and pull with a small finger movement rather than the wrist. Turning the model upside down often makes curved lines easier.
Use a larger brush with a sharp point, around a size 2 to 4, not a tiny one. It holds more paint so the tip stays wet. Go up a size if the room is hot, dry or has a fan running.

Load the belly so the tip does not run dry halfway along a line, then draw the excess off the tip on kitchen paper; a blob on the tip floods off the edge. Paint that is too thick drags and ridges, too thin floods. Add a touch of water or flow improver if it drags.

Use the lightest touch for fine lines. Hover just above the surface and come down until the tip barely touches; a ragged edge means you pressed too hard. For a dot, press very slightly more each time until it is the right size.
Use different parts of the brush. Hold it nearly flat and use the belly or side for base coats and layers, and the side near the tip for fine lines. Jabbing with the very point wears it out.
Plan each stroke: where the tip lands, which way it travels and how it lifts off. Then do the line in one stroke. Going over a line a second time is usually what thickens it.

Practise on a spare base, a button or a small stone: even lines, dots of one size, simple patterns. Paint slowly against a short timer and restart it after a slip. Checking each stroke against what you planned is how control improves; speed follows.

guides.title: Bullet strikes and impacts
guides.summary: Paint a short streak ending in a larger chip, with layered colours at the centre to show deeper damage.
body: Paint a short dark brown streak for the path of the shot, ending in a larger, roughly round brown chip where it struck.
Dot the armour's highlight colour along the lower edge of the chip and streak, so it reads as a dent catching light.
Dot a mid grey into the middle of the brown chip, then a small lighter grey at the very centre where the impact went deepest.
The layers read as paint, then primer, then bare metal. Keep strikes few and place them where shots would land, such as the front.

guides.title: Painting faces on busts
guides.summary: At bust scale a face needs real anatomy, colour zones, skin texture and fully painted eyes.
body: A bust face is big enough to show every mistake and every subtle change. Keep reference photos of real faces lit from one direction beside you.
Set the light first. Spray or paint a light to dark sketch from above, so the brow, nose, cheekbones and chin stand out and the eye sockets sit in shadow.
Use colour zones. The forehead leans slightly yellow, the cheeks, nose and ears warmer and redder, and the jaw cooler and greyer, most of all on stubbled faces. Glaze each zone thinly.
Build the skin from many thin glazes and layers. At this size, a soft wet blend helps, and fine stippling in a slightly darker tone reads as pores.
Paint the eyes in full: an off-white that greys towards the corners, an iris with a dark rim and lighter flecks, the pupil, one reflection dot and a thin wet line on the lower lid.
Add the details smaller scales skip: a dark line between the lips, faint veins, freckles, stubble glazed in a blue grey, #7d8590, and pink tear ducts.
Step back often, and check from across the room or in a phone photo. Realism comes from value and soft changes far more than from tiny detail.

guides.title: Working on busts and large-scale models
guides.summary: Big models show everything, so prep carefully, plan one light, blend smoothly and use more colour steps.
body: Prep matters more at this size. Clean every seam and mould line, fill gaps with putty and sand smooth. A scratch you would never see on a small model is plain on a bust.
Plan the light from one main source, usually high and in front. A zenithal spray or a brushed value sketch gives the map for the whole piece.
Work big areas with long, smooth fades. An airbrush, wet blending or many thin glazes all do it. Thin paint dries quickly, so work one small section at a time.
Add texture on purpose. Large surfaces look like plastic if they are too smooth. Stipple fine texture on skin, cloth weave or worn leather.
Use more steps than at small scale, five to eight from shadow to highlight. Add colour shifts and reflected light in the shadows for realism.
Finish each area before moving on, and paint the face or focal point when your hand is steadiest.
Fix the bust to a plinth or a temporary holder early, so you never hold the painted surface.

guides.title: Painting camouflage
guides.summary: Pick three or four tones from one colour family, block in bold shapes over a shaded base and keep the light consistent.
body: Choose colours to match the bases and setting: sands and warm browns for desert, warm greys for urban, greens and browns for woodland. Pick three or four tones from one family and make each clearly darker than the last, or two will read as one.

Decide where it goes. Camo over a whole figure hides its shape, so on troops keep it to one part, such as the helmet, smock or trousers. Vehicles and cloaks can take more. On cloaks, pattern the outer face only.

Look at references. Camo is soft blobs, hard-edged blotches or sharp angular splinters. Keep shapes bold, ragged and varied in size; avoid circles, dots and anything that repeats. At small scale or on busy curved parts, use fewer tones and simpler shapes.
Shade and highlight the base colour first, so the camo already sits in light and shadow and you do not have to shade every patch.

By brush, thin each colour a little so it leaves no brush marks. Outline each patch with the tip, then fill it, in two coats. On a vehicle, sit the turret on the hull and paint across the join, carry patches over tracks and wheels, and vary the layout from one vehicle to the next.

Add the lighter tones the same way, letting some meet, and leave the base colour as gaps. Sharpen wobbly edges by painting the base back in. A very thin dark outline crisps patches at small scale. For soft camo, stipple the joins or spray very thin paint in ragged shapes.

For hard edges on vehicles, spray the first colour, cover what should stay that colour with reusable putty, tape strips or brushed liquid mask, spray the next, mask again, then peel gently. Crisp edges also show chipping better than soft camo.

Highlight all the camo as one area with one colour, or, with masked camo, shade and highlight each colour in the same places. Seal with satin varnish before washes and weathering; a thin all-over wash also unifies the pattern.

guides.title: Painting cast shadows
guides.summary: Paint the shadow one part throws onto another, mapped with a one-direction airbrush spray or copied from a lit photo.
body: A cast shadow is the dark shape one part throws onto another, such as an arm across a chest or a beard over the body. It is an advanced effect that makes the light feel real.

To map it, prime black and spray thin white from one fixed direction only. Get closer near overhanging parts so the spray does not creep under them; the shadow they cast stays black. Two or three passes are enough.
Without an airbrush, set a lamp where you want the light, take a photo, and use the shadow in the photo as your guide.
Base coat with a thinned mid colour, stroking away from the shadow so you do not erase its edge.
Fill the shadow shape with a dark version of the local colour, checking the map or photo often, and keep small lit details such as fingernails sharp.
Keep the edge slightly soft: a couple of strokes of the next colour stop it looking cut out. Leave a small gap between the highlights and the shadow so there is a short transition.

guides.title: Changing a detail with paint
guides.summary: Move a shallow edge, eye or shape slightly by painting in new shadows and highlights where you want it.
body: On fine sculpts with shallow detail, you can fake a detail in a slightly different place with paint alone.
Paint a thin dark line where you want the new edge, eye line or fold to be.
Highlight just above or beside it so the eye reads it as a raised rim or a real shape.
Paint over the original detail with the surrounding colour so it fades away.
It is risky. Try it only where the sculpted detail is very shallow, and check the model at arm's length before committing.

guides.title: Wooden chests and crates
guides.summary: Over brush brown wood, mix up the metal fittings, wash it all and finish with one dusty dry brush.
body: Over brush the wood a mid brown, around #6b4a30, then dry brush the edges with a lighter brown.
For paler wood, start from a warm pale tan, around #d2a27c, wash a dark brown into the grain and joints, dry brush a light tan and pick out only the sharpest corners with a fine brush.
Vary the metal on bands and fittings between dark iron, silver and gold so a group of chests looks varied.
Wash everything with a brown wash, thinning it on the model where it pools.
Dry brush a dusty beige lightly over everything. It is a fast highlight for both wood and metal.
Tint a few chests with a thin green or a different brown so they stand apart.
For any parchment on top, paint short streaks of a light bone and add a few fine marks in thinned black.

guides.title: Making a paint job look clean and crisp
guides.summary: Neat strokes, dark lines between parts, shaded recesses and thin edge highlights make every part of a model read clearly.
body: Two things make a model look crisp: clean paint, with no stray strokes or colour spilling onto the next area, and clear definition, where each part is separated by even lines and sharp highlights. Without them a model looks blurry.
Base coat each area fully opaque, in as many thin coats as it takes to remove any patchiness. A light undercoat helps coverage.
Thin paint to roughly half paint, half water for most steps. It flows where you put it and keeps detail sharp. If it runs off the tip, it is too thin.
Keep a dark line between parts. Paint a very dark colour into the recesses, or leave a little of a dark undercoat showing as you layer. The deepest gaps between plates can stay black.

Edge highlight every sharp edge, even lightly, and put a thin light edge wherever two areas meet, such as a cloak against a shirt, so they do not merge. Keep the final, brightest highlight to the corners and peaks that define the shape.
Keep large surfaces smooth. Patchy blends distract, though deliberate texture is fine.
Do not pick out every tiny sculpted element. A busy motif on a focal area can read better painted as one tone, and leaving off an optional part such as a cape can keep the model cleaner.
At the end, tidy spills with the neighbouring colour and trim highlights that came out thick. Plain dark areas such as trousers need little detail and make the bright parts stand out.

guides.title: Colour modulation on vehicles
guides.summary: Light each vehicle panel on its own, dark at one end and light at the other, so big flat panels look lit at arm's length.
body: A vehicle in one flat colour looks dull at small scale. Modulation treats every panel as its own surface, lighter at the top or one end and darker at the other, and exaggerates that contrast on purpose.

Plan the panels first: front plate, top, sides, rear, hatches and engine covers. Prime grey or black, then spray the whole vehicle in a shadow mix, the main colour darkened with a dark brown or black.

Spray the main colour on the upper part of each panel, largest panels first. Tilt the model so the spray only catches the edge you want lighter, or mask the neighbours with tape, paper or putty. This first highlight sets the map for the rest, so take care over it.

Mix the main colour with a pale bone, pale yellow or white and spray it over a smaller area inside the last one. Build three to five tones this way, with every earlier tone still showing. On flat tops, push the light towards the front or back.
Put the brightest part of one panel next to the darkest part of its neighbour. Lighting big plates at the top and small hatches at the bottom makes each panel stand out more.
Brush the lightest mix onto rivets, hatches, handles and top edges with a fine brush.
It will look too stark at this stage. Filters and weathering pull it back. On camouflage, light every colour in the same places, and varnish before masking for a second colour or using enamels.

Without an airbrush, build the same tones with careful dry brushing, or dot a dark brown oil where you want shadow and a light yellowish brown oil where you want light, then blend with a brush barely damp with white spirit.

guides.title: Coloured undercoats and undershading
guides.summary: Use a coloured undercoat or one shadow colour under everything to set the mood and tie the model together.
body: Black and white suits cool colours but can flatten warm ones like red and yellow. A coloured undercoat gives every later colour a shared shadow.

Prime, then spray or brush one dark colour over the whole model, such as a navy or a deep red. Use warm darks such as a red brown under warm colours and gold, and cool darks such as a deep blue under blues and steel.

Add a lighter colour from above to set the light. Some pairings: dark purple then ochre for opposite colours; dark green then light green for a grimy mood; deep red then warm flesh for warmth; very dark blue then pale blue for cold.
Build each area up from that dark, leaving it showing in the deepest recesses. The shadows then have depth and colour instead of flat black.

No airbrush? Over black primer, brush one rich colour over the lower half and another over the upper half, blending roughly at the middle. Use strong, saturated colours or slightly thinned inks; pale or greyish ones do little.

With one-coat contrast-style paints, a dark coloured undercoat followed by a grey and off white dry brush gives coloured shadows for free, and missed spots show far less than over black. Very matt primers soak up thin paint, so avoid them here.
It works under dark colours too. Paint black or dark armour as normal over it and the hint of colour in the recesses shows the shape.
For skin, a green undershade under pinks gives rich, natural browns in the shadows, as red and green are near opposites.

guides.title: Loose colourful underpainting
guides.summary: Sketch or smear varied colours under the final layers for mood and variety, then unify them with glazes.
body: Lay down bright, varied colours first as an underpainting. They set the mood of the shadows; they are not the final colours.
Set strong pure colours out on the palette before you start so you never stop to open a pot.
Base coat a rich dark colour. Smear and dab the colours on loosely with a brush, fingertip or airbrush, placing lighter ones where light lands. Squint to see the big shapes.
Skip a white zenithal if using fingers, as fingers drag white into the recesses.
Paint the real mid tone very thin first, stroking from shadow towards light, so the underpainting shows in the darks. Then add a more opaque coat only where full colour should show.

A quick version: make a thin mix of the base colour, about half water, for the shadows and a thicker mix for where light falls. Leave the deepest recesses, and a thin line where materials meet, unpainted.
Unify loose areas with a glaze of one-coat paint thinned with three or four parts medium.
Pick out highlights with a brush, choosing the light colour that matches what shows through. Spend most highlights on the face and key details; troops can stop before this.

guides.title: Combining techniques
guides.summary: Pick techniques area by area for the result you want: fast methods for the bulk, careful ones where it shows.
body: Start by asking what effect each area needs and what the brush has to do to get it, rather than sticking to one method for the whole model.

Work broad first, then refine. Dry brush or wash the bulk of the model quickly, since those methods cover a lot but will not tidy small details. On a large model, a careful dry brush that follows the big forms can do most of the work.
Add black lining or a targeted wash where parts need more separation.
Edge highlight or layer by hand where it matters most, such as the head, arms, chest, weapon and upper edges. The back and feet can often stay as dry brushed.
Glaze over rough patches, or add bright or fluorescent tints for colour variation and light effects.

Vary the finish. If every surface is wet blended or airbrushed the model looks samey and soft. Mix smooth areas with texture from lines, dots and stippling, or brush blend a few features on an airbrushed model.
A thin filter sprayed or glazed over everything at the end can tint the whole model at once, such as a cool blue for moonlight.
If no named technique fits, try something. Dabbing opaque paint for a pattern or smudging a glaze with a finger are both fair.

guides.title: Comic book and cel-shaded style
guides.summary: Flat colour blocks, hard steps between light and shadow and bold dark outlines make a model look drawn.
body: The aim is a model that looks drawn rather than sculpted. Think in simple shapes, flat colour, a few hard-edged tones and bold outlines, not smooth gradients.
Paint each part in one flat, solid colour first. Keeping it flat means any later slip with the outlines can simply be painted over.
Give each colour only two or three tones, a shadow, a mid tone and a light, with sharp edges between them and no blending. Place the lights and darks deliberately for strong contrast.

Outline the main shapes with dark lines, heavier around faces, weapon edges and armour edges. Black acrylic ink flows better than black paint for outlines and shadows; shake it well, as thick ink can crack as it dries.
Ink in two passes: first by eye, then again under magnification for the fine lines. Turn the model upside down at the end and catch any edges you missed.
Add crisp edge highlights in a lighter tone. Small groups of three or four parallel diagonal lines on flat panels or glass read strongly as comic shine.
Keep everything neat, as the style depends on clean, confident shapes. A stray line does not always need hiding; it can often be worked into a shadow.

guides.title: Matching bases across a collection
guides.summary: Use the same basing materials and colours on every model, and carry the ground onto their feet to tie them in.
body: Bases set the scene. Every base in a collection should look like the same ground, even if the models are painted months apart.
Write down the materials and colours you use: texture, rocks, rubble, tufts and rim colour. Use the same ones each time.

If the collection mixes pale, dark and coloured models, choose a neutral mid tone for the ground, such as a mid grey with a pale dry brush. Dark models stand out on light ground and light models on dark, so a middle value suits both.
Same materials does not mean identical bases. Base a batch in one go, but cluster rocks unevenly, break some smaller, leave rocks or tufts off a few and vary how dusty each one is.

Tie each model to its base. Snow on feet and cloak hems, or dust and mud on lower legs, makes them look like they stand there. Carry a hint of the ground colour onto the lower parts, such as a cool blue from snow.
Paint the rim the same colour on every base. It is the simplest way to make a collection read as one.

Detailed bases take a long time across a big force. Save them for key models and keep the rest simpler. A large model can have a bigger feature, such as a slab of rubble it climbs over, as long as the ground and colours match the rest.

guides.title: Contrast first, smoothness later
guides.summary: Set strong lights and darks first with bold strokes, then smooth the transitions only as much as you need.
body: The difference between light and dark areas does more for a model than how smooth the joins are. Strong contrast with rough blends beats smooth blends with weak contrast, and strong values even trick the eye into reading a surface as smooth.
Instead of creeping up through many close layers, paint the base, then jump straight to a clearly lighter highlight on the brightest areas.
Use opaque paint and confident strokes to define each shape. Stark steps are fine at this stage.
Then mix a midtone between the two and paint it only over the join. Add another if needed. Covering midtones do most of the smoothing, so you need far less glazing.

Push the most important points, such as the face, nearly to white. Add a little soft bounce light near the bottom of shapes rather than going to pure black. Contrast can come from hue too, such as a cool tint on a weapon next to warm skin.

Crisp edge highlights pull the eye and make a blocky blend underneath hard to spot. Tidy the areas around a blend before judging it; mess nearby makes it look worse. Stippling the mixed colour along a hard join is a cheap fix.
On small parts there is no room for many layers anyway: a base, a sharp highlight and one transition is enough.
For tabletop work you can stop before smoothing at all. Slightly thick, quick layers with clear values look good and save hours.

guides.title: One-coat paints over a coloured base
guides.summary: Put a one-coat paint over a pale or matching base colour instead of white for a richer, smoother result.
body: One-coat contrast-style paints work over almost any light colour, and the colour underneath changes the result. Over black they barely show, especially yellows and light greens.
Base coat a pale or mid version of the same colour. The closer the base is to the one-coat colour, the smoother it looks, and the top coat only has to add depth in the recesses.
Unthinned one-coat paint over a pale tinted base comes out vivid, almost luminous.
Base coat a gradient, such as pale yellow shifting to peach, and one colour over it gives a blend for free.
On large flat areas these paints often go blotchy over primer. Base those in a normal paint of a similar colour first and the one-coat paint goes on far more evenly. Do not let it flood or pool.

A drop of water lets it run into the recesses and leaves more of the base showing on flats. A satin base keeps it workable; a matte base soaks it up and dries faster. If it comes out too dark, mix in a normal paint of the same colour.

Instead of a white dry brush, try a pale tinted one, such as a pale lilac (#c8b4dc), then a pale yellow (#f0e6a0) on the top edges only. The colour on top stays rich. Paint any spill back with white before a light tint goes over it.
A thinned one-coat paint over a solid one of the same colour adds depth. A matt varnish at the end evens out the patchy sheen these paints can leave.

guides.title: Order of work with one-coat paints
guides.summary: Over a pale primer, paint the light, weak one-coat colours first and the strong dark ones last.
body: Prime off-white or pale bone so the colours stay bright.
Paint the pale, weak colours first, such as flesh, joints and pale weapons, then small bits like tongues.
Clean up any slips onto pale areas with a pot of paint in the primer colour. A see-through paint cannot cover a mistake.
For an all-over tint, mix a weak colour with about one and a half parts clear medium and paint it over everything.
Then do the strong, dark colours, such as dark shells and black claws, with a small brush. They cover slips from the earlier colours. A second coat fixes patchiness.
Finish small details like eyes and teeth with normal opaque paint.

guides.title: Corroded, pitted metal
guides.summary: Dull the metal with washes, dab on warm rust and cool green patches, then add a broken bright edge.
body: For real pitting, add texture before you paint. Dab a crackle or fine texture paste onto the areas that should be corroded, and wipe it off the raised parts so it stays in sheltered spots. A dark brown mixed into the paste works too.
Base coat a mid steel in two coats.
Wash it all with a dark brown-black wash, then a brown wash once dry. Old metal is not shiny, and this dulls the sheen while letting some metal show.

Add colour with ordinary paint thinned to a wash, about four parts water to one of paint, rather than ready-made washes. It gives stronger colour and a flat finish. Push rust orange around rivets and into corners on steel, and a turquoise on copper and brass.
Dab the colour on with the brush tip instead of stroking it. Dabbing leaves mottled patches and small tide marks, which is what pitting looks like.
Put warm rust browns and oranges in some patches and cool greens in others, with plain metal between. Build each in a few layers, each smaller than the last, so some spots are stronger than others.

On big terrain pieces such as doors and panels, a sprayed silver works as the base. Build the rust with many thin coats of a rust brown wash in chosen recesses, then brush rust-coloured pigment where corrosion would gather.

Where it still looks flat, dab a little more dark wash here and there. Finish with a few broken bright metal touches on the sharpest edges, as small dots or a rough, almost dry brushed line rather than a clean edge.

guides.title: Creature and beast eyes
guides.summary: Paint monster and animal eyes bright and glossy: a coloured eye shaded to the rim, or white under a clear gloss colour.
body: For a yellow or amber eye, block it in with a strong yellow, around #f2c230, over a light undercoat so it covers easily. Leave a thin dark rim showing.
Shade around the edge with a little orange, and blend up to white towards the middle so it seems lit from within. A thin red or chestnut wash also settles round the rim and ties the eye to the skin.
Add a black slit or round pupil if it suits, and a tiny white dot in one corner for a wet look. A slit is one thin, straight vertical line.

For small beady eyes, paint them pure white, then two coats of a clear glossy colour such as red, green or blue. The white underneath makes them glow against dark skin. For quick red ones, fill with a deep red, add a brighter red leaving a dark rim, then one tiny pinkish dot.

For a dark, gem-like eye, fill it with black, paint a curve of turquoise along the lower edge, a smaller lighter blue patch at the very bottom, and a tiny pale grey dot high on the opposite side as the reflection.
Black eyes look wet and glassy with a dab of gloss varnish over flat pure black. The same works on fang tips.

On a big monster a clean bright eye matters more than detail. A deep orange with one ivory dot, or a bright red fill for a fierce glare, reads well. Large eyes make or break the model, so consider painting them early.
Keep the surrounding skin darker so the eye reads, and gloss varnish the eyes if the rest of the model is matte. Tidy any slips by running a dark wash into the recess around the eye.

guides.title: Clean armour by recess shade and edges
guides.summary: Base each panel a mid tone, shade only the recesses, then add two or three fine edge highlights for crisp armour.
body: Base coat each armour panel in a mid version of its colour, two thin coats.
Run one or two darker recess shades into the creases and panel joins, keeping them off the flat surfaces.
Tidy any spill with the base colour.
Add two or three edge highlights, each brighter and finer than the last, on the sharpest edges and corners. The last one is only on the very top points.

For quicker models, an all-over wash can stand in for the hand shading: base, wash, then edge highlight only the sharpest edges. A heavily thinned brown dropped into the recesses afterwards adds grime.
On a many-coloured scheme, finish one colour fully before starting the next. Paint trim last, once the panels are done.

guides.title: See-through cube and floating eye monsters
guides.summary: Tint clear cubes thinly and show what they swallowed; make a floating eye monster's big eye the brightest, glossiest point.
body: See-through cube in clear plastic or resin: wash it in warm soapy water, then tint it with a thinned glossy ink in a slime green, #7fbf4a, or a blue green, #4fa79a. Build the tint up in thin coats. Thick coats go cloudy.
Paint anything trapped inside before tinting: bones, a helmet, a few coins. Keep their colours muted so they read as swallowed. Add extra tint low down and in the corners, where the jelly is deepest.

Opaque cube: fake the clear look. Base a mid green, #5c9a45, darken the lower half and the centre, lighten the top edges toward a pale lime, #c8e38a, and paint faint outlines of trapped objects in a faded tone. Finish with gloss varnish.
Add drips and a small puddle on the base with thick gloss varnish or clear gel tinted the same colour. A few tiny pale dots along the top edges sell the wet shine.

Floating eye monster: the big eye is the focal point. Paint the white a pale yellow white, #ede3c4, shaded pink near the lids, then a strong iris such as a hot orange, #e0731f, or an acid green, #8cc63f, with a black pupil. Gloss only the eye.

Body: pick a fleshy tone that contrasts with the eye, such as a purple brown, #6b3f52, or a sickly olive, #7f7a45. Shade the underside heavily, since light comes from above, and add veins or blotches with thin glazes.
Paint the small stalk eyes as a set: the same iris colour, but smaller and duller, so the big eye still leads. Darken deep inside the mouth and pick out teeth in a dull bone, #cfc2a0.
