Mount floating models on a clear rod or a rock pillar, and keep the base calm and muted so the monster stays the star.

guides.title: Designing your own symbols
guides.summary: Make a custom badge by keeping a familiar icon shape and swapping in one new element, kept bold and simple.
body: Look at existing icons and heraldry for shapes people already recognise, such as jaws, wings, skulls, stars or crossed blades.
Keep one familiar element and replace the main object with something that fits your own idea, or combine shapes from two designs, such as a round emblem with an arrow taken from another.
Keep it bold and simple, with few lines. Fine detail is lost on a small shoulder plate or banner, and you may paint it dozens of times, so it must be easy to repeat.

Sketch several versions and reject any that are fiddly, lack clear shapes to colour, or look silly. Redraw the best one smaller and smaller until it is the real size of the shield or plate, and check it still reads.
Paint it with a light outline before filling it in. Straighten wobbly edges afterwards by cutting back in with the base colour.

Another way is to build it from spare transfers. Cut shapes such as blades or skulls from other sheets and place them one at a time. Keep any brush that has touched solvent away from them, as it can dissolve them.

guides.title: Damp drybrushing
guides.summary: Keep a little moisture in the drybrush and build several light passes for smooth, less chalky gradients.
body: With a completely dry brush, only dusty pigment reaches the model, which is where the chalky look comes from.

Put one drop of water on a sponge and work it in with a finger. Touch the brush to it before loading and again after. Touched to the back of your hand the brush should feel faintly cool, not cold and wet. In hot, dry weather add a second drop.
Never dunk a drybrush in the water pot. Soaking it lets pigment run up to the collar and floods paint into the recesses.
Work the paint into the bristles on a hard, smooth surface such as laminated card, not paper towel, which soaks the moisture out.

Test on your hand, then brush lightly where light would fall. Each pass is faint, so build up several, letting each dry first. When paint stops leaving the brush, go back for moisture, not more paint.
Rinse and dry the brush, then go again with a paler colour over less of the area, catching only edges and corners at the end.
It suits cloaks, skin, cloth, bone and rounded armour. Get used to normal drybrushing first.
A larger brush gives a smoother result than a small floppy one, and a soft round makeup-style brush is smoother still than a stiff flat one.

guides.title: Damp patches and drips on models
guides.summary: Show wet on a model with darker, glossier patches, pale-edged water stains and drops of gloss.
body: Water makes surfaces darker and shinier. A damp patch is the same colour one or two steps darker, with satin or gloss varnish over it.
Wet from the ground up: hems, boots and lower legs are darkest at the bottom and fade upwards. Glaze a thin dark brown, #3b2e22, then gloss it.
Dried water leaves a stain. Paint a ragged pale line, a dusty off-white, #c9c3b4, along the top edge of a darker patch as a tide mark.
For drips, run thin streaks down from edges, rivets and seams. Use a darker, cooler tint of the surface colour and soften the top with a damp brush.
Add drops with gloss varnish or clear resin dotted on the lowest points, such as under a chin, a hem or a plate edge. Build them up slowly so they do not run.
For rain, gloss the top surfaces lightly and leave the undersides matt. Light catches wet, glossy surfaces first.
Keep it believable. Water gathers at low points and on flat tops, and it runs straight down.

guides.title: Speed painting with a dip
guides.summary: Base coat a step lighter, dunk the model in a tinted varnish dip, scoop out pools, then matte varnish it.
body: A dip is a coloured varnish that the whole model is plunged into. It shades everything in one go, and strongly. It works best on models with plenty of recesses.

Prime light, such as bone or white. Base coat every area neatly, a step lighter than you want it to end up, including small details. Use an off-black rather than pure black so the dip still shades it.

Pick the tone to suit the models: light for pale, deeply textured ones, medium as the safe choice, dark for a heavy, inked look. Dark brown suits warm, earthy schemes and black suits cold, metal-heavy ones. Use one tone across a whole army.

Work outside or with good airflow, as the fumes are strong. Cover the desk and wear gloves. Stir the tin rather than shaking it, hold the model by its base in old pliers and swirl it for 10 to 20 seconds. For a model too big for the tin, brush the dip on generously.

Flick or tap it firmly over kitchen towel or against the tin edge to throw off the excess, then stand it on a non-absorbent surface for 5 to 10 minutes. Too much left on fills detail and pools at the bottom.

Check hollows such as collars and under arms for puddles and lift them out with an old brush or a dab of make-up sponge before they set. Never wipe dip with tissue; the fibres stick for good. Paint the base afterwards, as dip runs down onto it.

Leave it a full day somewhere still and dust free. It dries very glossy, so finish with matte varnish in dry air, as damp air can frost it; test a spray first. Repaint a few raised areas in the base colours to bring highlights back.
Clean brushes and spills with odourless mineral spirit, not water. The downsides are the drying time, shading you cannot control and fine detail that can fill in.

guides.title: Directional edge highlights
guides.summary: Highlight the edges facing the light brightest, keep downward edges dim, and save the strongest lines for the focal point.
body: The same bright line on every edge looks graphic but not believable. Pick one light direction, usually above and slightly in front, and keep every highlight consistent with it. Lining every edge is still a valid stylised choice if you do it on purpose.
Edges that face up or towards you get the strongest highlight: head, shoulders, the tops of arms, hands, knees and toes.
Edges facing down, underneath or between the legs get a softer, darker highlight or none at all. As a beginner, highlighting about a third of the edges is a good start.
On rounded edges, put the brightest point nearest the light and let it fade along the curve. Add an extra bright dot on the corners that face the light.

Vary the width as well as the brightness: a slightly broader line on upper edges and a hairline where the plate turns into shadow. For a softer look, paint a wider band on the flat beside the edge first, then the fine line on the edge itself.

Edges beside an already bright surface gain little and can be skipped. Edges beside dark areas show the most. On narrow trim where two edges sit close, lining both looks like neon tubing; shade one side instead.
Soft or rounded edges may not need a line at all; a dark line beneath can define them instead. A slightly warmer or cooler light tone often looks more natural than adding white.
Keep most lines a little muted and push the brightest ones around the face or focal point to draw the eye there. Broken dashes instead of full lines suggest wear.

guides.title: Dirty, dusty cloth hems
guides.summary: Build mud, dust and damp stains up from the hem in thin layers so robes and cloaks look worn and used.
body: Look at photos of real long cloaks or costumes first. Grime is heaviest at the bottom and fades upwards, with lower points catching most.

Glaze a thin khaki-brown, around #6e5a3c, up from the hem several times, strongest at the bottom and fading higher. A touch of green or grey looks more natural than plain brown. Pull each stroke down to the hem with little paint on the brush, and let each pass dry.

Think in two bands: a soft damp stain soaking higher up, and darker real dirt lower down. Tide marks are fine here; real fabric gets them. Vary the strength from patch to patch so it never forms a regular pattern.
For a very dirty hem, push thinned black or dark brown down so it gathers at the edge. A dragging hem can go almost black.
For a quick dusty hem, dry brush or stipple a sandy brown that matches the base very lightly around the hem and boots, fading a little way up. Build it slowly so it reads as dust, not a stripe.
Dried dust is lighter, so finish with a thin pale sand only at the very bottom. A quick option: dab pale dots near the hem and smudge them with a fingertip.

For splashed mud, flick thinned dark brown at the hem so most spots land low and fewer reach higher. Oil paint also works: over matt varnish, dab dark brown oil at the hem and fade its top edge with thinner.
Add a few small light nicks with a dark dot beside some, mostly near the hem. Keep them small and few; big scratches look out of scale.

guides.title: Blending with a drop of thin paint
guides.summary: Thin the lighter colour right down, wick most off the brush and drag a small drop across the join until it disappears.
body: Paint the lighter layer where light falls, at a consistency that covers in one to three coats. Each later layer covers less area.
Thin the same paint to a watery mix, roughly six parts water to four of paint. Erring thin only means more passes; erring thick gives coverage, not a blend.
Wick the excess onto a damp tissue so only a small drop is left in the brush. A loaded brush floods the area.
Start the stroke on the darker layer and pull towards the lighter one. Most pigment is left where the brush stops, so end the stroke right on the join.
Everything the brush crosses gets tinted a little, so start the stroke where a faint tint does no harm.
Let it dry fully and repeat a few times until the edge vanishes, then lay the next layer. Small steps in brightness blend far more easily than one big jump.

guides.title: Fast drybrushed shells and carapace
guides.summary: Drybrush a very dark mix as base and shade in one, then three drybrushes, each lighter and lighter in touch.
body: Mix the main shell colour about half and half with black for a very dark base. It replaces both a base coat and a wash.
Put it on with a drybrush pressed straight down onto each plate, so it reaches round the sides while the undersides stay black.
Work a mid tone on quite heavily in small circles so every flat area picks it up.
Dust a lighter tone lightly with a large drybrush to pick out the edges.
Flick a very pale tone only onto points, spines and blades so they look sharp. A gloss varnish on the shell afterwards gives an insect-like sheen.

For a black or very dark shell, keep the steps subtle. Mix a little colour into black, wipe almost all of it off and catch only the edges, then repeat with the pure colour. Clean the brush first, as stray pale flecks show badly on dark plates.
If the drybrushing looks dusty, a thin black wash over the shell softens it and deepens the gaps. Then tidy the edges and dot the sharpest points again with a fine brush.
Do the drybrushing before any markings or stripes, as it would spoil them. Striations can then be hatched in thin pale lines from each plate edge inwards and glazed over.

guides.title: Drybrushing
guides.summary: Wipe almost all the paint off a soft, round brush and skim it over raised detail so only edges and texture pick up colour.
body: Use a dedicated brush, never a good one. Soft round drybrushes or cheap synthetic makeup brushes give a smoother, less grainy finish than small stiff flats. Keep a few sizes. A stiffer flat can be aimed more exactly where skin sits next to armour.
Let the coat underneath dry fully. Choose a colour one step lighter than that area and load just the tip.

Wipe it on card or a towel that does not soak up much, until almost nothing comes off. Test on the back of your hand; it should feel slightly cool and barely mark. A trace of moisture stops the chalky look. If it leaves a solid stripe or streaks, wipe more off.
Skim lightly over the model so only raised edges and texture catch. Brush across the recesses rather than along them, usually downwards from the light. Circles suit rough areas like bases.
Light pressure gives soft highlights; heavier pressure gives a scratchy look that suits rock and vehicles. Support fragile parts with a finger while you work.

Build up over two or three passes. The first can carry a little more paint; for each paler pass wipe off more, use a softer touch and cover a smaller area. If it ends up too bright, a wash tones it down and the raised detail still reads.

It suits big models with broad raised surfaces, fur, chainmail, rock, terrain and texture, and highlights drybrushed first show through one-coat contrast-style paints. On smooth, sharp armour plates it looks dusty and patchy, and on small busy models it is hard to control, so do it early.

Drybrush after any darkening wash, since the wash dulls highlights. A light grey drybrush over a dark primer also shows shallow detail you might miss, and a light neutral flicked over a many-coloured model ties the colours together with a dusty look.

guides.title: Drybrushing cloth
guides.summary: Drybrush a deeply folded cloak or robe with a big, slightly damp soft brush in light passes for fast, smooth highlights.
body: Busy, heavily folded cloth is slow to layer by hand but drybrushes well. Do it early, before other details, as it is messy.
Use a medium or large soft round brush, even on a small cloak. A small brush leaves streaks.
Keep the bristles faintly damp by touching a damp sponge now and then. Wipe off on coated card, not tissue, and twist the brush as you wipe so no lumps hide on one side.
Test on your thumb. If you see streaks, take more paint off.
The first pass matters most. It gives the smooth base coat a dry, slightly rough layer for later passes to grip.
Stipple onto the raised folds, then flick along sharp creases. Work up two or three colours, each a touch lighter, without fully cleaning the brush so they blend.

Let the cloth drybrush catch straps, pouches and boots too. It acts as a pre-highlight under a thin dark paint later, and a very light pass of the cloth colour over black gear looks like faded canvas.

Finish the very top edges with a soft, pale colour, or switch to a normal brush and highlight them by hand. A thinned neutral or shade-coloured wash over the whole cloth afterwards ties the passes together.

guides.title: Drybrushing edges instead of lining
guides.summary: A nearly empty drybrush catches only sharp edges, giving fast, worn-looking edge highlights where hand lines feel too shaky.
body: Drybrushing raised edges is much faster than painting lines by hand. The result looks used and weathered; hand-painted lines look crisp and new. Pick the look you want.
Load the highlight colour, then wipe nearly all of it away. The brush should feel cool, not wet; moisture leaves marks instead of crisp edges.
Test on the edge of the palette. If it catches only the edge, it is ready.
Stroke across the edge in one direction. Each stroke catches edges facing where it comes from. Change direction for the opposite edges.
You get two values from one paint: bright edges and a faint tint on flats.
For metal, base the part black and drybrush a metallic with almost nothing on the brush, top to bottom. Edges shine and recesses stay dark.

You can drybrush the edges again at any stage, such as after a wash or tint, to bring them back. A little leftover wash mixed into the highlight ties it in. Drybrushing dulls colour, so a thin glaze of the main colour afterwards can restore it.

Some edges the brush misses will still need a quick hand highlight. A few hand lines in the same colour on the most prominent edges, such as shoulders and the fronts of legs, sharpen the whole result.

guides.title: Drybrushing large flat areas
guides.summary: Use a big, soft drybrush in many light passes to build a gradient or glow across wide areas without an airbrush.
body: Use a large, fluffy drybrush rather than a small stiff one. The soft bristles leave a smoother, more even dusting. Soft round makeup brushes made for blush work well.
Load very little paint and wipe nearly all of it off. Keep a hint of moisture in the bristles. Taking too much paint at once is the main thing that goes wrong.
Work the light colour in from where the light or glow should be strongest, spreading outwards. On panels, go from the top down. Many light strokes, twenty or more per area, are still quick.
When the brush runs dry, touch it to the damp pad rather than taking more paint. The moisture reactivates what is already in the bristles.

Add each lighter colour mixed with a little of the one before, over a smaller area each time, and go back and forth between the dark and light colours to balance the blend. Use your other palm as a soft mask where you do not want strokes running over an edge.

On vehicles, start with the base mixed half and half with a lighter colour. The drybrush catches rivets, panel lines and edges by itself, which saves most of the edge highlighting. Any roughness can be hidden later with oil shading or a filter.
Very soft brushes can be too subtle for the last crisp highlight. Finish with a smaller firm drybrush, and pick out any edges it missed with a fine brush.
Stop when the change from dark to bright looks soft and even from normal viewing distance. On a smooth vehicle it can look close to airbrushing and also hides a patchy base coat.

guides.title: Drybrushing metal
guides.summary: Build metal up in a few drybrushed steps from a dark base to near-pure silver on the highest points.
body: Shake metallic paint very well. Base coat the metal over a dark undercoat, or brush on a darker metal first. Black underneath makes silver look its most silvery.
For the first pass, darken the metal by mixing in black rather than using a darker metallic. The recesses then stay dark and matt while raised areas shine.

Drybrush with only the tiniest amount on the bristle tips. Too much silver turns stark fast, so test first and repeat passes instead. Brush across ridges, not along them, and come at round details from all directions.

Add more pure silver and go again over a smaller area, ending with near-pure silver only on the most raised points and edges. Start each pass where you want it brightest, such as the head and top surfaces.

For quick trim, drybrush gold over all the raised areas, then run a thinned black one-coat paint over the flat panels so it fills the cracks and leaves the trim clean. Touch up dull gold with a small brush. Do not paint solid metal over drybrushed trim later, or you undo the work.

For quick silver armour, drybrush freely over everything, then paint thinned black back into the joints and soft areas. It also suits long runs of cables or mechanical limbs that would take hours to edge by hand.

On small vehicles and small-scale models, prime black, drybrush a dark gunmetal over everything, wash black, then drybrush a brighter steel on the raised parts. Paint the flat plates in their colours afterwards and leave the raised rims as metal; every pipe, bolt and trim is done at once.
For a deeper finish, flow a thin wash into the recesses only, holding the part flat. Change your rinse water afterwards so metal flakes do not get into the next colours.

guides.title: Drybrush strokes and pressure
guides.summary: Flick one way across edges for clean highlights, work circles for texture, and set pressure so it does not leave blobs.
body: Light, grazing flicks across an edge, at a right angle to it, catch only the edge and act as an edge highlight. Come at each edge from both sides; dragging along its length smears.

Heavier round strokes with more paint left in the brush cover flat panels too, leaving dark only in the recesses. Use this to restore a base colour after a wash. Gentle stippling with a firm, slightly damp brush leaves soft dots that can be smudged in small circles to blend.

Directional strokes suit armour plates, wood grain and folded cloth, where you want a neat result. Circles suit fur, rough skin, rocks and terrain, where texture faces every way. Paint leaves the brush when bristles hit a ridge, so brush across the detail you want to catch.
Vary pressure across the model: light flicks where it should stay darker, such as the back or limbs, and firmer circles where colour should build up, such as the chest or belly.

Hold the brush further back and loosely, with a relaxed wrist; a tight grip near the bristles makes you press too hard. Test every pass: press on your thumb for smears, then brush a textured spot to check it only catches edges.

A typical armour sequence: base coat, an all-over black wash, a heavy drybrush of the base colour, then a light drybrush of a paler tone. Before stepping up to a much lighter colour, buff the whole area softly with the current one so the next step blends.
Next to finished areas, roll an old medium round brush in paint and wipe it sideways so the tip stays blunt. Push it along the texture at an angle, away from the neighbour.
Use normal paint, not washes or one-coat paints. Let the layer underneath dry fully, and clean and dry the brush between colours, or you get streaks.

guides.title: Dust and dirt on legs and feet
guides.summary: Stipple or glaze the base colours onto feet and lower legs so the model looks like it walked across its ground.
body: Finish the base first, then use the same colours again so model and ground match. Wet ground calls for darker damp dirt, dry ground for pale dust. Boots that will end up caked do not need careful highlights first, and if the model is glued on later, add the mud before gluing.
For dry dust, take a small drybrush with almost no paint and stipple the darker base colour at the feet, fading it out around mid-shin.
Lightly drybrush the paler base colour over the same area to soften it. When you shade and drybrush the base itself, catch the feet a little too. Keep dust off bare skin, where it only looks dull.

For damp dirt, thin a mid khaki-brown into a wash and glaze it downwards over feet and lower legs, pulling the brush towards the ground. Repeat until it is as dirty as you want, then add a darker brown only at the very bottom.

A quick way: thin the base texture paint or base colour about half and half with water and stipple or slop it over the feet. Once fully dry, wipe the raised areas with a damp cotton bud so the grime stays only in the recesses.

For mud, stipple a light, crusty dry mud on knees and thighs, a dark glossy wet mud lower down, and dab a thinned mid mud where they meet. Enamel or oil dirt dabbed on and blended with a brush damp with white spirit stays workable for hours.

Real dust is chalky and dull, so keep it desaturated. It shows best over dark colours. The same works on tyres and tracks: wash them with very thin base colour and lift off the excess, leaving it in the treads.
Build it slowly. It is easy to add more and hard to take away, though over varnish it lifts off easily with a damp finger. Vary the amount across a group so the models do not all match.

guides.title: Dusty weathering with thinned paint
guides.summary: Run very watery sand, khaki or brown paint into recesses and low areas so armour, cloth and vehicles look dusty and used.
body: Thin a dull khaki, sand or drab brown with about two parts water to one of paint. Ordinary paint holds more pigment than a one-coat paint for this. Match the colour to the base.
Run it into recesses, deep folds and the low parts where dust would settle: hems, lower legs, boots and the lower hull. Use more near the ground and less as you go higher.

Start thinner than you think. You can always add more once it dries, and wipe off anything you do not like with a finger while it is wet. On knees and elbows, a mix of about five parts water should only tint the colour; if it covers, it is too thick.
On a small model it also works like panel lining, outlining shapes, and it softens shade lines that came out darker than you wanted.

On vehicle panels, a sandy one-coat paint thinned with about three parts medium and brushed downwards gathers at the bottom, so panels look dirtier near the ground. It stains transfers too, which ties them in.

With an airbrush, spray a sand-coloured enamel well thinned with white spirit low on a vehicle's sides. After about ten minutes, drag most of it off downwards with a flat brush barely damp with thinner, so the dust stays gathered low. Ventilate well.

Finish with a light dry brush of pale bone on the lowest parts, or dab paint straight from the pot for caked mud and spatters. On terrain, drybrush a tan over the lower third, pressing harder near the ground.

Keep dust out of places where parts rub together, such as a boot in a stirrup. It is easy to overdo, so check from arm's length before adding more. Photos of real dusty clothing show where it gathers.

guides.title: Brush strokes for edge highlights
guides.summary: Drag the side of the brush tip along sharp edges and pull the point along blunt or awkward ones, turning the part to suit.
body: Use a brush with a sharp tip and enough belly to hold paint. Thin the paint only lightly; watery paint runs. Drag the brush once over paper towel before every stroke so there is not enough paint to run into recesses. Reload often; once paint dries on the tip you press harder and the line goes thick.

On sharp, open edges, lay the side of the bristles near the tip along the edge at about 45 degrees and sweep in one smooth stroke. Only the very edge picks up paint, as the edge itself guides it. Avoid the fat part near the collar. Do every edge you can reach this way first.
Where the side cannot reach, turn the brush so it lines up with the edge and pull the tip along it towards you. Save the very tip for dots and short scratches.
Rounded or bevelled edges, common on older sculpts, will not catch the side of the brush. Paint the line on with the tip in short, slow strokes.

On long straight sharp edges, a slightly drier brush dragged lightly along works like a very controlled drybrush. Beside a raised trim, rest the side of the bristles against it and drag. On straps and belts, hold the brush almost level and drag the side along each edge for two clean lines.

Keep weapons and parts off the model on a holder or a blob of tacky putty so you can approach each edge straight on. Find the one stroke you control best and turn the model so each edge comes to it, instead of twisting your wrist.
On saw teeth and serrated blades, stroke in the direction the teeth point so paint catches only their top edges. A second, brighter highlight goes inside the line of the first so both stay visible.
If a line wobbles, straighten it afterwards with the colour underneath. Practise on an old sprue sprayed black.

guides.title: Edge highlighting
guides.summary: Paint a thin, light line along raised edges so each shape reads clearly, with the right colour, paint and a steady hand.
body: An edge highlight is a fine, lighter line along raised edges. It stops single-colour areas looking flat and shows the shape from a distance, like the outline in a drawing. Do it over a clean, solid base coat, and after any dark wash or lining, which dulls the model; the edges bring the contrast back.

Pick a colour clearly brighter than the base. A half-and-half mix of base and a lighter colour makes a good first line; the lighter colour alone makes a finer second one. A more saturated tone, a blue-grey, a pale cream or an accent such as orange each give a different feel. On red, a pale orange keeps it warm where white turns it pink.

Thin the paint only slightly, to layer consistency or a little thinner, by pulling pigment into a drop of water beside it. Paint test lines on the palette: if they drag or break, add water; if they spread or run into recesses, the paint is too wet or the brush overloaded.
Use a size 1 to 3 with a good point. Tiny brushes dry out at once. Most people carry too much paint, so touch the loaded brush on tissue until the tip carries little and the belly keeps a reserve.

Brace your wrists on the table and your hands against each other. Make a few practice swings just above the edge, then skim it lightly. Turn the model, not your hand. Keep the line an even width: too faint and nobody sees it, too thick and the model looks chunky.
Reload fresh paint every minute or so. Stop when mistakes start to creep in.

For extra punch, add a second, paler and thinner line on only part of the first, or a dot on the sharpest corners and points. Metal edges can go brightest of all. Bright edges draw the eye, so put the strongest where you want attention.
Practise on an old sprue sprayed black and highlighted in white. Every wobble shows, and the edges train each movement.

guides.title: Enamel streaks, rust and mud
guides.summary: Place enamel rust, grime or mud, let it set, then pull it into soft streaks or fades with a spirit-damp brush or bud.
body: Varnish the acrylic paint first so the spirit cannot lift it. Use old brushes kept only for enamels, and keep two jars of spirit that look different: a dirty one for rinsing and a clean one for moving paint on the model. Work with good ventilation.

For rust streaks, dot a light orange rust enamel round rivets and into recesses and let it set about five minutes. Pull a flat brush damp with clean spirit downwards over it, removing most of the paint, then soften both sides of each streak. Repeat to build strength rather than starting heavy.

Mix tones for variety: a rust, a pale rain mark and a dark grime. Start each line at a rivet, chip or top edge, on vertical faces only. A few single sharp lines left unblended below chips act as focal points. Go dustier for desert settings, greener and darker for wet ones.

Another way: paint thin lines of unthinned grime where rain would run, then pull them from the bottom upwards with a clean dry brush for natural stains. While wet, any excess lifts off with a clean brush or bud. A few streaks over transfers blend them in.

Streaks make no sense on flat tops. There, dab thinned enamel around hatches, rivets and fittings and fade its outer edge with spirit so the stain stays tight to the detail. Strong red rust over a white winter coat looks too heavy.

For grime, stipple a dark enamel into machinery, wait, then drag a spirit-damp cotton bud downwards. For mud, work a mud-coloured enamel onto the feet and lower legs, then dab spirit on to fade it upwards.
If rust blurs the separation between plates, dot bright silver back onto the sharpest edges.
Seal with matte varnish before the next enamel layer, or it will lift too. Spray varnish in dry weather and test on a spare first.

guides.title: Enamel washes and wipe-off
guides.summary: Varnish, coat the model in a dark enamel grime wash, then wipe it off raised areas with spirit for fast dirt and shading.
body: Seal the acrylic paint with an acrylic varnish first, ideally two coats, and let it cure. Spirit can lift unprotected paint, and an enamel-based varnish can soften under the wash. A gloss coat lets the wash run into recesses and wipe off cleanly; matt leaves more tint. Never thin enamels or rinse their brushes with water.
It works best over light or mid colours. On dark colours the wash barely shows.

Thin a dark brown or grey enamel wash slightly with spirit and brush it over the whole piece. A big flat brush suits terrain. Pooling two colours, such as an orange and a dark brown, and letting them mix on the model adds variety. Thinned black oil paint works the same way.

Let it set until it loses its wet shine, about 20 to 30 minutes. A hair dryer on low speeds this up, but a strong blast pushes the wash around. Enamels stay workable for a long time, so there is no rush.

Wipe it back with a cotton bud or makeup sponge dampened in odourless white spirit, rolled on tissue first. Wipe downwards, lifting it from raised and upward surfaces and leaving it in cracks and lower areas. Over metallics, roll or dab rather than scrub, or the metal comes off too.

A low pile glasses cloth or firm, tightly wound buds work best; fluffy buds and toilet roll leave fibres. Dabbing instead of wiping leaves a fabric-like texture. Strokes across a blade edge look like scraped-away rust.

Go easy with the spirit; heavy scrubbing eats through varnish, and a proper enamel thinner is gentler than harsh white spirit. Wait until every trace of enamel gloss has gone, then seal with a flat matt so later brushwork grips. Finish metal with a light silver drybrush on edges.
For subtle grime, skip the all-over coat and build a green or brown wash only where muck would collect, in several thin layers dried in between.

guides.title: Evening out a mixed sheen
guides.summary: Brush a thin coat of clear medium or matte varnish over an area so shiny and dull patches end up with one finish.
body: Washes, glazes, metallics and different paints dry with different sheens, and mixing paint ranges on one model adds more. Tilted to the light, the area looks patchy even when the colours are right. Reds, gems and one-coat paints are common offenders.
Before sealing, check the colour has not dried dull. If it has, glaze a little more colour first.
Brush one thin coat of clear matte medium or matte varnish over the whole area. Thin a glaze medium with a little matte varnish for a satin result.
Keep it thin. Thick matte coats can frost and grey the colour.

Let it dry, then add final bright highlights. They stand out more against an even matte surface, and a matt surface is easier to judge under a strong lamp. For gems or wet effects, a clear gloss coat over the evened area works instead.
If you spray matte varnish over the whole figure, paint the metallics afterwards so they keep their shine.
A matt finish scratches more easily than a glossier one, so a final varnish over the finished model both evens the sheen and protects it.

guides.title: Fabric textures
guides.summary: Add fine cross-hatching or tiny stitch marks with each highlight so cloth reads as linen, tweed or knitted wool.
body: Texture makes cloth read as a different material from the smooth skin and armour next to it. Keep it where light hits; skip most of it in shadow.
For heavy linen or hessian, thin a highlight colour and paint a few short fine lines one way over part of the cloth, then turn the model and add a few the other way.
Keep it sparse. You are suggesting texture rather than drawing a pattern, so the lines can be uneven. Repeat with each later highlight, only on the lit areas.
For coarse cloth such as a work jacket, put the highlights on in short, broken strokes or dabs instead of smooth layers. The gaps read as a rough weave.

For knitted wool, base a little darker than the midtone, then paint rows of tiny angled V strokes like stitches. Smaller stitches read as finer yarn. Keep the dark gaps between them very thin. For ribbed socks or cuffs, short vertical lines, evenly spaced and parallel, are enough.
Highlight knit by repainting stitches in lighter mixes, covering fewer each time. Where the light fades out, paint just the upper half of each stitch.
For a busy flecked fabric without freehand, dab a lighter tone of the same colour on with a small piece of sponge, as for chipping, then highlight a few fold edges with it.
If the texture looks too stark, glaze the whole area with the midtone to pull it together, and sponge or hatch again for more depth if needed.

guides.title: Where to highlight a face
guides.summary: Gather light on the forehead, brow, nose, cheekbones, upper lip and chin, and keep shadows soft where the face is soft.
body: Decide the main viewing angle, then look at the primed face under a single lamp, or photograph it, to see which areas catch the light. A light slightly to one side adds character. Think of the head as a cylinder lit from the front with a dome on top.

Start from the midtone. Focus light on the brow ridge, the bridge and tip of the nose, the tops of the cheekbones, the chin and the area above the upper lip. Together these form a double T: across the brow and down to the chin, then across the cheekbones. On a bald head, the crown gets plenty.

On each cheek, a reversed L reads well: a short stroke under the eye and a longer one down beside the nose. Do not forget small upward faces: the upper eyelids, the corners of the mouth and the sides of the nostrils.
Put the forehead highlight just above the brows, not at the hairline, and shade along the hairline.

Judge how deep each recess is. Deep ones keep more of the previous colour; shallow ones are mostly covered. Under the cheekbones is only a shallow dip and needs little shading; around the eyes and nose can take stronger shade.

Keep the shadow under the brow soft, and do not shade heavily under the eye. Dark bags make a face look tired or dead. A hard dark line beside the nose and mouth ages a face quickly. On softer faces, keep blue or green out of the lower face, where it reads as stubble.

A stronger jaw and chin highlight looks heroic; a slim line beside the nose bridge looks finer. Keep the side away from the light darker, with a few small highlights. Highlights kept high and central with darker outer edges slim a broad face.

Thin each highlight so it stays slightly see-through, and build each over a smaller area than the last, with no hard edge lines in creases. Tiny bright dots at the end give an oily shine. Young faces want softer steps and less contrast.

guides.title: Faces with one-coat paints
guides.summary: Over a pale primer, shade a face down with thinned one-coat flesh paints, then layer or glaze the highlights back up.
body: Start from a bone or off-white primer. This works backwards from the usual way: you shade down from light rather than build up from dark.
Dilute a pale flesh one-coat paint with water, about half and half, plus a touch of clear medium if you have it. Brush a light coat over all the skin just to tint it, without letting it pool.
Once dry, apply the same colour less thinned, only into the recesses: around the eyes and nose, under the cheeks, in the ears.
Repeat with a darker, richer flesh tone even more selectively: behind the ears, under the chin, along the hairline, in the eye sockets, under the nose and mouth.
Finish the shading with a thinned warm dark brown in only the deepest spots.
It looks messy at this stage. That is normal. Layer a pale skin tone, around #e8c4a6, back onto the forehead, nose, cheekbones and chin.
Glaze one more thin coat of the first flesh paint over the whole face. It softens the steps between highlights and pulls the skin together.

guides.title: Fast terrain painting
guides.summary: Prime dark, dust a lighter colour from above, drybrush roughly with big brushes and wash once to get terrain onto the table quickly.
body: With terrain, the effect across the table matters more than tidy edges. Give yourself a short deadline and a fixed few steps; extra steps are why terrain so often never gets finished.

Use cheap craft acrylics or household sample pots and your biggest brushes. Rough cast surfaces wear soft brushes out, so use old stiff ones there; soft makeup brushes make good throwaway drybrushes. Keep fine model paints for small effects such as a glowing rune.

Prime black, then dust a lighter grey or sand colour from above. The dark stays in recesses and undersides as ready-made shading. A second colour sprayed from below gives a quick two-tone gradient. Coloured spray primers save more time, and roofs, walls and floors that come apart can each get their own base colour.
Clip-together wall and corridor kits can jam once painted. Join them into long runs and paint each run as one piece instead of masking every connector.

Line the pieces up and do each step across all of them. Overbrush each material roughly with plenty of paint, dark to pale, covering less each time. Press harder on top edges and lighter lower down so it looks lit from above.

Do not chase every crack. A dirty brown wash or a wipe-off enamel wash fills the recesses for you. Thin brown or green filters at the top and bottom of plain walls add grime, and a light dark-iron drybrush over everything ties crates and walls together.

Drybrush metal in a dark steel with light passes of bright silver on edges, or paint it straight in rust. Pull out wood grain with a little pale drybrush over brown. Use a grey with a hint of green, brown or blue for stone rather than flat grey. Skulls go white, then a bone-tinted brown wash, then white drybrushed back over.

Finish with a few spot colours, such as deep red lights and valves and screens left dark as if switched off, but do not crowd it. Paint cut plastic edges black for a neat frame, and use the same colours and tufts as your bases so the table matches.

guides.title: Fast white from a white primer
guides.summary: Prime white, paint the other colours loosely, tidy once with white, then shade everything with one grey or brown wash.
body: Prime white with a matte spray. The primer is your main colour already, and white over a dark primer takes many coats.
Paint all the other parts first, such as the black joints, metal weapons and coloured markings. Do not worry about going over the lines.
Once every other colour is on, tidy all the slips at once with matte white. It matches the primer and vanishes after shading.

Shade with a thin grey or light brown wash, put on with a soft brush to avoid blotches. Glaze it towards the lower part of each panel and let it wick along the panel lines. It looks dark wet but dries paler; lift any pools on flat panels.
Line the panel lines with a darker warm brown or grey for crisp definition, tidying slips with white.

Skip edge highlights if you like. A light drybrush of white brings back clean white on raised areas and brightens edges. Small dark grey chips sponged on the edges define them instead and suit battered armour.
With an airbrush there is another route: base a mid grey, spray white from above so the top is brightest, then glaze a thin tinted one-coat paint or ink over it.

guides.title: Feathering
guides.summary: Two brush blending: place paint where the highlight is strongest, then pull its edge out to a soft fade with a clean damp brush.
body: Feathering is like wet blending with one colour: you spread one wet layer so it fades out at its edge. It works with layers, washes and one-coat paints alike, and suits skin, hair and weathered surfaces where soft shifts look natural.
Put a small amount of fairly thick paint exactly where the brightest point, or the deepest shadow, should be. Pigment-dense paint spreads further and more gradually than watery paint.

Rinse and blot the brush so it is just damp. Hold it at a low angle and dab and drag the edge of the paint outwards in quick short strokes, so it thins as it goes, like spreading the last of the butter.
Another way: lay a thin film of clean water beside the paint first, then pull the paint into it. It fades from solid to clear on its own.
Work while it is wet; acrylic dries fast under a warm lamp. Once it starts to grip, stop. Scrubbing lifts the layer underneath or leaves gaps.

Use two brushes, one to lay paint and one damp with water or a little slow-drying medium to pull it, or rinse the same brush. A firmer synthetic brush works well and spares your good one. With a wash, run the damp brush along its edge straight away, before a tide mark forms.
Add the next lighter layer and feather it over a smaller area. Many small dots build up better than one big highlight. Colours close together on the colour wheel feather together most smoothly.
Feathering rarely gives a perfect blend on its own. Tidy it with a few glazes or stippled midtones. Practise on a flat spare base, as flat surfaces show every mistake.

guides.title: Finding reflections on shiny parts
guides.summary: Prime a part satin black or metallic, turn it under a lamp and copy where the light lands as your highlight guide.
body: Prime the part in satin black or a very dark grey, base it in a satin paint, or spray a spare part bright silver. Shine shows where light naturally lands, which a matte primer or top-down white spray does not.
Shine one lamp from the direction your light will come from and turn the part to the angles it will mostly be seen from.

Photograph it from the front and back and keep the photos beside you. Raising the contrast on the photo makes bright and dark areas easier to read. Tilt the model under the lamp again wherever you are unsure.

Notice how extreme shiny metal is: bright spots sit right beside near black. Round and cone shapes get the strongest spots, sharp edges catch thin bright lines, and a plain cylinder reads well with one bright line down its length.
Shiny parts also reflect what is around them. Coloured card beside or under the part shows where a red cloak or blue water would appear in the dark areas.
Paint your highlights on those spots and along the edges that catch the most light. On larger flat areas, blend back into the base so it does not look stripy.

A primer photo treats every material alike and tells you little about flat blades, skin or glows. Use artwork or photos of real metal outdoors for those. For glows, light travels in straight lines and is brightest nearest the source.
Practise on parts with real volume, such as helmets, curved armour and rounded weapons. Without a reference, think in simple shapes: limbs as cylinders, the head as a sphere.

guides.title: Finding your own painting style
guides.summary: A personal style grows from solid basics, lots of practice and noticing what you keep leaning towards.
body: Style is the sum of your habits and choices. Give two painters the same model and colours and the results still differ. It ties your techniques together and can matter more than technical polish.
Learn the basics first. Sloppy brushwork or clashing colours are not a style, and rules are easier to break once you know them.

Copying is a fine way to start. Follow a scheme or method step by step to learn it. Later, borrow single ideas you admire, such as how someone shades cloth or highlights hair, rather than their whole look.

Style cannot be forced. Notice what you tend to do, such as hard contrast or soft blends, bright colour or grim tones, and which looks you keep coming back to. Then lean into it and improve those parts on purpose.

Realistic and stylised are both valid. Realism means very smooth transitions, light placed as it would really fall and close study of real materials, and it is slow. A stylised look might prime black, push shadows and highlights hard and keep the model near one colour with one or two bold accents.
Spend effort on the parts you want noticed and keep the rest simpler so it sits back. Do not wear yourself out second-guessing every shadow colour.

Paint often and learn one new skill per project. Compare old photos to see progress. Paint to your own taste rather than contest rules unless you plan to enter, and do not ask for feedback after every small step.

guides.title: Actually finishing an army
guides.summary: Choose a simple, repeatable scheme and a small palette, time a test model honestly, and stick to the plan.
body: Paint a single test model in the planned style and note honestly how long it took. Write the steps down in order. If it is too slow to repeat across the whole army, change the style rather than the goal.
Keep the scheme simple and the palette small, with one or two strong accents. One or two universal highlight colours used on every area save mixing and keep the army consistent.
Pick a look that suits repetition. Airbrushed and weathered armour is quick on big panels and hides small errors better than crisp line highlights.
Spend time on the large, eye-catching parts such as armour, faces, weapons and the base. Paint belts, pouches and buckles in one tone with a quick highlight.
Treat the group like one model and follow the plan. Your last model will look best; touch up the first ones afterwards instead of changing the plan halfway.

Shared markings, such as a repeated symbol or stripe, link models of very different sizes. Decide early how to do them: freehand across a whole army is slow and risky, so use transfers or keep the symbol very simple. Dark transfers are rarer than white ones.
Set a tight but realistic deadline. It stops you fussing over details that never show on the table. Plan drying time to overlap with other jobs, such as basing while vehicles dry.
Any workflow can work: one at a time, batches of five or ten, or one colour across everything. Anything that removes a chore, like ready-made bases, keeps the project moving.

guides.title: Finishing touches on a character
guides.summary: Painted eyes, a clean rim, a little grime and a last look-over make a model read as finished.
body: Eyes that are painted make a model look complete, even when the rest is simple. A tiny pale dot in each pupil as a reflection makes them look alive.
Finish the base and paint its rim; a bare base reads as an unfinished model. If unsure of the rim colour, black always looks neat and frames the model.
A thin brown-grey wash round the feet adds grime and ties the model to its base. It suits pale armour well. Put any transfers on before grime or damage so they sit in the same worn surface.

Push the highlights a little further than feels natural so characters stand out on the table. Give items near the face a proper transition and a bright dot or two. After washes, touch the brightest metal back onto rivets and edges.
Small items need only one coat, one lighter edge and a dark line where they meet skin. A skin tone or ivory can highlight browns and small items, so you do not need a lighter version of every colour.
Where areas meet, such as straps over cloth or armour against skin, a neat dark line keeps each part separate. It tidies a loose drybrushed model quickly.
Add one or two tiny accents in a contrasting colour, such as a few turquoise beads among reds. Spread small details round the model and give one on the back some care, so it holds up from every side.

Keep the last minutes to look the model over at arm's length. Glows should read as bright and painted metal as shiny; if not, push the contrast. Tidy slips with the nearby colour, then a matt varnish evens out any shiny patches.

guides.title: Painting your first model
guides.summary: Prime, base coat the main colour, wash and drybrush it, then block in and wash the small details and add a few highlights.
body: Pick a simple model. Clip the parts off with flush cutters, scrape away mould lines and glue it together. Glue sand to the base while it is bare, so model and base are primed together.
Prime grey. Stick the model to an old stick with double-sided tape, shake the can for two minutes and spray from about 30 cm in sweeps.
Base coat the main colour in two thin coats with a larger brush. Do not worry about going over neighbouring parts yet.
Wash it with a black or brown wash, lift any pools and leave it about 45 minutes. It will look flatter and darker; the next step fixes that.
Drybrush the main colour back on top, then a lighter tone over the edges. Do this early, because drybrushing is messy.
Now block in the small details, such as joints, leather and metal, with a smaller brush, and wash those neatly. Change your rinse water after metallics so flakes do not get into other colours.

For first highlights, mix a little yellow and off-white into the base colour and thin it more. Touch it on raised parts like brows, knuckles and muscles, or along edges and corners on hard surfaces. A base, a shade and one highlight per area is plenty while learning.
Stop once you like how it looks. Paint the base and rim, then spray one or two light coats of matt varnish from 15 to 30 cm, and the model is done.

guides.title: Fluorescent paints
guides.summary: Fluorescent colours only glow over solid white, so paint the source white first and glaze or spray the colour over it.
body: Fluorescent paints are very translucent. Paint the glowing area a solid, opaque white first, in two coats if needed. Over black they do almost nothing and over light grey they look patchy. Do the glow at the very end, after the rest of the model.
The undercoat tint shows through. An icy blue white under the colour makes it feel cold; a warm ivory makes it feel warm.
Shake the pot very hard; if clear goo comes out, keep shaking. Use fresh, clean water, as dirty water dulls these paints quickly.
Paint the surfaces facing the source a very light grey and the source itself pure white, so the colour reads brightest there.

Brush the fluorescent colour over the white. It is already thin, so barely dilute it, and build three or four coats, letting each dry. Alternating thin white and fluorescent layers gives a stronger glow. A little yellow in a green makes it look hotter.

With an airbrush, spray the white most solid at the source and fading outwards. Thin the fluorescent about half and build it in several passes over the white and a little beyond; the overspray on nearby surfaces reads as a haze of light.

Use them as a small accent. Orange suits fire, green suits toxic glows, pink suits magic and yellow an intense light; fluorescent blue tends to be dull. A touch mixed into a pale highlight mix, or glazed over a finished gem, keeps it vivid rather than chalky.

For eyes and gems across many models, dot them all white and mist the colour lightly over them. Fluorescents also light up under ultraviolet light. If a photo looks flat, dim the lights and lower the camera exposure.

guides.title: Freehand flames
guides.summary: Start each flame as a thin S curve, broaden it into a tongue, then cut the shape back sharp with the background colour.
body: Paint freehand at the base coat stage, before shading and highlighting, so tidy-ups match and you do not waste highlights you will cover.
With thinned orange or dark red, paint one line up the middle of the panel to set the height. Then paint a few S-shaped curves of different heights rising from the bottom edge on either side.
Widen each curve into a tongue of flame, broader at the bottom, and add a few small flicks and dots for sparks higher up.
Build up coats until solid. Fire is hottest at its base: keep a deep red, around #b02a12, at the tips, orange as the main body, then yellow low down and a touch of near white where it is hottest.

For a looser, flickering look, keep the colours wet on a wet palette and use a small round brush with a fat belly. Lay very thin coats from deep red through orange to yellow, each straight after the last so they run together. Work fast rather than carefully.
Cut back into the flames with the background colour to sharpen the shapes. If you cut in too far, restore the shape with the flame colour.
A thin yellow glaze over the finished pattern pulls the colours together. A coat of varnish between stages makes slips easier to fix.

For a subtle touch on black, use a muted ochre or orange on a small panel. Practise on a test model or paper first and expect a few attempts; breaking any design into simple shapes makes it manageable.

guides.title: Freehand lettering and text
guides.summary: Plan the word on paper, place the middle letter first and then the ends, and suggest tiny writing with broken dashes.
body: Pick a word that fits the scroll's length. Write it out on paper first, or print it in a suitable font as a reference. Check which way up the part will sit; an upside-down word on an angled scroll is an easy slip. On a plank sign, mask a clean box for the text rather than following the boards.

Count the letters and paint the middle one faintly in the centre of the scroll. Then place the first and last letters faintly at each end, and fill in between. Writing from the left almost always runs out of space.

Place every letter as a thin skeleton before thickening any. Then thicken and shape each one with slightly less thinned paint so it covers. Do the straight downward strokes first, then add the curves using them as guides.
Keep the style simple. Plain capitals with one main stroke doubled and short bars at the top and bottom read as old ornate script; fussy calligraphy does not work at this scale.
Black paint with a drop of black ink, glaze medium or drying retarder flows off a fine tip and stays wet longer. Test the line width on the palette first, and brace your hands together.

For tiny text on parchment, mix black and dark brown half and half, thinned to flow. Make straight, evenly spaced rows of short marks, letting the brush wobble a little and breaking each row at irregular points so it reads as words. Solid lines read as stripes.

A red first capital, or a small gap left for a symbol, makes fake text more convincing. Tidy thick or wobbly letters with the scroll colour, then glaze a thin pale cream over raised folds so the text sits into the paper.
If painted script will not come right, cut narrow strips of text from a transfer sheet, soften them over the curves and hide the film with a spot of matt varnish.

guides.title: Freehand lightning
guides.summary: Paint lightning as short jagged forking lines, building each lighter colour as a thinner line inside the last.
body: Look at photos of lightning first. It forks: one bold line runs the full length, smaller branches leave it, often at the sharp bends, and branches sometimes rejoin.
Use your finest brush and keep it to a few panels per model, or one blade. A dark base gives the most contrast.

Start with the darkest glow colour thinned to a glaze. Wash it round the point the energy comes from, then draw rough branching lines of short straight segments that change direction often. Keep this first pass faint. On a blade, a heavily thinned brighter wash left to dry in cloudy patches gives edges for the bolts to follow.
Go over the shapes again to make them bolder once you like them. Painting these first lines a little wider and softer gives a glow that spreads onto the surface around the bolt.

Each lighter colour goes as a thinner line inside the last, so earlier colours stay visible at the edges. Take the palest only along the main bolt, stopping and restarting it for a flicker; the branches stay dimmer.

Finish with white dots at the bends and where lines join, and a fine white line down the thickest strokes. Let the brush wobble slightly; perfectly straight lines look wrong. Extra branches hide a wobbly main line.

For a quick version, use an opaque white that flows well off the tip and paint thin scratchy lines in one pass. Faint bolts left underneath read as distant lightning. A thin glaze over the finished bolt shifts its colour, such as yellow over blue for a greener light.
Varnish the area first and a slip wipes off with a damp cotton bud, if you are quick. Judge it from normal viewing distance; close up it always looks rougher than it is.

guides.title: Freehand painting
guides.summary: Break a design into simple shapes, place it from the centre, paint it rough and tidy it by cutting back with the background.
body: Paint freehand straight onto a smooth base coat, before shading, so any wobble can be fixed with the base colour. If you can, paint a banner or shield before gluing it on, and wear a glove or wrap the painted parts you hold.
Work out the simple shapes the design is made of: lines, triangles, squares, crosses. A spiked border is a line, a row of triangles and a curve cut into each. Sketch it on paper at size first.

Plan motifs to follow the edges, hems and raised areas of the sculpt. Mark the centre with a dot and work outwards, judging spacing by eye. Leave more room at the edges than you think; designs often drift to one side.

Thin paint to flow, but not as thin as a glaze; lumpy or chalky lines mean it is too thick. Keep it wet on a wet palette and use a size 1 or 2 with a sharp point, upright, in short pen-like marks. Start thin: a line can get fatter but never thinner.

Place everything faintly first, in a colour close to the background, such as pink before red on white, or with a sharp pencil on the dry base coat. Then go bolder. Paint downstrokes and turn the model for sideways parts.

Block the shape in slightly rough, then carve it into shape by painting the background colour back into its edges. For a design that stands out, block it in a darker related tone, such as brown under cream, then paint the final colour inside it, leaving a thin dark edge.

A coat of matt varnish under the design, or a drop of drying retarder in the paint, lets a wrong line wipe or scrape off. Practise on scrap plastic card primed and painted close to the model's colour.

If a design is too hard, simplify it or use a transfer. Shade the design to match the light on its surface: white where lit, light greys in shadow. A few chips over wobbly spots hide them and make it sit on the surface.

guides.title: Freehand stripes, checks and patterns
guides.summary: Mark out checks, chevrons and stripes with thin guide lines, follow the folds, then shade and highlight the pattern as one surface.
body: Paint patterns at the base coat stage, before shading and weathering, so they get the same wear as the rest. Use an edge, such as a hem or a panel rim, as the guide for stripes and borders, and let the brush width set the stripe thickness. Work top to bottom so your hand does not smudge it.

For checks, paint one thin line down the middle and one across, then halve each part again until the squares are the right size. Fill alternate squares, checking first so you do not double a colour. For chevrons, paint thin guide lines and thicken them over a couple of coats.

Start pale parts in a mid grey, then an off-white, and edge them in pure white; grey slips are far easier to cover. Thin the paint so it flows from the tip and build coverage over several coats. For alternating bands, base the whole band in one colour, then pick out every other segment.

Break helmet and shield markings into triangles and strips. Paint one side, then mirror it. For small rank stripes, paint one chunky chevron and split it with fine lines of the background colour. A row of small crosses on a dark trim band, worked from the middle out, makes a quick border.

Hold the model at one fixed angle and pull every stripe the same way, towards you. Curved swoops forgive more than straight lines. Trim thick or wobbly lines back with the other colour; it often takes a few rounds.

On cloth, let stripes follow the folds and let small motifs disappear into deep folds. A coloured stripe can go on dark first, with the bright colour only on its raised parts. Keep patterns small and spaced on creased robes, but make tartan and checks slightly larger than life.

Animal prints: zebra is wavy dark lines out from the centre, fewer than you expect. Leopard is small uneven dark rings with an orange dot inside. Tiger is short angled black stripes tapering at both ends. Turn a stray mark into another spot.

Shade and highlight the pattern as one surface: one dark glaze into the folds across every colour, one thin light mix on the raised areas. Keep patterns to one or two areas, and let a few chips across the edges hide what is left of the mistakes.

guides.title: Freehand symbols and heraldry
guides.summary: Build small symbols from a centre line outwards with thinned paint, then thicken the lines once the shape is right.
body: Paint symbols at the base coat stage, before the wash, while slips are easy to trim with the base colour. The wash then sits them into the model. Thin the paint a little so it flows in fine lines; it takes extra coats but is far easier to steer, and thick paint drags and wobbles.

Draw the symbol on paper first, large and then smaller. A light pencil sketch on the model also works; tilt it under the lamp to see the lines, and wipe leftovers off with a damp tissue. Small dots at the key points, joined with smooth lines, also make a good outline.

Find the centre from a straight edge, such as the top of a banner, not a ragged bottom. On a curved plate, look straight at it and place a dot in the exact centre first, as lines drift. Paint one line down the middle, following the cloth.

Add a crossing line, then any diagonals through the same centre. An eight-pointed star is just four lines. Join the tips of a cross for a diamond, or mark four sides and join them for a circle. A skull is a circle, an oval below and a slanted box for teeth, with eyes cut in early as small triangles.

Add lines either side of the centre and fill between them. Rivets and sculpted details make handy reference points. For white symbols, fill in mid grey first, then two or three thin white coats. At tiny scale, a black shape under white marks makes them read.

Grow each shape a little at a time, slightly bigger than needed, and trim it back with the background. Only then thicken the lines and add a lighter mix as a highlight. A black or contrasting outline added last hides earlier slips. Repaint any edge highlights the symbol crossed.
For heraldry that reads at a distance, treat white and yellow as metals and red, blue and black as colours. Put a metal on a colour or a colour on a metal, not colour on colour.
Judge it at table distance: the rough shape is what reads, and a crude hand-daubed look need not be perfect. Unlike a transfer, a painted symbol can go darker in shadow and lighter towards the light.

guides.title: Fuel, oil and grease stains
guides.summary: A few small, glossy dark stains around fuel caps, engines and hubs stand out against matt dust and make a vehicle look used.
body: Fresh fuel, oil and grease are dark and wet looking. What sells them is the gloss against a matt, dusty surface, so add them last, after dust, pigments and any matt varnish.
Put them where liquids would leak or spill: round fuel caps and filler points, on engine decks, at wheel hubs, below joints and hatches and round moving parts of weapons.
Use a dark brown-black, around #1e140c, in oil paint, a glossy enamel effect or an acrylic mixed with gloss varnish. Thin it with its own thinner for softer, older-looking marks.

Dot a small amount at the source, then pull a short run downwards with a fine brush for a drip. Soften the outer edge with a brush barely damp with thinner so it fades, and leave the centre darkest and shiniest.
Layer old and new. Older stains can be a duller, lighter brown with a matt finish, with a fresh glossy mark over part of one. Spilt fuel round a cap shows best as a slightly paler, see-through ring.
Keep it to one or two fresh stains per vehicle. Too many make it look messy rather than used. Do not varnish over them with matt, or the wet look is lost.

guides.title: Painting ghosts and ethereal spirits
guides.summary: Build pale, glowing spirit bodies from many thin glazes over white, darkest low down, or drybrush white over a dusty colour.
body: Spirits read as pale, glowing and see-through: light on top, with colour deepening lower down and in the recesses. Many thin glazes give that look far better than one heavy coat.

For a glazed glow, base the ghostly parts white. Mix a translucent bright colour, such as green, about half and half with glaze medium; neat paint darkens the model instead of glowing. Glaze the whole area once with a big-bellied brush so it goes on smooth.

Add a second glaze starting lower down, then a third lower again, so the colour deepens towards the bottom. Use the colour neat only on the very bottom edge, and add extra glaze to recesses that stayed too pale. Let each coat dry first.

For a dusty, drybrushed spirit, prime white or light grey and spray the parts a dark purple mixed about two to one with white. Then spray white from about 45 degrees above so the top surfaces start pale.
Glaze thinned dark purple into the folds and recesses, then push a thinned deep violet into the very deepest spots: between fingers, eye sockets, overlapping layers and where chains meet the body.
Drybrush white lightly with a soft makeup brush, then a brighter white more gently still. With either method, finish by picking out faces, knuckles and the top-most edges in slightly thinned white.

guides.title: Glazing stroke direction
guides.summary: Start each glaze stroke where colour should be faintest and lift off where it should be strongest, since pigment gathers there.
body: Most pigment is left where the brush lifts off the surface. So start the stroke where you want least colour and finish where you want most.
To shade, start a little way into the panel and pull towards the bottom edge, recess or underside, lifting off there.
To highlight, pull upwards from the middle towards the centre of the lit area instead.

Thin the glaze until it spreads into a pool on the palette rather than pulling into beads. Soak most of it from the brush onto tissue. Each coat seems to do almost nothing; keep repeating and the gradient appears.
Hold the brush at a low angle. Pulling it towards you is easier to control than pushing. Turn the model rather than changing your stroke.
To fade colour up to a detail, end the stroke against the detail rather than outlining it. Spots where earlier coats pooled show where more colour wants to go.

To smooth, glaze the midtone the opposite way over the middle, spreading it rather than letting it pool. A visible glaze edge can also be feathered out with a damp brush while wet. Start each new coat a little further from the edge than the last so the steps stagger.
Put less on to begin with. If a blob forms, soak it up with a clean brush tip. Then run a darker mix into the deepest recesses at the end.

guides.title: Glazing
guides.summary: A glaze is paint thinned until it tints like coloured film: wick most off the brush, apply thin coats and let each dry.
body: A glaze is a see-through layer that tints, shades, highlights or enriches what is under it without hiding detail. A bit more water and it becomes a wash; less and it becomes a layer. Use it to soften a harsh highlight, lift a dark recess, warm or cool a colour, or smooth the step between two layers.

Mix paint with water, or with glaze medium, which keeps it smooth and slower to dry. Somewhere between three and fifteen parts liquid to one of paint; test rather than trust a ratio. If it barely shows, add paint; if it covers, thin more. If glazes start lifting or cracking earlier layers, drop flow additives and thin with plain water.

Strong, pure colours glaze best. Pale colours contain white and go chalky when thinned, so layer the light areas and glaze stronger colours over them, or thin pale paint with medium rather than water. An ink or one-coat paint in clear medium makes an easy glaze, and ink stays see-through over many coats.

A glaze needs a light surface to show. Over black it does almost nothing; over white, ivory or a light metal even a thin one stains strongly, so glazing a pale base down in stages is a good way to build rich colour or tinted metal.

Load a good brush with a sharp point, then touch it on tissue until it is damp with colour, not dripping. This is what separates a glaze from a wash: it must not run into recesses. Keep the same light pressure through the stroke, and start too thin rather than too thick.

Start where the colour should be faintest and lift off where you want most, since most pigment lands where the brush lifts. Let each layer dry fully; watch the sheen go dull. A hair dryer on low, held well back, speeds this. Glazing over half-dry paint goes lumpy. Build several layers, each covering a little less.

Common mistakes: paint too thick covers instead of tinting, so add water; you cannot really over-thin, it just takes more coats. Too much liquid pools and dries with tide marks; pressing too hard leaves strokes. If highlights end up dull, bring the brightest points back at the end. Matt varnish removes shine left by glaze medium.
Judge it at arm's length. To save time, lay shades and highlights as layers and glaze only the transitions. The last glaze sets the overall colour, so put the one that matters most on top.

guides.title: Glazing for smooth gradients
guides.summary: Build smooth gradients, deep shadows and soft layer joins with many thin, nearly dry glazes, steering colour with pressure.
body: On big panels, thinned paint applied as glazes builds a smoother, steerable gradient than a flooded wash, which pools and dries unevenly.

Frame the area first: decide where the brightest and darkest points are. Each glaze stops a little short of the last, light over less and less area for highlights, dark over less and less for shadows. After five passes the strong end carries five times the colour. Using straight paints this way, not mixes, makes the recipe easy to repeat.

At first you will see almost nothing. Let each layer dry fully before the next; wet layers on top of each other lift and streak. Your darkest point can only be as dark as the glaze colour, so switch to a deeper one if needed.

For very smooth blends, wick almost all the glaze off the brush. Then pressure decides how much colour comes off: press harder at the end of the stroke to build colour there. Blotches mean the brush was too wet or the mix too thick; fix them with more, thinner glazes, not heavier ones.

A thin glaze of the base colour, about as thin as milk, brushed on like a base coat, knocks back over-bright highlights and blends the steps between layers. Work both ways: dark up into the light, then thin light back down, until smooth. It also tidies rough drybrushing and scratchy wet blends.
Pale colours full of white go chalky when thinned this far, and pale cold greys show every step. Build highlights with thicker layers and glaze the darks and saturated colours over them.

Let glazes dry naturally or with cool air; hot air dries them too fast. A drop of flow improver or medium cuts tide marks and stops thin paint tearing, but slows drying. A satin medium can leave shiny rings on a matt surface.

If the colour drifts too far, a thin glaze of the colour you want pulls it back, and a final very thin glaze of a matching wash unifies the tones. Judge at arm's length. It is slow, so save the full method for centrepieces and use it to fix rough transitions elsewhere.

guides.title: Gloss coat before a wash
guides.summary: Seal the paint with gloss or satin varnish so a wash runs into recesses and spills wipe cleanly off flat areas.
body: On matt or chalky paint a wash soaks in and stains the flat areas. Over a smooth gloss or satin surface it slides along into recesses and panel lines, and spills wipe off without leaving a mark.

Once the base colours are dry, varnish with gloss. A paint that dries satin does a similar job without a separate coat, and matt and gloss varnish mixed give a satin. Gloss is also the right surface for transfers, so apply them now.

Brush on one thin, unthinned coat, as brush marks disturb how the wash flows, or spray it thinned to about milk. One or two coats at most; more makes the wash run in odd patterns. Let it dry fully before washing.
Pick a wash just a little darker than the area, with a hint of the same colour. It gives softer definition than harsh black lines. A matching one-coat paint can give a richer shade than a plain wash.
Touch the wash into the recesses and panel lines only, and let it run along them by itself. Keep it off broad flat areas.

With an acrylic wash, wipe spills with a clean dry brush or a damp cotton bud before they dry, one section at a time. Oil and enamel washes suit this best, as mistakes wipe off with a bud barely damp with white spirit; the varnish also stops the spirit lifting the paint. Wipe gently either way.
On a large creature, gloss it heavily, wash one section, then wipe the raised areas clean with a damp cotton bud and move on. Lift any pooling you missed later by dampening and wiping gently.
Finish with a matt or satin varnish. It removes the shine, seals any transfers and washes that redissolve in water, and gives a surface that new paint grips, which gloss does not.

guides.title: Glow in the dark and UV paints
guides.summary: Glow paints shine after charging in light, UV paints light up under a black light, and both need a white base.
body: Glow in the dark paint soaks up light and gives it off in the dark. UV reactive paint glows only while an ultraviolet lamp shines on it. They are different effects, though some paints do both.
Both work best over a smooth, solid white. Over dark colours the glow is weak or lost.
Glow paint is usually grainy and pale in daylight. Stir it well, apply several thin coats, and keep it to small areas such as eyes, runes, gems or slime.
Charge glow paint under a bright lamp or daylight for a few minutes. It is brightest right after and fades over minutes to hours.
UV paints look like normal bright colours in daylight, so they can be part of the scheme itself. Many fluorescent paints react to UV too.
Plan for both views. Paint the daylight look of the glow with normal colours, then add the special paint on top, so the model still looks right with the lights on.
Varnish can dull the effect. Test it on a scrap piece first, or varnish the model and add the glow paint last.

guides.title: Glow spilling onto surroundings
guides.summary: Glaze the glow colour onto nearby surfaces, strongest close to the source and fading away, but never as bright as the source.
body: A glowing object looks real when nearby surfaces catch its light. Only surfaces that can see the source catch it; anything turned away, or hidden under an overhang, stays dark. Finish the source first so you know how bright the light is.

Highlight the edges and surfaces facing the source first, in a pale blue grey or white, then glaze the glow colour over them. Another way: tint everything the light would touch with a thin wash of the glow colour, then build brighter coats over smaller areas closer to the source.

Use mid strength mixes of the glow colour, not the brightest one. Only the source itself should be that bright. Keep the rest of the model a little darker than usual; a glow only reads against darkness.

Glaze very thinly over the facing surfaces, pulling each stroke towards the source and starting each layer a little closer, so it builds without hard edges. For fire, work dark red, then orange, then yellow, each kept closer to the source.

Pale surfaces such as bone, teeth, rope and skin catch the glow strongly; surfaces in the opposite colour, such as red cloth under green light, show it dimly. Mixing the glow colour into a surface's own colour gives a softer change than pure glow. Do not leave out the face and chest above a glowing weapon.

Pick out small undersides that face the light: under the brows, lips and knuckles, and along rope strands. Add faint touches even on fairly distant parts that face the source, but only on edges that face it; lining every edge sends the eye all over the model.

Keep a dark band between the glow and the normally lit areas, or the colour reads as paint rather than light. Under a strong coloured light, paint everything inside the glow zone in that one colour, whatever its own colour.

If a glow spreads too far, glaze the underlying colour back over it, pulling outwards. A sunken source such as lava in a crack lights only what is right beside it. Work slowly; with glows, less is usually more.

guides.title: Glowing energy blades
guides.summary: Plot light and dark zones along a blade, build them with glazes, and finish with stacked bright edges and white glints.
