body: Base coat the blade in the glow colour, such as a mid turquoise, around #2a9a9a, with several smooth thin coats. Any texture shows through every glaze. A vivid, pigment-heavy colour has more punch than an ink, and greens and turquoises glow more readily than reds or purples.

Decide where the light falls. Plot rough, uneven oval light zones that alternate from side to side down the blade, with dark zones between. A reliable layout: each cutting edge, or each face, gets brighter towards the opposite end, one towards the tip, the other towards the guard. On a faceted blade, set light facets beside dark ones.

Build the light zones with paint heavily thinned with water or clear medium, pulling towards the centre of each zone and lifting off there. Each pass stops a little shorter. Then repeat with a paler mix over a shorter length, and near white only at the very ends.
Glaze darker tones into the dark zones the same way, keeping any central groove dark and ending with thinned black only at the darkest points. Smooth the steps with very thin in-between glazes.

For a simpler version, keep the blade deep and stack ever finer edge highlights along the edges and central ridge: broad first, then thinner and lighter. Or paint a white core line down the middle, a mid band either side and the darkest colour at the edges.

For a quick version, paint the blade pale or white and glaze a transparent icy blue one-coat paint over it, adding coats towards the darker end. Lay the weapon flat while it dries so the colour does not pool at one end.

For a crackling blade, base it near black, sketch bolts in two thin coats of the glow colour, brightest near the source, glaze the whole blade with the colour, then trace thin white inside the bolts. A thin off-white line along both edges separates the faces.

Contrast sells it: deep darks right beside bright lights. Keep white thin and only on the hottest spots, such as the tip or a gem, or it looks harsh. Glaze a little glow onto the hilt and hand to show the light spilling.

guides.title: Glowing eye lenses
guides.summary: Paint a lens like a tiny gem, dark at the back to bright at the front with one white dot, and glaze a little glow around it.
body: For a gem-style lens, start over black. Paint the darkest colour, leaving black in the back corner, then each lighter colour over a smaller area towards the front and along the bottom edge. Keep a thin dark outline so the lens stands out from the helmet.

Finish with a single tiny white or pale grey dot in the dark upper corner as a reflection. That one dot does most of the work of making it look like glass; keep it tiny or it reads as a blob. A fine pale line along the bright lower edge adds to the effect.

For a glowing lens, paint the lens and socket a deep colour such as red, then build up in steps: bright red, orange-red, orange, yellow, and a pale yellow dot in the middle. A glow colour that contrasts with the armour, such as green on red or red on blue, stands out most.

For quick bright lenses, paint them white, cover with a strong see-through colour or a fluorescent, brighten the inner corner with a paler mix and add the white dot. A little coloured wash let onto the socket round the eye reads as light thrown onto it. Skip the eyes when washing the model.

For a glassy finish, paint the lens bright silver and flow a coloured clear lacquer over it in one stroke, without fiddling. Clear lacquers are often alcohol based, so use a synthetic brush. For a dark glass lens, paint solid black and add a dab of gloss varnish in the centre.

Glaze thin versions of the darker colours onto the helmet just below the eye, then tiny touches of the brighter ones right under the middle. A touch on the brow edge above helps. The glow should fade softer and darker as it spreads.

Carry very little paint and brace your hands. Paint lenses before the helmet so slips get covered, or tidy round them with black. Check from the normal viewing angle, as some helmets hide the top of the lens. Draw a stray drop off at once with a clean damp brush.
Do not start human eyes with pure white; that makes them stare.

guides.title: Painting a glowing light source
guides.summary: Paint the source solid white, pick its brightest point, then glaze colour over it, deepest away from that point.
body: Change your water first. White must stay clean, and a stray hair is hard to remove from bumpy coils.

Cover the glowing part in white. Over black this takes about three coats that are neither thick nor watery. Keep coats thin on fine coils so they do not clog. A thin white ink runs into recesses and covers well where it settles.
Decide where the single brightest spot is, such as the centre of an orb or the base of a coil. Long tubes can have several hot spots, dark, light, dark, so they seem to pulse.

Glaze a deep tone of the glow colour over all of it, ending each stroke at that bright spot. Follow with a more vivid version, each pass stopping a little short of the last. Keep every layer see-through; transparent colour over white glows far brighter than opaque paint. Punchy colours with big steps, such as red, orange and yellow, read best.

Add a pale cream or near white step by step, covering less each time, and leave the brightest spot almost white. Be bold with this last step; timid final highlights make a glow look flat. A white glaze in the deepest corner of a coil reads as the hottest point.

For small recessed lights, vents and barrels, fill with a deep colour, paint a smaller bright circle inside leaving a dark ring, then a white dot in the centre. For narrow slits, paint a dark halo round each and step lighter and warmer inwards to near white at the opening.

Dark next to bright makes a glow stronger. Line round glowing parts with a thinned near black, separate coils with a fine darker line along their tops, and darken the ends where the glow meets the casing.

Then cast a faint glow onto the casing and nearby edges, such as fingertips, with thin glazes of the glow colour. A quick halo stippled around the source with a small drybrush also works. Repeat the glow colour in a few places so it shows from every side.

guides.title: Glowing magic effects
guides.summary: A pale warm base under strong pinks and a fluorescent top layer makes magic glows on terrain or spells read bright.
body: Base coat every glowing part in a bright warm ivory first. Strong colours stay vivid over it and turn dull over a dark base.
Coat the area with a one-coat magenta or similar strong tint. It settles in the recesses and gives you shading in one go.
Layer up with an opaque hot pink, then a fluorescent pink, then fluorescent mixed with ivory only in the centres where the light is strongest.
Pick a glow colour opposite the surroundings on the colour wheel. Pink magic on green stone, for example, stands out hard. Greens and blues feel eerie and otherworldly; oranges and yellows feel warm.

For shifting, unstable magic, shade the recesses dark, then paint patches of two opposite colours side by side, such as green and purple. Soften the joins with thin glazes and add tiny dots of a very bright tone in the hollows for sparkle.

For an eerie glow across a whole piece, mist thin ink in the glow colour in patches and under overhangs such as a leaf canopy, so the light seems to come from the piece itself. Very thin ink on a big brush works without an airbrush.
For magic smoke, flip the usual lighting: keep recesses lighter and raised parts darker, fading from the glow out towards black.

guides.title: Glowing orbs and spheres
guides.summary: Make an orb glow from inside by keeping the bright colour in the grooves and placing the light low and towards the centre.
body: Paint the orb white so the next colour comes out bright.
Layer a vivid colour, such as a warm salmon pink, over it until it is opaque.
If the orb has carved grooves, paint a dark red brown on the raised parts only. The bright colour left in the grooves looks like light from within.
On a smooth or large sphere, place the main glow low and towards the middle, not hard against the edge.
Add a second, thinner band of light along the rim on that same lower side.
Put a small white reflection on last, on the side facing the light. Look at a real glass ball for reference.

For a quick glow, paint white a little past the orb, cover it with an opaque wash of the glow colour, then build white back in thin layers, each smaller, towards the centre. Catch nearby edges with a chunky highlight in the glow colour, then a paler one.

For a tiny orb, gem or eye, work in shrinking dots: the bright colour, a smaller yellow or paler dot inside, then a tiny near white dot. On a pair of eyes, match the dot sizes, enlarging the smaller one if needed.

guides.title: Glowing runes
guides.summary: Glowing runes need dark stone around them, a white underlayer, a strong tint on top and a glazed fade into the stone.
body: A glow only reads in shadow, so paint the stone or armour around the runes dark before you start. A wash beforehand marks the carved lines out clearly.
Run thinned white with a touch of yellow into the carved lines. Neatness does not matter yet.
Run a strong see-through colour, such as a pink, over the top in two thin coats rather than one thick one, which clumps. The white underneath makes it pop.
Tidy between the lines with the dark stone colour.
Glaze outwards from bright to dark, pulling each stroke towards the rune so colour builds up at its edge and fades into the stone.
Put each lighter step deeper into the groove: the mid colour stains the edges, a paler mix sits lower, and near white goes only in the very deepest part.
Retrace the lines last with a fluorescent mix. The rune itself must be the brightest thing in the area. Skip edge highlights on the rune panel; the glow does that job.

A quick shortcut for carved lines: over a gloss coat, brush a pale blue and white gouache mix into the grooves, wipe the surface clean with a damp brush, then seal with matt varnish so it cannot wash out.

guides.title: Gold from a tint over silver
guides.summary: Brush a yellow or ochre one-coat paint over silver to get shaded gold, then dry brush silver to finish both metals.
body: Base the area in silver or gunmetal. A heavy silver dry brush over black also works and leaves dark recesses. Do every metal this way, including the parts meant to be gold.

Brush a yellow or ochre contrast-style paint over the parts that should be gold. The metal shines through and the tint shades the recesses. Pick a golden yellow; very pale yellows look like toy plastic. Test the mix on a silver patch on your palette first.

For a duller, deeper gold, add a little brown ink to the yellow. Where it sits over dark shading it turns slightly green, which adds depth. A second coat gives a stronger, richer colour; leave some of the pure yellow showing so it still reads as gold.
Other warm metals work the same way: a brown wash over silver reads as bronze, and a warm flesh-toned wash as brass.
Tidy slips with silver, or wash the silver areas last with a cool dark wash, which covers any gold that strayed.
Finish with one soft dry brush of bright silver over everything. It highlights the silver and the gold in the same pass. For brighter gold edges, mix a little of the yellow into the silver.
Optional: glaze a thin red brown over the gold for a warmer glow, add black only in the deepest recesses, and stain alternate rows of scale or chain a slightly different yellow.

guides.title: Graphic, box-art style
guides.summary: Bold light and shadow, smooth gradients on panels and crisp edge lines give a clean, illustrated look.
body: Prime black, even under areas that will end up white. It gives deep shadows to work up from.

Choose the focal point first and put the strongest contrast and detail there. Decide where the light falls and be braver with contrast than feels natural; timid contrast reads as flat from arm's length.
On chunky, awkward shapes, mark the light and dark blocks first, then blend between them. On large flat panels, blend a smooth gradient from dark to light.
Finish every panel with a neat, thin edge highlight to sharpen the shape. Paint small details such as eyes, trim and markings neatly and completely; the style favours clarity over grit.

Choose colours for impact rather than realism. Metal can skip metallic paint: four flat tones from lit to deep shadow, leaning on blue greys, blues and purples rather than neutral grey. Gold can be a warm light brown over a cool grey shadow.

Invert the light in places: a dark colour on a lit surface with light edges makes small details such as dials stand out. Use off-white or bone rather than pure white for bright symbols, and a duller tone on far-off parts suggests distance.
Theme and finish the base to match the model, so the whole piece reads as one clean picture.

guides.title: Painting green skin
guides.summary: Green skin can be washed down from a bright base or layered up from a dark one; both work with a warm or pink touch.
body: Bright greens cover badly over black. For a vivid skin, start over white or light grey, and mix a little high-coverage green into the bright one for near one-coat cover.

Light method: wash the base with a green shade cut half and half with medium, dab extra into the deepest recesses, then repaint the base mix on the upper surfaces. Too much wash is fixed the same way.

Dark method: over black, base two coats of a drab dark green. Highlight with a paler, slightly cool mix over about 80 percent of the area, leaving the recesses, then smaller passes on the tops only. Quicker: a dark green one-coat paint over grey primer, a green wash to even out blotches, then bright green on brows, knuckles and sinews.

For a smoother shade, mix a green shade into the base a little at a time and push each darker mix further into the muscle recesses: under arms, inner neck, between fingers. Yellowish greens blend easily; minty, white-heavy greens show every layer line.

For a smoother shade, mix a green shade into the base a little at a time and push each darker mix further into the muscle recesses: under arms, inner neck, between fingers. Yellowish greens blend easily; minty, white-heavy greens show every layer line. If highlight steps look stark, glaze over them with about 4 parts medium to 1 part bright green.

Red sits opposite green and makes natural shadows. Drybrush dark red all over, then yellow from above, and cover with a see-through green. Or glaze very thin red into the deepest spots for a rich shadow line without black.
Dab a little pink on nose, lips, ears and knuckles and blend the edge with a pink and green mix so the skin looks alive. Skin with no red in it looks dead.
Avoid a toy-like pure bright green. A slightly drab or blue-tinted mid-tone looks more serious. Purple or red clothing beside green skin makes both look stronger.

guides.title: Colour over a greyscale underpainting
guides.summary: Set the light and shade in greys or white first, then add colour with one-coat paints, inks or glazes on top.
body: Paint the lighting before the colour. Over black primer, a white spray from about 45 degrees above, turning the model, puts light on the tops just like sunlight. Make it bolder than feels right, as colour on top cuts the contrast. Under warm schemes, brown to warm white works better than black to white.

No spray or airbrush? Drybrush instead: heavy mid grey all over leaving black in the recesses, then lighter grey, then a light white on corners and edges. Stroke top to bottom, and across any detail that runs up and down, which catches it far better. Stop before it looks fluffy.
For worn armour, sponge mid grey and then a little white over a dark brown base, pressing lighter near the edges. The brown left showing reads as chips.

Cover each area with a see-through colour: a contrast-style paint, an ink or a glaze. The light and dark underneath show through as shading. Pick saturated, lighter tints; dark shading-type paints pool and bury the highlights, and browns and other neutrals turn muddy. Pale, opaque one-coats hide the underpainting: use two coats at most and run a thin dark glaze back into the folds.

Work from the lightest colour to the darkest, since a dark paint covers a lighter slip but not the reverse. The dark recesses hide where colours meet and small slips, so this is more forgiving than tinting over a plain light primer.

A darker tone sprayed from below, such as a deep purple, gives richer shadows than black, and coloured underpaintings work too, such as mid green drybrushed over dark purple. Underpaint every model in a unit the same way, especially the white, or the colours will vary across the squad.

It suits textured models such as creatures, fur and cloth. Smooth armour panels show drybrush streaks, so add a few clean edge highlights after. A second drybrush and tint round evens patchy areas; beyond that, touch-ups pay better.

Common mistakes: greys too timid, so the model stays murky; too much white, so the shadows vanish; painting over a grey that is still wet. Keep white to the few highest points and let each stage dry. If the underpainting goes badly, it is early enough to prime over and start again.

guides.title: Grime with mixed washes
guides.summary: Work two or three washes into the same area without rinsing and let them blend unevenly for an aged, grimy look.
body: Put a dark brown, a black and a dark olive wash on the palette, each with a little water. Black and brown stirred together also make one oily, dirty shade on its own.
Work them into recesses and texture, switching between washes without rinsing the brush. The uneven mix is the point, as grime is never smooth.
Leave large flat panels mostly alone and let everything dry fully.
For stained cloth, dab small puddles of thin brown and leave them alone. They dry with darker rings at the edges that read as old water and mud marks. Keep them near the lower edges.
With an oil or enamel wash you can cover the whole part, let it go touch dry, then wipe the flat and raised areas with a sponge dampened in white spirit. The grime stays only in the gaps.
Clean up splashes on bright panels by drybrushing the base colour back in soft circles.
Finish with a downward drybrush of pale bone for faint streaks and dust.
Hold back. Too many stains make a model look dipped and flat. Put grime where the model would really pick it up and keep some clean, bright accents so it still reads.

guides.title: Grimy, dirty metal
guides.summary: Dull steel and iron down with heavy washes or ink, then bring the shine back only on edges and worn points.
body: Real worn metal has little shine. Only edges and rubbed points catch the light, so plan to add the brightness last.
Fast route: black primer, a steel spray or base, then slap on a dark brown-black wash strengthened with a little black. A brown wash first and black after keeps it looking old rather than just dark.

Machinery route: block in all the inner workings in silver with an old brush, flood a black wash, pick out caps and joints in brass, then give everything a dark brown wash. The brown looks like oil and ties the metals together. Drybrush silver again to finish.
Ink or drybrush route: cover a dark silver with a thick deep brown ink and re-edge the raised parts, or drybrush silver mixed with plenty of black and a touch of blue over a dark brown base.

For variety, dab small patches of different washes, such as sepia, green, blue or orange, and soften their edges with a clean damp brush. The mix looks used and lived in. Touch a thinned rust brown round bolts where water would sit.
For grease on joints and pistons, add a gritty texture paint for caked muck and a glossy dark oil or enamel for fresh grease. Glossy spots on a matt model catch the eye.
Finish with a bright silver on the flat of the brush along a few edges. Outline rivets with a black wash and dot each one with silver. Against the dull metal they read strongly.
Overdone it? A wet brush scrubs off pigment, and the base metal can be overbrushed back over too much wash.

guides.title: Gritty, dark weathered style
guides.summary: Muted colours, deep shadows, heavy wear and varied texture give a model a bleak, war-worn look.
body: Keep the palette muted and desaturated: dull greens, browns, greys and off-whites. Avoid bright, cheerful tones, and save one stronger colour for a small accent.
Push the contrast hard. Deep shadows with only a few sharp, bright highlights on the highest edges give drama and keep the model readable.
Start with a clean, fairly bright base colour, then knock it back with earthy layers, washes or glazes. It looks worn and dirty almost at once.
Add damage next: chips and scratches on armour, cuts on skin, frayed cloth. Then bring light back with a zenithal highlight and a few glazes to restore some colour.
Give each material its own texture. Drybrush rough cloth and stone, keep metal dull with bright edges, and let leather keep a slight sheen.
Oil washes in the recesses give rich, deep shadow. One-coat contrast-style paints over a light undercoat build colour and shading quickly.
Finish with weathering powders, grime, mud and gore. Reference photos show where dirt and blood really gather: low down, in folds and round joints.
Think about the story. Place every mark for a reason, so the model looks like it has survived something harsh rather than being dirty evenly all over.

guides.title: Where hair meets skin
guides.summary: Separate hair from skin with each area's own darkest tone, not a black line, so the face is framed softly.
body: A hard black line where hair meets skin looks drawn on.
Run the darkest skin shade around the face where it meets the hair, as part of the face shading.
On the hair side, use the darkest hair shade, for example the hair colour with a touch of black.
The two dark tones together give a soft, natural break between the areas. A thin glaze of the hair colour on the skin right at the hairline softens it further.
For bright or dyed hair, base it in a neutral grey brown first and streak the bright colour over loosely. The neutral tone showing through keeps it from looking like a wig.
Keep the hairline dark even on fair hair. It frames the face, and the top of the head takes the strongest hair highlights.

guides.title: Hairspray and scratch-through chipping
guides.summary: Paint a top colour over a resist such as hairspray or chipping fluid, then scrub or scratch it back to reveal real chips.
body: Paint the colour you want revealed first, such as a dark dull brown or a dull silver, with some orange-brown stippled in for rust.

Seal the base with a thin satin varnish so scrubbing later cannot strip it. Then add hairspray or chipping medium in two thin, even coats, letting the first dry. Keep it out of the recesses: pools lift as big flakes. Sprinkle coarse salt on while wet for larger patches.
Gloss or satin varnish over the base also works as a resist. The top colour then wears off it when you rub edges with a damp cotton bud, rubbing from the front as well as along the edge.
Water based medium can bead on shiny metallics. Latex masking fluid dabbed on with a sponge avoids that; rub it off with an eraser once the top coat is dry.

Paint the top colour soon after the resist dries, in thin coats, ideally with an airbrush. Keep any highlights to one thin coat. After about 20 minutes, wet a small area and scrub with a damp old brush or a toothpick. The longer you wait, the smaller and harder the chips; leave it for days and little will lift.
Without a resist, scratch fully dry paint with a hobby knife tip or sandpaper: fine for grazes, coarse for long scratches, the knife for nicks. Always cut away from your hand.
Go slowly and check often. Keep chips small at this scale and place them where wear makes sense: edges, fronts, panel bottoms.

If huge flakes lift, the resist pooled. If nothing lifts, the top coat is too thick or you waited too long. If too much comes off, use less water and a lighter touch. Test on scrap first, and for full control sponge or paint the chips instead.

guides.title: Hazard stripes
guides.summary: Paint yellow first and black over it, using tape or pencil as a guide, and keep every stripe the same width and angle.
body: Put stripes where moving parts would be dangerous: joints, pistons, ramps, weapon housings. Paint the whole band yellow first over a white or mid grey undercoat. Black covers yellow in one coat; yellow over black takes many.

If the stripes must go over black, a dull orange ochre covers far better than a bright yellow and still reads as yellow next to the black. Outline each ochre stripe with a golden yellow to brighten it.

Mark out the stripes. Pencil lines drawn on the dry yellow are quickest, but draw them before any gloss or glaze, which pencil will not mark. Thin masking tape at about 45 degrees gives straighter lines; for even gaps, lay three strips side by side and pull out the middle one.
Against tape, dab or sponge the black on with little paint so it does not creep underneath. Fill with dark grey first and then black if you want a slight lift on the stripes.

Freehand, pick one angle that suits your painting hand and use a thin, free-flowing black; thick paint drags and leaves ragged edges. Paint the middle of each stripe and widen it, or paint its two edges as fine lines and fill between. Make stripes about as wide as the gaps, and fix slips by cutting back in with yellow.

Taped method for terrain: over black, lay evenly spaced tape strips, sponge yellow between them, peel once dry, then sponge a little black back on for wear. On tiny parts, striped transfers over gloss varnish are far easier than masking.
On cables, plot thin slanted stripes faintly with half-thinned black so they spiral round, then thicken them. One thin white stroke along each cable over both colours makes it look glossy.

Judge the stripes only once the trim around them is painted. Shade the yellow with a thin orange-brown and leave small black areas unhighlighted. Add a few chips across the edges, dark rust on the yellow and grey on the black: they hide wobbles and make the stripes look used.

guides.title: Highlight before or after the wash
guides.summary: Highlight before a wash for softer, smoother transitions, or after it for sharper, stronger contrast.
body: A wash tones down everything it touches, highlights included.

Highlight first and wash over the top when you want soft, smooth transitions and a unified look. You can push these highlights brighter than looks right on purpose; the wash pulls the harsh spots back into the rest.
Wash first and highlight after when you want crisp, strong contrast.
The same choice applies to drybrushing. Wash then drybrush keeps raised areas bright and the surface dry and dusty. Drybrush then wash darkens and ties all the colours together.
A middle route: wash part way through, before the last one or two drybrush or highlight passes. Wash marks form on raised areas, and those final passes cover them.
Either way, you will often need to bring back the brightest edges and points after the wash.

If the wash buried the highlights, it was too strong or too thick. Thin it, keep it to recesses and panel joins, and once fully dry lay the base colour or highlight back over the raised areas. Losing some highlight this way is normal.

guides.title: Highlighting rounded and organic shapes
guides.summary: Rounded parts and organic shells have no sharp edge, so glaze soft highlights onto the highest part of the curve.
body: Curved parts like rounded helmets, shells, bellies and orbs have no edge to catch a line. Edge highlights look odd on them, so build a gradient instead.

Thin the highlight colour heavily and build it on the highest part of the curve, each stage over a smaller area. Finish with one small, bright highlight at the very top. Glaze a little of the mid colour around the outside to smooth the join.
Let strokes follow the form, moving in curves on a round shape. Start each stroke in the shadow and end it in the light: the brush leaves most of its pigment where the stroke ends.

On a cylinder, such as a leg plate, keep a bright band down the length and darken both sides. On a round helmet, paint each lighter layer as a smaller circle centred on the dome, then pull the light out toward the brim and run the side of the brush along the rim. A dome can also take two lights, front and back, with a shadow band between.
On a shiny or glowing sphere, the brightest light sits as a band near the edge, so build a halo round the side and keep the middle a little darker.
On creature shells, break the highlight into short, choppy strokes along ridges and upper edges. Smooth continuous lines look machined. Touch the brightest point with a pale bone.

Method choice: drybrushing smooth curves is quick but tends to look streaky and chalky, layering in bands is slow and can leave steps, and an airbrush gives the smoothest fade but needs masking. Glazing sits between them and needs no mixing.

guides.title: Highlighting metallic paint
guides.summary: On metal, put bright silver only where the light really catches instead of edge highlighting every plate.
body: Start dark. Mix silver with black, a deep blue or green for cold steel, or a red brown for warmer steel. Each step then takes more silver, so it gets lighter and shinier at once.
After the wash, dab the base metal, such as a gunmetal, back onto the raised curves of each plate.

Turn the part under your lamp: the metallic already shows where light catches. Stab a bright silver just there, such as the dome of a helmet or the top of a shoulder plate. A big jump from base to highlight reads shinier than many close steps. For gold, highlight with gold mixed with a little silver.
Metallics blend poorly. Place clean highlight shapes and soften a hard edge with small scratches, or stipple an almost dry bright silver down into the mid tone.

For sharp edges, drag the side of the brush tip along so the edge picks up paint by itself. A thin, runny, fine-pigment metallic gives the cleanest lines. Where there are many segments, edge only a few plates and rivets; lining every edge looks busy and less like metal.
On round studs and spheres, paint a round highlight near the top and a thin curved reflection along the bottom. On small chains, one dot on the top of each link is enough.
On blades, keep the highlight clean near the hilt and break it into small scratches further down for a used look.
Keep the very brightest silver to tiny dots and catches, so the metal does not pull the eye away from the face or focal point.

guides.title: Highlighting tiny repeating details
guides.summary: Keep highlights on vents, grilles and rivets very fine, or the whole area turns paler than the rest.
body: Vents, grilles and rows of small detail have many edges packed close together.
If each highlight is as wide as on a large panel, the area adds up to a much lighter patch than the rest of the model.
Use only the very tip of the brush and keep the lines as fine as you can. Skip some edges if needed.
Very small buttons and studs are not worth basing and washing. Leave them in the surrounding colour and dot each with bright metal at the end.
For a panel full of studs, paint slightly thinned colour over the lot, then wipe a fingertip across the stud tops while wet to show the metal underneath.

Slim, realistic sculpts have small clips, buckles and straps that vanish unless picked out, so expect more of this work than on chunky models. Make panel lines and highlights thinner to suit, and slow down.
Good light and magnification make a real difference on areas like this.

guides.title: Highlighting by basic shape
guides.summary: Treat each part as a sphere, box or cylinder and give its highlight the same shape as the surface it sits on.
body: Most parts are a sphere, a box or a cylinder, or a mix of them. Work out which shape each piece is, then apply that shape's rule.

Sphere, such as a head, knee guard or shoulder pad: a round highlight towards the top that softens into shadow, with a faint reflected light underneath. Paint it as a round patch, not a stripe. On a round helmet, paint rings that shrink toward the crown and add a line along the lower edge.
Box, such as straps, belts, holsters and gun parts: the face pointing up is brightest, the sides are midtone and the underside is darkest. Edge highlight the sharp edges.
Cylinder, such as arms and legs: run a stripe of light down the side facing the light and a weaker one down the opposite side, with shadow between.
On curved plates, if you are unsure, let the highlight follow the plate's edge and widen where the plate flares out.
Pull each stroke towards the spot you want brightest, so the paint thins out there and the transition looks smoother. On long plates, keep the last, brightest layers to the top part to draw the eye.

Repeated and textured parts follow the same idea. On a ribbed tube, run a thin light line along each ridge. On wood, use straight strokes of lighter brown along the grain. On webbing and pouches, light only the edges.

guides.title: How long a model takes to paint
guides.summary: Rough times per model: under an hour for quick tabletop, a few hours for good tabletop, days for display.
body: These are rough guides for one infantry-sized model, painted by someone with a little practice. Beginners often take twice as long, and that is normal.
Quick tabletop, with primer, one-coat paints or a wash and a few picked-out details: 20 to 60 minutes. Painted in a batch, it can drop to 15 to 30 minutes each.
Good tabletop, with base coats, a wash, one or two highlights, eyes and a finished base: about 2 to 4 hours. Leaders and heroes often take 4 to 8.
Display standard, with smooth blends, fine edge highlights, freehand and a detailed base: 10 to 30 hours or more. Busts and big display pieces can run past 40.
Big models scale up fast. A large monster or vehicle is often 3 to 6 times the time of an infantry model at the same standard, though drybrushing and an airbrush cut that down.
Drying time adds up. Washes, varnish and glue need time to set, so a model with 3 hours of work may take two or three evenings.
Time yourself on one model before planning a whole army. Multiply by the number of models, then decide where to save time and where to spend it.

guides.title: Improving step by step
guides.summary: Get better by picking one small, reachable goal per model, reviewing each finished piece and testing on spares.
body: Big skills like smooth blending are made of many smaller ones. Trying them all at once is overwhelming, and the newer you are, the smaller each goal should be. Painting the same way every time builds speed but little else.

Good first goals: darker shadows, brighter highlights, or dark lining between areas to push contrast. Later, try placing light and shadow yourself instead of leaving it to washes, which settle where gravity takes them rather than where light falls.

When a model is done, study it honestly for a few minutes and compare it with your last one, not with the best work online. Name what you do not like and its cause: flat look, shadows too light; chalky highlights, white added too fast.

Set one goal for the next model and write it down. Give that part extra time and keep the rest quick. If it makes another part slightly worse at first but the model looks better overall, that is progress.

Practise on spares. Paint just the skill on a leftover blade or head for 10 or 15 minutes, note what went wrong, and try twice more. You do not need to finish it. To break habits, set a limit: one brush, fewer than five colours, or greys only.

Paint often and paint many models. Short sessions most days build brush control faster than one long weekend, and most learning happens in base coats, blocking in and layering, not the final tiny details. Now and then, give one model far longer than usual and push every part.

Study finished work you admire and ask why it works; copying a scheme is a normal way to learn. Ask for feedback on one stated skill, from a better painter who can explain why, not friends who just agree. Painting with others, in person or at a class, speeds things up too.
Better gear will not fix technique. Get results with what you have, and upgrade a tool only when it is clearly holding you back.

guides.title: Inverted edge highlights
guides.summary: Highlight the lower lip of grooves and the inner edge beside trims to separate parts and liven up big plain panels.
body: Large plain plates, such as a chest or a shoulder pad, can look empty, and a dark panel next to a coloured trim can blur into it.
As well as the raised edges, paint a fine light line along the lower lip of grooves and indents, where light would catch the inner edge.
Do the same on the panel right under a trim. The area then reads brighter and more detailed.
Beside a trim, the line can be a different colour. A thin warm brown along a black panel next to green trim adds a touch of colour and makes each part easier to read.
Keep these lines thinner and a little dimmer than the main edge highlights, so the raised edges still read first.

guides.title: Iridescent colour-shift effects
guides.summary: Light a wing, shell or scales in one hue from above and another from below for a shifting, pearly look.
body: Base coat in a strong colour that sits between the two shift colours, such as a rich purple between pink and blue. One coat of a well covering paint is enough.
From the top side, drybrush a pink-purple over everything you can see from that angle, then work small circles all over to pick out texture. Build up brighter pinks over smaller areas.
Clean the brush and work from the opposite direction: a deep blue, then turquoise, then turquoise mixed with a pale yellow, pushed into the shadow side.
Finish both colour zones with the same pale yellow. A shared final highlight ties the two colours together.
Keep the colours over big areas and the pale highlight small, or the effect goes washed out.
The same plan works on beetle shells, scales and feathers. Pick two neighbouring colours on the wheel and give each its own light direction.

guides.title: Broken, jagged edge highlights
guides.summary: Tap the edge highlight on in short broken strokes so armour looks chipped and battered instead of neatly lined.
body: Instead of pulling one clean line, lay the side of the brush on the edge and make small taps and flicks along it.
Use paint at normal layer consistency, neither thick nor watery.
It does not have to be neat. Gaps and uneven bits read as scratches, chips and wear, which suits battered armour.
It is quicker than a smooth line and more forgiving when your hand is unsteady.
Put most of it on upward facing edges and corners, where light and wear would hit first.
Using the side of the brush gives a more even width than the tip, for smooth edge lines as well.
For a chipped paint look, add small dark brown chips inside or beside some of the light marks and leave others light. A brighter off-white on a few of the cleanest edges finishes it.

guides.title: Knowing when to stop
guides.summary: Stop when the next step risks spoiling what already works, and judge from table distance whether more is worth it.
body: Do the steps with the biggest effect first: a good base, a shading wash, then raised areas re-layered. For troops that is already table ready; edge highlights are an extra.
Then look at the model at arm's length, not in a zoomed phone photo. Many fine details vanish at table distance, and in a unit the models are seen together.
Decide what the piece is for. For tabletop, get the colours down with clear contrast and move on. For display, keep going to the top of your current skill.
More layers are not always better. A clean base and one neat highlight often read better than several edges on every area. Hidden parts can stay dark and simple.
Edge highlights are low risk. Highlights in the middle of flat areas are high risk because mistakes show. Do risky steps with well thinned paint, so a slip only leaves part of a mistake.
If you are going round in circles correcting an area, it is done. Extra correction layers clog detail. On small things like eyes, get to acceptable and stop.
When the next step feels likely to go wrong, stop. You can always add more later. Leave small flaws, note them, and do better on the next model.
Save slow extras like warm glazes and colour variation for leaders and centrepieces.

guides.title: Bands of colour blended with glazes
guides.summary: Paint solid bands of each colour first, then soften the joins with glazes or well unloaded thin paint.
body: Blending with glazes alone over one base works but takes a great many layers. Laying down solid bands first is much faster.
Paint stripes of each colour in order, for example icy blue, light blue, turquoise and dark blue down a blade. The smaller the step between bands, the easier they blend.
For layered highlights, pull each stroke towards where the light should be, as paint builds up most where a stroke ends. Going a little brighter than you want is fine; the glazes will pull it back.

Glaze the next colour, or a half and half mix of the two bands thinned until see-through, over the line between them. Use a feathering stroke that lifts off in the middle of the join. Touch the brush on a paper towel first so the thin paint does not flood.
Run a clean damp brush along the edge of the glaze so it leaves no hard line.

Repeat, narrowing the glazed strip each time, until the join is smooth, then move to the next pair. Five to eight passes over a hard step is normal. Let each pass dry; working into a wet glaze turns it muddy.
Glaze dark colours and layer light ones. Dark mixes thin into smooth glazes, while pale mixes full of white turn chalky when thinned that far.
Alternative: paint a new layer solid, then water the same colour down, wick it well and drag from the darker area towards the layer, pressing harder at the end.

guides.title: Chips that show layers
guides.summary: Make deep chips read as layers of paint, primer or bare metal by putting a dark or metal centre inside a paler ring.
body: Mix a pale version of the armour colour, about half base and half white, or use a sand or beige. Sponge it on edges and where damage makes sense, starting on the back in case the sponge is overloaded. Put extra where highlights would fall so the damage doubles as a highlight. On black parts, chip with grey instead.

Enlarge some chips with a brush, vary their shapes and reach spots the sponge cannot. Many painters chip armour with the brush alone, dragging its side along plate edges, and keep the sponge for heavy wear such as exhausts. Stop once you are happy, as chips are hard to undo.

With a small stiff brush, fill the middle of some pale chips with a dark grey, dark brown or a red primer colour, smaller so a pale rim shows. The rim reads as primer and the dark centre as bare material. An orange-brown centre reads as rust and shows better than dark brown on black.
For a dent or gouge, paint a fairly straight light line first, then a bigger, uneven dark shape just above it. That is easier than tracing a light edge under a dark blob.
Dot a thin line of the armour highlight along the lower edge of some bigger chips, not all, so they look recessed at different depths.
For paint knocked back to metal, dot dark steel along the chip edge and bright silver only at the hardest point of impact.
On vehicles, think about the story: legs on a walker, around the tracks on a tank. Keep scratches fine and few; they keep the model in scale.
Test chip colours on a hidden part first. A colour too close to the base coat looks dull, and a touch of warmth often helps.

guides.title: Layering
guides.summary: Stack lighter, smaller and thinner layers over a base coat to build highlights, with no washes or blending needed.
body: Start with a well covering base coat in a shadow tone darker than the main colour. If you base in the main colour and only work upward, the base becomes the shadow and the model looks pale. Spread it well so detail is not hidden.
Paint the midtone over about 90 percent of the area, shifted to the top of each form, leaving thin dark lines between shapes.
Next layer about 30 percent, then about 10 percent. Cover more than you think: beginners often shrink each step too fast. Treat a limb as a tube and run the highlight along its top.

Thin later layers until slightly see-through, about one part water to one of paint, and touch the brush on a towel first. They blend better and are easier to correct. Lay the paint and leave it: brushing over paint that has started to dry leaves stroke marks. Paint dries darker, so judge once dry.

Going for contrast first is fine; visible steps can be glazed later. If you cannot see where a new layer goes, it is not bright enough. Layering alone is enough to paint well, so learn it before other blends.

Building a bright colour from black, start with a deep in-between tone, such as dark burgundy before red. Lighten with ivory or a pale yellow rather than pure white, which makes colours chalky and leaves hard steps. If you do use white, thin more and take more, smaller steps.

Where a panel line crosses a plate, skim the side of a lightly loaded brush over it. The bristles bridge the groove and the line stays dark. On big areas like cloaks, a large brush and confident strokes cover most steps.
Finish with a few very thin glazes over any rough steps. Push the brightest points close to white, as off-white looks darker on the model than on the palette, and save them for small focal areas.

guides.title: Sketching light and volume first
guides.summary: Block in the darkest and lightest tones and the light direction quickly, then refine between them.
body: Light and shape matter more than small details, so get them down first. If the light is placed wrongly or the colours are dull, no amount of careful refining will save the model.

With a large brush and well covering paint over a midtone base, block in each volume: darker away from the light, brighter where it hits. Work from the largest areas to the smallest. Treat a busy part, such as an ornate blade, as one simple shape and paint its small details back in later.

Set the deepest shadow and brightest highlight early. One way is to paint the top highlight first over everywhere the light touches, then lay mid tones and shadows over it. Everything else is then quicker to fill in.

With an airbrush, spray white ink or each light colour over black from the light's direction. A light pass gives grey and more passes give white, and the sprayed zones mark where later highlights belong.
Exaggerate colour at this stage if you like. Deep reds, magentas and blues mixed wet make a rich dark without black, and become undertones later.

Use the sketch to test ideas fast, such as how bright a red should be or where reflections go. A second rough pass lets you move lights that looked wrong. Changing your mind now costs minutes, not a repaint.

Rough does not mean random. Each stroke still has a purpose. Push contrast further than real life, since small figures lose it at a distance, but do not run the full light range round every muscle; the figure darkens away from the light. Skip the sketch for things you already know how to paint.

To refine, mix half steps between your sketch colours and fill the gaps, then glaze thin dark down into the shadows and thin light up onto the highlights. Pale colours look brighter wet, so judge each pass once dry.

guides.title: Light bands and spots on armour
guides.summary: Glaze bands of light down curved plates and soft spots on round ones so dark or shiny armour shows its shape.
body: Edge highlights alone leave a dark curved plate looking flat. A band of light down the curve shows its shape and makes it look glossy.

With each highlight colour, glaze a thin stripe down the curve, such as down a shin and onto the foot. For smoother, more reflective plates, block the bands in thickly and wet blend their borders, keeping a gradient of mixed steps on the palette.
Make the bands different sizes and let one dominate. Two equal highlights, equally spaced, look fake. Leave the darkest colour between them as the deepest shadow.
On round parts like knee and shoulder pads, place thin paint, draw it towards the centre and lift off so it gathers in the middle. Repeat once dry.
Light every band and spot from the same direction.
Last, place a few tiny dots of a very pale colour on the sharpest corners and inside the light spots. Too many make the model hard to read.
These spots suggest a shiny surface. Leave them off if you want matt armour.

guides.title: Loaded brush blending
guides.summary: Carry a thin colour in the brush and a thick one on the tip to blend a gradient in a single stroke.
body: Load the brush with your thinned main colour, usually the darker one, and take most of it off on a paper towel. Keep the load modest: an overloaded brush floods the surface and the colours merge.
Touch just the very tip into a thicker highlight colour.
Place the tip on the brightest point and drag or push the stroke away from it. The main colour takes over as you go and the blend happens on the model.
Use one smooth pass, then reload and repeat. Scrubbing back and forth leaves jagged lines. A thin glaze over the join afterwards makes it smoother.

Getting the right amount on the tip is the hard part. Practise on simple flat areas such as blades, or on busts, and expect messy results and touch-ups while learning. Once you have the feel, it is handy in small areas.
You can also tip with a darker colour and work up from the shadows, or use two colours of similar brightness. Finish with very thin filters in the shadows for variety.
Contrast between the two colours matters more than the exact colours. A wet palette keeps both at the right consistency; on a dry palette, work fast.

guides.title: Maggots and grubs
guides.summary: Paint maggots in two colours, highlight along the ridges and finish all with one pale highlight so they sit together.
body: Maggots come in several colours. Two shades together look more natural than one uniform blob.
Leave a purple shade between them from earlier shading, then paint some a creamy sand and others a pink.
Highlight along the sculpted ridges: pale yellow on the cream ones, pink mixed with pale flesh on the pink ones.
Give all of them the same final pale flesh highlight on top.
For worm-like tentacles, paint and highlight them pale flesh, then stain the base half with a slightly thinned pink one-coat paint and feather its edge with a damp brush so it fades out.
Keep them low-key so they do not pull attention from the face.

guides.title: Masking stripes and shapes
guides.summary: Use tape or a stuck-on token as a mask for straight stripes, halves and circles, then hide any bleed as chips.
body: Use thin, low-tack hobby masking tape; household tape is stiff, lets paint creep under and can rip paint off. Let the paint underneath cure fully and test a hidden spot first, as tape lifts paint that has not gripped. Stick the tape to cloth first to reduce its tack, and a thin coat of varnish underneath helps it peel cleanly.

Lay one strip, then butt a second against it as a spacer so the edges of the stripe stay parallel. Line tape up with panel edges and use tape widths as a ruler. Run a fingernail along the edges and into recesses, and cut the tape rather than tearing it on the model.
Brush only along the gap, never across the tape edge, or dab the paint on with a small sponge. Thin runny paint creeps under tape more easily.
Peel when the paint is touch dry. Fully dry paint can lift with the tape; wet paint smears. Dry with air, not a hair dryer, as heat softens the tape's glue.

For circles, stick a round token or coin on with reusable putty and sponge around it, or cut a hole in a piece of tape. For custom shapes, tape a printed outline over masking tape and cut round it with a sharp knife. Masks work best on flat surfaces.
Some bleed is normal. Over gloss, wipe it off with a damp brush while fresh. Otherwise tidy it with the base colour, or sponge the base colour along the edge so it reads as chips.
Dry brush lightly over the finished stripe so it matches the rest of the surface.

For a light shape on a dark ground, such as a cross or pale stripes, paint the light colour over the whole area first, seal it, tape the shape, then paint the dark around it. Light under dark covers far better than the reverse.

guides.title: Unit numbers and matching squad markings
guides.summary: Plan markings for the whole squad at once, mark the spot and paint each step on every model in turn.
body: Decide the system first: what goes where, and what changes from model to model. Write it down, such as a number on the left shoulder and a stripe on the leader's helmet.
Mark the same spot on every model with a light pencil dot or a dot of thinned paint, so numbers do not wander.
Paint markings as a batch. Do the base shape on every model, then the outline, then the highlight, so colours and line weight match.
For numbers, build each digit from plain straight strokes, then tidy the edges with the background colour. Keep every digit the same height and width.
Mix plenty of each marking colour and keep it in a sealed dropper bottle or pot, so models painted later still match.
Stencils, transfers and paint markers help with repeated shapes. Even with transfers, a thin coat over them in the same colours ties them together.
Line the squad up side by side before varnish. Fix any that stand out; consistency reads better than detail.

guides.title: Painting membrane wings
guides.summary: Paint bat and dragon wing skin with streaks along the stretch, a soft gradient to the centre and dark lined veins.
body: Base the membrane neatly up to the wing bones. Thin the paint and expect two coats over black. Pull every stroke the way the skin hangs, usually from the bones downwards; the faint streaks read as stretched skin.
Drybrush route: drybrush the skin tone softly so it fades out towards the bones, work more paint into the middle of each panel, then a paler tone over the centres only.

Stipple route: use a small stiff round brush wiped about twice as dry as for drybrushing. Stab the brightest spot first and spread outwards as the brush empties, each lighter step covering less. It gives a leathery texture with no careful blending.
Run the shadow colour, undiluted, into the corners where membrane meets bone and over the veins, so they are outlined again after the highlights.

To tint the skin, mix a wash about half and half with a one-coat paint medium. It stains flat areas instead of running into recesses. Paint it on the top of each panel and pull it down with a damp brush so it fades. Thinned black over a red drybrush gives dark red skin.
On dark wings, wash one panel at a time so nothing pools, and fix any uneven sheen with a very light drybrush of the base. Drybrush across ridges, never along them.
Edge torn ends and a little either side of each rib with a light colour, keeping it sparse. Finish with one thin glaze over the whole wing to tie it together.

For torn wings, mark the remaining skin first in a light colour, which is easy to correct, then paint the exposed flesh behind in a see-through warm brown so the texture shows. Shade the border so the torn edge reads.

guides.title: Paint from metal pigment powder
guides.summary: Mix loose metal powder into gloss medium or ink to make very smooth, shiny metallics with matching shades.
body: Loose metal pigment powder stirred into a gloss medium or gloss varnish makes your own metallic paint. It covers in one smooth coat, even over white, and is tough once dry.
Mix very thoroughly so no dry powder is left, and make small amounts at a time.
For a shade, mix the powder with plenty of brown ink. It turns into a thin, deep brown gold that blends into the base gold.
For a highlight, add a few drops of a bright silver metallic paint. It brightens the gold without turning it silver.
Real metal powder is not safe to swallow or breathe. Never point the brush with your lips, mix gently so it does not puff into the air, and wash your hands after.

guides.title: Fast armour from a metal primer
guides.summary: Spray a metallic primer, block in other colours, then shade the whole model at once with a wash or dark oil.
body: When most of the model is armour, prime it in the armour metal: a mid silver, neither too dark nor too bright, or a gold. The metal is then done in one step.

Block in the non-metal parts such as cloth, leather and handles, and pick out trim in a second metal: bronze trim on silver, steel on gold. For quick brass, brush a yellow-brown one-coat paint over finished silver.

Quick acrylic route: wash the whole model in a dark grey or brown shade, or a black one-coat paint cut with its medium, soaking up pools with a dry brush. A purple wash gives gold a rich, warm depth. The wash also takes the slick feel off sprayed metal so later coats grip.
Then one very light drybrush of bright silver highlights both metals at once.
Oil route: gloss varnish the whole model so the wash runs off flat areas and collects in recesses. A second gloss coat helps if a grainy primer traps the wash.

Mix a near black oil paint with odourless thinner and dissolve it fully so no blobs land on the model. Leaving the oil paint on cardboard for a while first draws out some oil and helps it cure faster.
Slap it on everywhere with an old brush. Mess is fine. Leave it to cure overnight, then clean off the flats if needed.
For leaders, glaze thinned base metal back over raised areas and dot bright metal on rivets. With an airbrush, a dark metal all over and a lighter tinted metal from above does the same job.

guides.title: Painting sharp metallic blades
guides.summary: Keep the flat of a metal blade darker and the cutting edge brighter, then add fine edge lines so it looks honed.
body: Base the blade in a dark silver with long smooth strokes from hilt to tip, then wash it black, working the wash into any sculpted nicks. A second wash on the flat once dry gives deeper, darker reflections.
Re-layer a mid silver thinly along the cutting edge bevel only, not across the flat. The bright strip beside the darker flat reads as a sharpened edge.
Glaze a bright silver near the tip in two or three thin coats, each covering less, so the tip ends up brightest.
Edge the cutting edge with the side of the brush, then the back edges. Turn the model and pull a fine line down the central ridge or the line where the two tones meet, keeping to the brighter side.
Leave sculpted scratches dark and add a thin bright line along one side of each, so they read as nicks in the metal.

guides.title: Painting metallic trim
guides.summary: Block in trim neatly, wash it in light level coats, and highlight it fast with the side of the brush.
body: Prime black so slips onto the armour are easy to cover. Use a mid size brush with a good point, light pressure, and two thin coats rather than one heavy one.

Choose the order that saves fiddly work. Painting a flat colour up to a raised edge is easier than painting a neat metal line along it. So on ornate armour, rough in the trim first, wash it, change your water to clear metal flakes, then fill the panels. Or prime in the trim metal, wash and dry brush it, then fill the panels.
On speed models, skip trim in deep shadow and overbrush detailed areas so paint stays on the raised parts.

Wash with the area held level so it does not run, and use two light coats rather than one heavy one, which leaves tide marks. Dab the wash into the middle of each section and round rivets; it pulls back from the edges, which stay bright like a free highlight.

Highlight by dragging the side of a lightly loaded brush along the trim at about 45 degrees with bright silver or gold. It catches only the edges, almost like a dry brush. Inner edges need the tip pulled down them with the model held steady.
Block in all gold and silver first, wash them together, then highlight each metal separately. If a metal still looks flat, push a deeper shade into its recesses and a brighter line on its edges.
Wipe a big slip away while wet with a clean damp brush. Once dry, cover plate colour on tinted trim with the metal underneath, then re-tint it.
For a dark, menacing look, use a dark iron trim edged in mid silver, with bright silver only on the sharpest corners and rivets.

guides.title: Midtones make blending easier
guides.summary: Lay a few in-between colours before you blend, and use mid-value highlights, which flow better than whites.
body: Mix two colours on the palette into a few in-between steps and paint them on the model side by side before blending. Keep these mixes close to undiluted so they cover; the width of each band sets how gradual the change is.

Whether you then wet blend or glaze, the smaller the gap between neighbouring colours, the easier the blend. If two colours are too far apart, add a middle colour, such as an orange between a pale skin and a red.
More steps do not make painting slower. Mix small amounts on the brush tip, and clean the brush only lightly between steps, as a little of the last colour helps the blend.
Decide how much area each tone covers before you start, block each straight into place, then blend only the borders. Planning this often halves the time spent smoothing.
If one colour overpowers the other while wet blending, add a touch more of the weaker one while it is still wet.
Whites and near whites tend to be thick, chalky and hard to blend. Mid-value colours such as turquoise, orange or ochre are usually more transparent and flow better.
If smooth highlights keep failing, darken the whole scheme and use one of those colours as the top highlight. Choose it to match a lighting idea such as moonlight or torchlight.
For light schemes, start from a lighter base near the main colour. Fewer layers means less paint texture and a smoother finish.

guides.title: Molten and heated metal
guides.summary: Glaze from red through orange and yellow to white at the hottest point, with patchy cooler browns at the edges.
body: Plan the heat first. Thick and central parts, like the spine of a blade or a gem or rune, stay hottest; thin outer edges cool first. Base coat bright red, or white if you will glaze see-through colours over it.

Thin orange until very see-through and glaze it on in many coats, each covering a little less and stopping short of the tip so red stays at the coolest end. A slow, wide orange zone looks more believable than a quick jump from yellow to red.

Glaze yellow mixes nearer the hot point, keeping them off the cutting edges. Finish with pale yellow and then white right on the hottest spot. Keep white and yellow small; too much looks less hot. Link two stray hot spots into one glow.
Ease any harsh step with a red-orange glaze. A wet palette keeps every colour usable for these fixes.

Real heat is uneven. Use specks and dots rather than a perfect gradient, and drop a few darker dabs inside lighter areas. For flakes of scale, keep the dividing lines very fine and the shapes random; heavy dark outlines look like crazy paving.
For cooler metal, dot a red brown roughly along the edges and the far end of the ridge, then a darker brown in fewer places. Use black only with the brush almost dry.
For glowing cracks, run thinned white into the cracks and yellow over it, paint the raised parts inside them orange then red, and glaze a deep red around each crack.
Expect to go back and forth, and check photos of hot metal halfway through. Stop early; this is far easier to add to than to take away.

guides.title: Moss and damp rot on models
guides.summary: Blotch thin dark green around joints and fittings, brighten the centres with yellow-green and stipple a little texture.
body: Moss grows where water sits and light is low: round metal fittings and joints, at the bottom of uprights and on the shaded side. Photos of rotting wood show it is often a warm yellowish green.
Thin a mid dark green to a semi-wash and blob it on in chosen patches, especially round rivets and joints. Blotchy and uneven is right.
Wash a brighter yellow-green inside those patches, drawing the brush to the centre so the colour is strongest there.

Stipple a few tiny, slightly thicker dabs of the yellow-green inside the larger patches for a furry texture. Quick route: stipple bright yellow-green, drybrush lightly with off-white, then a dark brown wash cut with medium.

Enamel route: apply a dark green enamel wash neat where water collects, fade its edge with a brush dampened in odourless thinner, then add a brighter green only in the faded band. Use a worn synthetic brush, as the thinner ruins natural hair.
Pigment route: at this scale moss reads mostly as a tint. Dab green pigment into recesses and work most of it off, then add a touch of red, which turns a natural brown where it meets the green.
Textured moss effect paints work faster and brighter on a warmed, slightly wet, sealed surface. Thin coats dry lighter and thick blobs darker.
Enamels and pigments dry matt, so add gloss if you want it to look wet. Using greens already on the model ties the rot into the scheme.

guides.title: Veiny, bruised and mottled skin
guides.summary: Dab or glaze reds, purples and thin skin tones onto skin for veins, bruises and a natural blotchy texture.
body: Start on the underside or back, where mistakes are hidden.
Put a cool blue-green shade only into the deepest recesses, then small touches of pink-purple and red-brown at the bottoms of muscles.
For a vein, paint a wiggly tapered line across light and dark areas, then push a little shade along its underside.

For bruised, sickly skin, brush thinned purple and red washes onto pale skin one small area at a time, let them mix, then dab with a damp cotton bud for a blotchy texture. Purple and flesh one-coat paints mixed wet with a clear medium do the same on tentacles.

For sore, raw skin, cut a deep red wash with about the same amount of clear medium and paint it round boils, wounds, eyes and implants. Pull the edge out with a damp brush and build two or three thin coats. Stop before the skin turns too colourful.

For general mottling, thin a slightly lighter skin tone to a glaze and dab it on with the brush tip instead of stroking. For unnatural monster skin, mix two or three thinned colours wet patch by patch, then highlight each zone with a lighter version of its own colour.
For leathery texture, sponge faint pale dots over the skin, or flick tiny strokes all one way with a fine brush, then glaze the main skin colour over to knock it back.
An old brush that has lost its point is good for placing paint in lots of small spots. Pick out tendons last with very thin pale paint.

guides.title: Mottled, pitted armour
guides.summary: Blob thin washes on at random and let the tide marks dry, then dab lighter tones on top for a pitted, organic surface.
body: Base coat in several thin coats, for example a cool blue-green, then wash a very dark version over everything.
Thin the dark colour to a wash and blob it on at random with the brush tip. Let it dry with tide marks; they are the texture. Use bigger, heavier blobs low down and smaller, fewer ones up top.
Repeat with the dark colour in the shadowed areas only, then thinned black only in the lowest gaps.
It looks messy at this point. Keep going.
Dab the thinned base colour over the areas you would highlight, overlapping slightly into the dark. Follow with lighter, warmer mixes in smaller, more controlled dabs higher up.
Soften harsh dabs with a very thin glaze of the top colour, drawing the brush to the centre of rounded areas.

guides.title: Painting mouths, tongues and gums
guides.summary: Tint a pale grey base with a purple-pink one-coat paint, re-highlight and glaze back for a wet, fleshy mouth.
body: Base the tongue, gums and inside of the mouth in a light grey at the same time as the teeth. The pale base keeps the tint over it bright.
Paint a purple-pink one-coat paint over these areas. It settles into the texture and shades the flesh for you.
Highlight the tongue's tip, the ridges and any warts or bumps with the light grey again.
Glaze a thinned coat of the purple-pink back over the top so the highlights blend in without going too dark.
Keep the back of the throat darkest, with a touch of deep red or purple, so the mouth has depth. A dab of gloss varnish on the tongue makes it look wet.

Over a dark base instead: deep red on the tongue and inner mouth, bright pink on top leaving the red in the throat and at the edges, light pink on the top of the tongue, and one pale pink dot where it is wettest.

guides.title: Mud and splatter on vehicles
guides.summary: Pile textured mud on tracks and wheels, then flick dry light mud and wet dark mud, heaviest low down.
body: Mud goes on last, after washes, chips, streaks and pigments. Check it suits the setting: a desert vehicle should be dusty, not muddy. Use at least two related tones: a light one reads as dried mud, a dark one as wet mud.
For thick mud on tracks and wheels, mix a mud paste or pigment with a little fine sand and short grass fibres. Add the bits slowly, as too much texture looks out of scale.

Brush the lighter, dry mix on the upper running gear and mudguards with an old brush. Put a darker, coarser wet mix on the lower running gear, and pile most at the front and rear, where tracks throw it. Rework it while soft.

For splatter, mix pigments with thinner or a mud enamel until it flows like runny honey. Load a short, stiff brush, hold it close to the model and draw a toothpick or stick across the bristles. Practise the flick on paper first.
Thin mixes give small, flat spots, like splash from a ford. Thick mixes give lumpy road mud. Tilt the model on a sponge so the spots land at an angle, as they would from moving tracks.

Splatter the light, dry tone first over the lower hull, mudguards and wheels. A few minutes later add a darker tone over a smaller, lower area, leaving the first showing. Light then dark is enough for a quick job.
Lift spots that are too big or too high at once with a brush damp with thinner, stroking downward so they leave faint dirt streaks.
Finish with a glossy wet mud in track recesses and a few spots on the heavy mud for a fresh look, plus a few glossy oil stains. Leave it all to dry overnight.

guides.title: Drybrushing with several colours
guides.summary: Use three to five drybrush steps and keep colour in the highlights so drybrushing does not go grey and chalky.
body: Drybrushing straight up to pale bone or ivory makes an area look washed out and grey.

Start from an even two-coat base of a dark version of the colour, then drybrush a mid tone. Satin-finish paints drybrush better than very matt ones. On big monsters, prime in the skin colour and make the first pass with more paint left on the brush.

Lay the steps out in order on the palette and move to the next lighter colour without rinsing the brush. The leftover paint softens each step. Or keep one dry brush per colour, which saves cleaning and drying one brush between steps.

Each lighter colour covers less, staying on the highest folds and edges, with lighter pressure each time. Because the brush dilutes it, you can push the top highlight further, such as red up to orange and yellow. Aim the last passes from the light's direction.
Where a model has several colour zones, drybrush each with a lighter tone of its own colour, then a very light pale bone over everything to tie them together.

For more depth, smudge a deep blue or a weak black with an old soft brush into areas you want darker before the last pale pass. Anything that lands on raised parts gets covered, and the pale then looks brighter.

To smooth harsh steps, mix half and half of two colours on the brush, wipe most off and stroke over the join with a small soft brush. Going back with a darker mix works like a glaze. Weak colours such as orange need extra passes to show. If colours turn muddy, the last one was not dry.
If an area loses its colour, go back in with a more saturated drybrush.

guides.title: Muzzle flash and firing glow
guides.summary: Paint rough white rings round a barrel end and glaze warm inks over them for a firing glow.
body: Paint rough, scratchy concentric white circles around the end of each barrel.
Glaze yellow over them, then orange, using inks or thinned one-coat paints.
Keep the centre brightest and let the colour fade outward.
A small effect like this gives a large model a second point of interest.

On a clear plastic flash part, satin varnish it first and wash it orange all over. Glaze orange ink over the centre and tip, then yellow ink into the heart of the burst, and white ink mixed with gloss medium round the barrel.

guides.title: Non-metallic metal basics
guides.summary: Painted-on metal reads as metal through where you place the light and very strong contrast, not smooth blending.
body: Non-metallic metal means painting reflections with ordinary paint, so you decide where the shine goes. Metallic paint is quicker and suits gritty pieces and big batches; painted-on metal gives controllable reflections, matches the hand-painted light elsewhere and does not glare under lamps.
Four things sell it: strong contrast, the right shape for each part, how much of each surface is lit, and a weaker bounce light. Missing bounce light is the usual reason a first try looks flat.

Paint the rest of the model first if the metal will reflect it. Pick the main viewing angle: the shine sits where light bounces to the viewer, often on the front of a curve rather than its top. Like all painted light, it only works from one direction.

Over black, sketch hard patches of each value where light and shadow fall, without blending. A rule of thumb: put the highlight 30 to 45 degrees down from the top of each curve. Check the pattern in a black and white photo so colour does not fool you. Get the placement wrong and nothing else saves it.

Push contrast hard. Shiny metal jumps from near black to near white over a short distance, so put the darkest dark right against the brightest light. Keep little of the surface in the midtones, or it reads as stone.

Use about three highlight steps, each a big jump. A little black in each mix keeps steel from turning pale blue. If the colour of gold or copper washes out, sweep a thin, saturated filter of its hue over all but the brightest spots.

Smooth the joins, then highlight every edge, brightest on the most exposed ones. Add the cooler bounce light opposite the main light, separated by dark, and a few tiny near white dots. It looks wrong until these last steps.

Learn on a small part like a blade, helmet or gauntlet, where the light pattern is easy to see. Stop once it reads as metal: over-blending spoils more pieces than rough, high-contrast work, and a sketchy or stippled finish still looks like metal. A stylised glow is easier to learn than a chrome look that mirrors sky and ground.

guides.title: Painted metal in coloured light
guides.summary: Shift painted-on metal towards the light colour, such as blue-green, with a touch of pale yellow for the top glints.
body: Mix a dark blue-grey with the cold light colour for the shadows, then work up towards pure blue-green.
Shiny metal needs higher values than nearby matt cloth or leather, so add a little pale yellow for the top steps.
Keep about a fifth blue-green even in the brightest dots and edges so they still look cold.
Line the metal highlights up with the lit areas on armour and cloth nearby. Light falls in straight shafts.
On a side facing a second, warmer light, keep a little warmth in the metal to show both sources.

The same idea tints any painted metal. A dark brown in the shadow greys gives a warmer, earthy steel, and a little light blue glazed round the brightest areas suggests sky reflecting in it. Keep these tints subtle.

guides.title: Finishing painted metal: edges and glints
guides.summary: Graded edge highlights, a few white glints, gloss shadows and a dim bounce light finish non-metallic metal.
body: Edges are part of the contrast, not an extra: light gathers on the edges of shiny surfaces. Paint each edge one value step above the brightest part of the plate it sits on.

Grade them. Use the palest tone on upward facing edges and drop a step on downward ones. Lower on the model or in shadow, edges go no brighter than the midtone. On later passes, cover only the middle of each edge and fade towards the ends.

A pale tinted grey can stand in for white; next to the dark metal it still looks white. A quick edge pass partway through shows how the metal is coming along. A dark line round each metal part separates it cleanly from its neighbours.
Smooth the zones with glazes of three to five parts water to one of paint: the shadow tone first, then the midtone, then the high tone into the highlights.

For glints, stipple tiny dots of the palest tone on the brightest points, then a pinpoint of white in the centre of each, such as at the tip of a blade. Keep them few and irregular or they look planned.

Bounce light sits on the side facing the ground or a nearby surface. Build it like the main light but stop at the midtone. Ground light reads cool, so finish it pale blue; beside a coloured cloak, tint it that colour. Always keep a dark band between it and the main light.

Glaze thinned black ink into the darkest areas: gloss looks darker than matt and adds contrast. Thin tints, such as purple in the shadows and teal in the midtones, add colour. Restore any white highlights afterwards.
Expect it to look wrong in the middle stages. It usually comes together with these last steps.

guides.title: Non-metallic gold
guides.summary: Paint gold, bronze and copper with the same light rules as steel, but carry the colour in rich browns and ochres.
body: Place the light exactly as for steel, with big jumps in brightness.
Choose warm or cool gold before you start. Warm gold runs from a deep red brown through a warm yellow brown to warm yellow; cool gold runs from black through a muted yellow.

The midtones carry the colour, so work browns, ochres and olive greens through the middle while keeping shadows dark and reflections very light. Letting some tones lean slightly green and others slightly orange adds realism.

Warm yellow alone is rarely bright enough, so mix in a pale yellow for the final edges and dots. Gold blended straight from brown to white looks bland: glaze a yellow brown through the middle. If it turns too yellow, a very thin blue or green glaze before the last highlights calms it.

With each brighter mix, highlight the edges, then the main reflection, then the tips of details. Follow each curve with your strokes and use the side of the brush on long edges. Five or six layers usually do a helmet-sized area.

Add smaller secondary reflections on the far side, split from the main shine by a band of shadow, and glaze a thin orange over them. A small dark spot just before the end of a reflection makes it more interesting.

Quick version: base in a dirty yellow, which is yellow with a little brown and a touch of blue. Wash a thinned brown into the hollows, then add three ever-smaller highlights with white and a little blue mixed in, ending in white dots. Where the light sits matters more than how smooth it is.
For copper and bronze, mix steps from dark brown through orange to a pale peach. A few warm gold accents nearby make the copper read as a different metal.

guides.title: Reflections in painted metal
