guides.summary: Break painted metal into scattered patches, add weaker counter reflections and pick up colours from nearby objects.
body: Place reflections for the viewer. A shiny surface sends light towards the eye, so the main reflection sits more on the front of a shoulder pad than on its top. Parts of the same shape and angle get the same pattern. A black primed model under a lamp shows where reflections fall.

Mix seven or eight steps from your darkest to lightest paint and base in the darkest. From the mid-tone up, place each lighter step in several small, uneven patches, skipping spots. Think roller coaster, not smooth wave. A new light spot sits two or three steps above its surroundings.

At first it looks blotchy. Glaze or feather only the edges of each patch, getting thinner and more targeted as you go. Scatter a few small points of light near bright areas, never in the darkest zones.

On flat blades, avoid neat stripes or a checkerboard, and do not mirror one face on the other: they tilt differently, so make one brighter. Push the main band slightly off centre. Triangles of light work well on flats; fine hatched lines suggest brushed steel. On a round barrel, run a thin reflection down the middle.
Add counter reflections from bounced light: clearly dimmer than the main ones, with a band of shadow between them. Those on the underside stay much darker. Skip them on dull metal.

Shiny metal picks up nearby colours. Place a reflection only where a straight line runs from the object to the metal, start it darker than the object, and stop a step below its brightest tone. Reflected colours are greyer and duller than you expect.
Keep reflections soft and fuzzy unless it is chrome, and leave a thin dark line where an object touches the metal.

For a mirror finish, paint a bent scene over a white undercoat: a dark brown horizon line, ground below it in browns lightening to sand, and sky above in blue fading to near white just over the line. Faces tipped down show mostly ground, faces up mostly sky, and tubes carry the horizon along their length.

guides.title: Painted metal on flats, cylinders and domes
guides.summary: Break each part into a flat, cylinder or dome and place painted metal light and dark bands by that shape.
body: Ignore fine detail and ask what simple shape each part is. Arms and legs are mostly cylinders, chest plates are flats, shoulder pads and helmets are domes.

Cylinders show light, dark and light again, not one highlight shading across. On a lying tube, paint a sharp bright line about the middle with the darkest tone right below it and a soft reflected light on the underside. On an upright one, put a bright band in the middle, dark either side, and a lesser light near the far edge.

On a dome, put a bright hotspot slightly off centre facing the viewer, not on the very top, and fade it outwards. Add a smaller, weaker reflection on the opposite lower side. A rivet needs only a white dot on top and a touch of warm colour underneath.
Hollows work the other way: on a dished plate, the side nearest the light is in shadow and the shine appears on the far side.

Flats act like mirrors and are the hardest. Keep them mostly dark, or flip the neighbouring edge: shadow where it is bright, light where it is dark. A shaft of light down a flat usually spreads like a triangle, broad at one end and narrow at the other.

Avoid light and dark bands of equal width. Vary their size and taper them into triangles; on a cone, the bands narrow toward the point. On a flat round shape facing you, place opposing highlights like clock positions, such as 12 and 6. If two strong reflections would merge into one wide patch, keep the one that matters and tone down the other.
Darken the dark areas first, as early dark mixes look bright until the pale tones go on. Expect to resize the lit areas and glaze to smooth them. Planes facing down stay mostly dark.

guides.title: Non-metallic steel
guides.summary: Build painted-on steel from black and a muted blue, with smooth high-contrast bands and pure white reflections.
body: Look at photos of polished plate armour to see where light and dark fall on curved plates. Mix the whole ladder of greys before you start, with a tiny touch of blue to keep the steel apart from any rust.

Over black, paint the main reflections in several thin coats of white; starting from white is faster than building up to it. Or base in a dark blue-grey and trace the light in the palest colour. Squint: if the jump already reads as metal, the placement is right.
Cover the white areas with about nine parts white to one dark blue, and the rest with pure dark blue or a blue-grey and black mix.
Mix three midtones, roughly 7 to 3, 1 to 1 and 3 to 7, and paint them in bands across each join from lightest to darkest. Mix extra for fixes.

Glaze each midtone gently over its transitions until smooth. End dark glazes in the shadow and pale glazes on the highlight, since most pigment lands where a stroke ends. Follow curves with curved strokes and flat parts with straight ones.

Add counter reflections from the lightest midtone, leaving dark space between them and the main reflections. Finish with bright edges and pure white on the strongest reflections, and line panel edges dark. Make one key item, like a blade, shinier than the rest.
If flat grey looks like grey paint, glaze very thin blue, purple and green over it, with a thin blue-green on upward mid tones for sky. Fine straight striations suggest brushed steel.

Warmer option: purple-grey shadows and pale yellowish grey highlights. For old, worn steel, keep most of it in dark and mid greys with a few small, hard brights. Keep any rust in the dark parts, never over the white reflections.

guides.title: Blending with oil paints
guides.summary: Dab dark, mid and light oils where shadow and light fall, then pull them together with a clean, dry brush.
body: Base the area in acrylic, a little brighter than the mid tone you want. The acrylic only needs to be dry. A satin or gloss surface lets the oils move more freely.

Mix a spread of tones on a plain, non-absorbent palette and place them roughly on the model: the lightest where highlights go, then mid tones, then shadows opposite. Place all the dabs before blending; the highlights act as the guide. On a panel, a blob of mid tone with a dot of dark and a dot of light is enough.

Quick armour route: paint thinned dark oil over the panels and wipe most of it off with a sponge or cotton bud, leaving it in the shadows. The oily film left behind lets a light oil dabbed on the highlights blend easily. For big armies, stop after the wipe-back.

Blend with a separate brush that is completely dry, with no thinner and no paint in it. Fuzz over each border, pulling from light into dark or along the folds on cloth, and wipe the brush on a lint-free cloth after every stroke. Never rinse it in spirits mid-blend: the solvent dissolves the paint and the brush erases instead of blending.
Do not buff too far into a highlight or it dulls. If an area goes wrong, add a little of the colour it needs into the wet paint and smooth again, or wipe it with thinner and start that patch over.
Very strong pigments, such as intense blues and magentas, spread through everything they touch. Use them in tiny amounts, or pick a softer shadow colour for skin.

A large, cheap synthetic brush with a big belly smooths fastest, an angled flat is precise along edges, and a soft brush gives the softest blends. Mid-grade artist oils are much easier to work than very cheap ones.

Let an area set for 10 to 30 minutes until tacky before adding colour on top, and work elsewhere meanwhile; rushing makes oils muddy. Thicker oil sits over thinner, not the reverse. For a crisp edge, lay paint thickly along the line instead of blending it.

guides.title: Oil filters and dot filtering
guides.summary: Thin oil tints and dots of oil dragged together unify, warm, fade or dirty a model, and wipe off if you dislike them.
body: A filter is a very thin oil tint over a whole area. Thin a dark brown, or a red-brown to warm a cold scheme, with white spirit until very see-through but not separating. Leaving the oil on card for a while first draws out some oil.

Brush it on area by area rather than flooding it. It ties the colours together and tones down a scheme that looks too bright or clean. Use it slightly thicker in recesses as a wash, and once dry, repaint a few highlights on metal and leather to lift them.

For dot filtering, pick a few oils: a dark brown, a rust orange, an off white and one close to the main colour, so you have lighter, darker and warmer tones. Dot small spots at random over one panel. Go easy with white and pale colours, which are much stronger than the rest; black can overpower.

Blot almost all the spirit off a soft flat brush, so it leaves no streak on card, and pull it through the dots in one direction, usually top to bottom. Use many light strokes until they fade into soft streaks. On curves, turn the model so the streaks follow the curve.

For soft stains, dab small dots of thicker oil into a still-wet filter near hems and edges. They spread as if muddy or worn. For a local colour shift, put a little oil in one spot, such as a hatch corner, and blend its edge out until no line shows. A red brown on a sand panel reads as dirt.

Common problems: big blobs turn into heavy streaks, too much spirit turns dots into a pooling wash, and dirty spirit spreads a murky tint, so change it often. Do not scrub. Seal any scratch with a dab of gloss first, as spirit under acrylic can lift it.
Anything you dislike wipes away with clean spirit. Use a synthetic or old brush, as solvent damages natural hair. Let it dry overnight, then varnish satin or matt.

guides.title: Using oil paints on models
guides.summary: Oils go over dry acrylics; let them cure, seal with matte varnish, then go back in with acrylics and inks.
body: Oils work over acrylics that have dried for about half an hour. Thin them with odourless mineral spirits and clean the brush with spirits, not water. Dry acrylic is not harmed by them; damage comes from scrubbing, or from thin paint on unprimed plastic, so always prime.

A satin surface lets oils move freely, gloss helps washes run into recesses, and very matt surfaces grab the paint. Use a paper palette or baking parchment, which soaks up excess oil; no wet palette is needed. Stiff synthetic brushes and cosmetic sponges for wiping back cover most jobs. Work with a window open and low odour spirit.

Oils stay wet for hours, so you can blend and wipe them back long after acrylics would have dried, and a mistake resets with a brush of spirit. They suit smooth skin and highlights on purples and blues that go chalky with white. Keep crisp lines and texture for acrylics.

Oil work tones down what is underneath, so push the acrylic shading and highlights a little further beforehand. Keep the brush loaded with paint, not solvent: a wet brush dissolves the layer below. Change colour by wiping the brush on paper towel rather than rinsing it.

Let oils cure fully before painting or varnishing over them, usually a day or more. Thin layers dry faster than thick, and earth browns faster than greens and blues. Touch a hidden spot: if it is at all sticky, wait, as varnish over tacky oil can wrinkle or cloud. Keep a second project going while one cures, covered from dust.

Oils, reds especially, can dry shiny. Spray a matte varnish to seal and flatten them; it also gives acrylics something to grip. Varnish between oil stages so new oil work does not disturb the layer below.

Then add edge highlights with an opaque pale acrylic. Smoothed oils look a little desaturated, so glaze thinned inks over selected areas to bring colour back, and spend the extra time on the face and focal point.
Oils dull metallic shine slightly. Finish by touching pure gold or silver back onto the upward faces.

guides.title: Oil pin washes
guides.summary: Run thinned oil paint into recesses over a gloss coat so it flows along the lines and leaves the flats clean.
body: Gloss varnish the area first with an acrylic gloss. The wash then slides along the surface instead of soaking into the paint. Never put an oil wash over an enamel-based gloss: the spirit melts it and the wash fuses in for good.

Thin a near black oil, such as a dark brown or dark greenish grey, with odourless mineral spirits until it runs. Brown looks softer and dirtier than black, and a mid grey suits white armour. Better grade oils hold together when thinned this far; cheap ones go patchy and leave specks.
Mix only a little at a time in a clean well. The spirit evaporates fast and changes the mix, and old dried oil left in a pot can stain parts so they will not clean back.

Touch the brush tip into panel lines, round rivets and into recesses only. Capillary action carries it along the line. A slightly thicker mix stays put and stays dark. Too thin and it runs out of the lines and muddies the panels.

After 20 to 30 minutes, lift stray marks with a brush or cotton bud just damp with clean spirits. Wipe across the recess, not along it, so you do not drag the wash out, and keep each touch brief. If a pool has dried as a ring, buff it with small circles of a clean dry brush. Pull a few short streaks down for a weathered look.

Leave it overnight, then matte or satin varnish to kill the shine and give acrylics something to grip. Redraw any lines you lost with a fine brush and dark brown acrylic, and finish the last highlights by brush. If the wash dried bitty or too pale, give it a second pass before varnishing.

For quick verdigris, pin wash a thinned turquoise oil into cracks on bronze and brass. Keep dark washes off bright metal you want to stay shiny. Dark lines even work on white areas, where they read as cast shadow.

If the wash stained the paint, the surface was not sealed. If base colour comes off, you rubbed too long, as spirit dissolves acrylic. Even dried oil wash lifts with spirit and can be redone. Clean brushes straight after, as solvent wicks into the ferrule.

guides.title: Oil streaking and staining
guides.summary: Dab oil paint where grime gathers, pull it down into streaks with a damp brush, and layer rust tones on top.
body: Work over a gloss coat, which lets the oil move easily and protects the paint if you need to wipe back. Leave the oils on card for a while first to draw out excess oil so they dry faster and handle better.

Dab small amounts of neat oil on rivets, in recesses, under chips and damage, and along the tops of flat panels. A dark brown suits most areas; put a pale dust brown on dark panels, as light over dark and dark over light both show. Keep the brush fairly dry so each dab stays put.

Clean the brush, leave just a little spirit on it, then press gently on the dab and pull straight down. Shape each streak so it is dense at the top and fades out lower down. Press lightly, as heavy pressure can lift earlier oil or scuff the varnish.
Soften the edges and lift excess with a clean dry brush. Dab with a fat brush to break one big streak into many small ones. Expect to reshape a streak several times.

Wet oil looks stronger than it dries, so go a little heavier than seems right. A streak you dislike comes off with a cotton bud dipped in a little thinner. Wipe, do not scrub. Wait 30 to 60 minutes before adding a second layer.
Once dry, add an orange brown as fresher rust, especially round pistons, joints and moving parts where grease collects. It shows strongly over pale areas and transfers.
For sun faded paint, place small dots of oil a shade lighter and a shade darker than the panel, then pull them down with a just damp flat brush into soft vertical streaks.

For patchy discolouration, put a dab down and flood it with spirit so it spreads thinly and pools in recesses. For grime on flat tops, dab a little brown or red oil round hatches and corners and blend it out with a wetter brush in random motions.

guides.title: Subtractive oil painting
guides.summary: Coat a light-primed model in oils, then wipe paint off the raised areas so the bright primer shows as highlights.
body: Prime in a colour, then spray a lighter tone and finally white from above. These become your highlights.
Let the primer cure fully, ideally overnight, before any oils go on.
Thin the oils with odourless mineral spirits to about normal layer consistency.
Block in colours with a large brush. Where two colours meet, brush back and forth to blend while still wet.

Wipe paint off raised areas with a makeup sponge so the bright undercoat shows through. Cotton buds and tissue leave fibres behind. Let the spirit evaporate for about 30 minutes first, until the surface is no longer slippery.

Variant: over white primer, brush a dark brown and olive oil mix over everything, a value darker than the final colour. Once the spirit flashes off, sponge the raised areas back like a reverse drybrush, leaving a thin film where colours go next to help them grip.

Work on the parts you need to hold last so you do not smudge wet oil. This suits big models such as monsters well. The same idea works with acrylics: brush a one-coat paint thinned in plenty of medium over an area and wipe the high points straight away with a fingertip or soft cloth, not a brush.

guides.title: Oil washes
guides.summary: Mix oil paint with spirit into a wash, flood it on gently, let it settle, then wipe the raised areas clean.
body: Mix artist oil paint with odourless mineral spirits or white spirit until no lumps remain. Never thin oils with water. A dark brown, sepia, purple or a colour that suits the scheme, such as grey green over green, is more interesting than plain black.

Thin it about like skim milk for shading, or roughly equal parts paint and spirit for a strong wash. Use little or no spirit for heavy grime. Very thin mixes can split and look grainy, or need two coats. Test on paper towel: a clear ring of spirit running ahead means add paint; if it will not spread, add spirit.

Gloss varnish helps the wash flow and wipe off, but is optional over smooth metallic paint. Acrylics underneath need only about half an hour to dry. Use an old synthetic brush, and keep spirit away from putty adhesive, which turns to sticky goo.

Brush it over the area gently with a big soft brush, ending each stroke in a recess. Spirit does not dissolve acrylic, but scrubbing a wet surface can lift it. If a puddle forms, blot the brush on paper and touch it to the pool to soak it up.

It flows into recesses evenly and dries without tide marks. Wait until the spirit evaporates, from a few minutes to an hour. The longer it sits, the more it tints the colours below. On a batch, go back to the first model every 10 to 20.

Wipe the raised areas with a small makeup sponge, turning to a clean side often and pressing lightly so you do not drag it out of the recesses. Cotton buds leave fibres. A brush with the faintest trace of spirit lifts oil cleanly off highlights. On metal, dab it off only where you want shine.
Once dry, matte varnish to lock it in, or paint acrylics straight over it. Do not leave a very thin mix overnight before cleaning up; it gets hard to shift after a few hours.
White oil wiped back off the raised areas leaves a haze in the recesses that reads as mist or smoke.
keywords: how to make an oil wash

guides.title: Order of painting
guides.summary: Work big to small and messy to neat, so each later step tidies the overspill from the one before.
body: Start with the biggest, messiest step while nothing else is finished: the colour that covers most of the model, or any drybrushing or sponging. Paint it quickly over everything nearby, belts and straps included. Only avoid parts already finished.

Then work down to smaller, neater areas. Each one covers the slips from the step before, so you never have to fix them separately. Before you start, drop any step that a later one will cover or that will barely show.
Paint pale colours and poor coverers such as yellow, red and white before dark, strong ones. Dark paint covers a pale slip in one coat; the reverse takes many.

Many paint metallics before the black or matte areas next to them, since black covers stray metal easily and the reverse is hard. Others leave metal until last so its flakes cannot get into other colours, then touch clean metal back onto rivets after the wash. Either way, change your water after metallics.
On armour covered in raised trim, rough the trim in first, then fill each flat panel neatly up to it. Filling a simple panel is much quicker than outlining fiddly trim.
Work from the top down and the centre out, and do the hardest to reach parts first. Your fingers then rest on unpainted areas and the brush does not have to reach past finished ones.

Group details that share a wash: off-black and silver with a black wash; gold, deep red and bone with a brown one. Base each group, then wash it in one go. Paint markings before the all-over wash so they get shaded with the rest.

Black out or base the neighbouring areas before you judge highlights, as bare primer makes anything next to it look wrong. Drybrush a textured base early, as it throws dust and stray paint over finished work. Some prefer to paint the base last, so it can be chosen to suit the finished figure.

guides.title: Object source lighting basics
guides.summary: Painted light follows simple rules: the source is brightest, light fades with distance, moves straight and is blocked.
body: The light source must be the brightest thing in the area, close to white at its core. Nearby lit spots can match it but never exceed it. Brightness comes from contrast, not hue: any colour glows if its core is near white and its surround is dark.

Light fades with distance. Surfaces close to the source get strong, crisp light; those further away get less, and softer. Even far off, raised lips and edges still catch a little while flat areas go dark.
Light travels in straight lines, so recesses and surfaces facing away stay dark. You can bend this slightly where it helps.

A lit surface mixes the light colour with its own. A red leg lit by cyan looks more cyan near the source and more red further off. Use the mid tone of the glow colour for light cast on surfaces, and keep its brightest shade for the source itself.
Shiny materials such as metal pick up a visible reflection even further from the source than matt ones, with small sharp glints. Matt cloth and wood only take the glow close by, and softly.
Light mixes lighter, not darker. Where a red glow and a blue glow overlap, paint a light purple on just the parts lit by both, not the deep purple you get mixing the paints.

It needs to be believable, not realistic. Above all, the space around the lit parts must be darker. To practise, paint a white spot on black card with greys fading out from it, then glue a small ball beside it and light only the side facing the spot.

guides.title: Ways to paint a glow
guides.summary: Build a glow by dry brushing out from the source, by many thin glazes, or by a pale mix tinted with a filter.
body: Dry brush method: base the glowing object in a mid tone of the glow colour, then dry brush that colour over raised areas inside an imagined sphere of light, heavier near the source. Stipple towards the source and drag strokes away from it, along the line the light travels.
Thin the same colour about one to five with water and glaze it over the lit area. It tints and smooths the chalky dry brush look. It looks messy wet but fine dry.

Dry brush lighter tones, each softer and closer to the source. Let every step dry fully first; brushing into wet paint is the most common way to spoil it. Finish with sharp highlights on edges near the light and a very pale mix in the centre of the source.
If a colour stops showing over the layer below, put a careful touch of white where the light is strongest and glaze the colour back over it. Work quickly; overworked glow looks painted on.

Glaze method: thin the glow colour about ten parts water to one paint. Start each stroke a little away from the source and end on it, so most paint lands nearest the light. A glaze alone tints but does not brighten, so on dark surfaces paint lighter highlights first where the glow hits.

Let every glaze dry fully before the next or you lift the paint underneath. Keep each pass a little tighter to the source than the last, so the overlaps build brightness at the centre. Repeat many times, then add a thin bright line right next to the source.

Filter method: mixing orange into blue or green gives mud. Highlight with pale yellow mixed into each base colour instead, then glaze or spray a transparent orange over it. Or build the glow in heavily thinned white, with a little base colour in it for cleaner blends, and glaze the colour over. Touch-ups are hard after filtering.

With an airbrush, finish the details and take off clear effect parts first, then spray the glow from the source side and keep the far side dark. A coloured primer sprayed from the light's side gives rough placement without one. Thin fluorescent glazes over the gradient intensify it. Brush the brightest spots afterwards.

guides.title: Planning object source lighting
guides.summary: Decide where a glow lands before painting, keep that area dark and test it with a small coloured light.
body: Paint most of the model first. The glow mixes with the colours underneath, but leave the zones it will hit dark to fill in later. A dark overall scheme gives more contrast and hides slips in the shadows.
Pick a base colour that contrasts with the light, such as navy under an orange flash. The glow need not be very saturated if everything around it is darker.

Hold a small coloured torch or light strip where the glowing object is, in a dim room, and take photos to see which surfaces catch it and how far it spreads. Photos of other lit models help too: note how much is dark, mid and bright.

Only surfaces facing the source get light. The far side stays in shadow, and one part can shade another, such as an arm shielding the chest from a held spell. Hold the model so the source lines up with your eye; the surfaces you see from there are the ones to light.

Tone down the general top light and keep a dark band between top-lit areas and the glow. A glow from the same direction as the main light disappears. Keeping the normal light to a small patch on one side lets the glow take over.

Block the effect in roughly first, mapping it with a darker version of the glow colour, such as a deep red for fire: bright paint only where the light hits hardest, then weaker mixes fading outwards. Squint at it. If it reads as lit, the placement is right, and only then smooth it.

Do not expect to get it in one pass. Hold the model away, turn it, and adjust with glazes of the shadow colour. Where glow meets another colour, a middle glaze of the two smooths the change. On small details use solid paint, as glazes run into the recesses.

guides.title: Over-highlighting then glazing back
guides.summary: Push highlights brighter than you need, then glaze the base colours back over them for smoother, richer results.
body: Too much highlight is the easiest contrast problem to fix, and too little is the hardest: darkening a blend takes a few glazes, lightening one takes many passes. So take highlights brighter and further than you think they should go. Rough layers or quick blends are fine at this stage.
Thin the original colour of the area, or a mid tone close to it, into a glaze. It does not need to match exactly. For skin, about eight to ten parts water or medium to one of paint works.

Brush it over most of the area, about three quarters of each shape, keeping off the top highlights. Let it dry, then glaze again. Repeat until the transition is smooth. Avoid washes here, as they spread and leave stains.
The glaze shrinks the bright area, ties highlights back into the colour, hides wobbly or slightly misplaced lines and lets subtle variation in the darks show again.
Bright layers seen through thin glazes look smoother and hold more colour than opaque layers alone. This is why the method suits skin, which is translucent in real life.
To go further, rebuild the highlight a little smaller and glaze again, thinning both layers and glazes each round. Three or four rounds is plenty.
Finish with a final dot or short line of the brightest mix on the sharpest points only. Stop whenever you are happy; every extra round is optional.

guides.title: Over-shade busy areas, then tidy
guides.summary: Shade fiddly areas like hands heavily on purpose, then clean up the raised parts with the base colour.
body: In crowded spots like hands, fingers and belts, it is hard to place shade precisely.
Shade generously so plenty of colour gets into the tight gaps between fingers and folds.
Once dry, go back with the base colour and tidy the raised parts.
It is quicker than trying to be exact, but a little care at the start still saves tidying time.

guides.title: Overbrushing
guides.summary: A soft, slightly loaded brush pressed flat gives cleaner, stronger coverage on texture than a stiff dry brush.
body: Stiff drybrushes can flick paint where you do not want it.

Use a larger soft brush, such as a soft round or a makeup brush, which leaves no streaks. Load it, wipe some paint off, but leave it wetter than a dry brush, and press the bristles flat. The paint should be neither watery nor thick.

Skim the flat brush gently over the raised texture, such as sand, foliage or detailed trim. On armour, stroke along the shape with the side of the brush and keep out of the recesses so the dark primer stays there as shading.

Go as heavy or light as you like. Each lighter pass should catch less of the texture and be a clearly lighter colour; overbrushing the same colour as the base does nothing. Because it builds coverage, a quick, light true drybrush of a brighter colour on top finishes it.
From a black undercoat, a heavy pass of a deep colour, a lighter pass over less of each panel, then a few edge highlights gives fast, gritty armour.
On big models, overbrush metal heavily over the base colour instead of picking out every panel. A little red left in the recesses of bronze or steel reads as dried blood.
A final light pass of one pale colour over a whole base, rocks included, makes the parts feel like one scene.

guides.title: Painting a test model
guides.summary: Try a new scheme on one model first, note what works, and make every mistake once instead of across a unit.
body: Before a unit or army, paint one model start to finish at the level you mean to repeat. Use a model from the army so you see the colours on the real shapes; a leader works too, since test models often end up the best painted. For a quick trial, glue a spare torso to a length of sprue as a handle.
Prime just that model or one frame first. If you dislike the primer or scheme, prime over it and try again; thin coats take many repaints before detail suffers.
Block in the main colours roughly, deciding placement as you go, then base the details, wash, clean up and highlight. Add the spot colour last. Test the base on it too, as a pale base can clash.
Keep it loose. Thin paint lets you move or paint over anything that does not work. When torn between two detail colours, paint one on each of two models and compare them at table distance.

Photograph each step and judge the model at table distance under ordinary lighting. Look for neighbouring areas that merge, such as dark metal beside silver, and push them apart. Check transfers will show: dark ones need a light area behind them.

Write down every paint, mix and step, and what you would skip or reorder for batch painting, such as moving colours before the all-over wash so it hides tidy-up. If you change a step later, update the list so the army stays matched.
Simplify: two or three main colours plus neutrals, and one brown for all the straps and pouches. A scheme too slow to repeat means the army never gets finished.

Follow the list on the rest; the first model is always the slowest. Try any new effect or medium on a spare piece of similar shape and size first. Some, like crackle, work on a flat test card and do nothing on a small curved model.

guides.title: Paint hidden areas first
guides.summary: Paint the innermost, hard-to-reach parts first so slips land on unpainted areas, not finished work.
body: Start with the places the brush struggles to reach, such as under cloaks, inside wings and the chest behind a held weapon, and get their dark shades in first. Turn the model and come in from several angles.

Mistakes there land on areas you have not painted yet, so they do not matter. If you catch a gun or arm in front, leave it; it gets painted later. Only take care near finished colours that cover badly, like yellow.

Then paint layers in the order they sit on the body: skin or bone, then clothing, then armour, then cloaks. On big models and mounts this usually means the skin or inner frame first, then metal, then straps, skulls and teeth.

Reaching over finished armour to paint the cloth beneath is how most slips happen. Doing the cloth first avoids it. The deepest layer can even be drybrushed and washed freely, since everything on top still needs painting.
Areas framed by others go first too. Wood inside a metal rim is easier first, because the metal then neatens the edge. The same goes for areas under straps, belts and pouches.
Over a white primer, paint deep undercuts and the insides of coats matt black early, so any gap you miss later does not glint white. Touch up spots the spray missed so the rest of the base is even.
Some gaps cannot be reached at all once glued, such as the space between an arm and the body. Keep those parts off, paint inside the gap black, then assemble.
Early base coats can be loose where another colour will go over the edge. Save fussy tidying for the end.

guides.title: Non-metallic blades
guides.summary: Paint blades with curved bands of light, one edge brighter than the other, and finish with sharp white edges and glints.
body: Flat blades are easier to blend than curved armour, and you choose where the reflections go. A few long, stretched reflections beat many small ones. Blacking out the flat, non-cutting part first keeps your eye on the edge.

Base polished steel in a fairly light grey, since most of it reads bright. Use the full range from near black to near white, but bias the blade towards the light greys or it starts to look like stone. Tinting the shadows with blue or purple makes it read as cold steel.

Paint the highlights as curved or diagonal bands following the light across the blade. Keep one edge brighter and the other darker, then swap them on the reverse side. Light gathers towards the ends of a surface, such as where an edge curves.

Keep the brightest colour broad inside each reflection, with only narrow midtones around it, each lighter layer narrower than the last. Sketch the bright spot first, then glaze back through the darker tones until it blends. Break up regular gradients with a small secondary highlight in a dark band.

Long smooth strokes along the length give a polished look; short cross strokes look worn. Keep the paint moist or the strokes dry dusty. A very thin glaze of one colour over the finished blend ties it together.

Painted metal need not be grey. A blade can reflect the colours around it: armour colours near the top, darker skin or cloth tones lower down, a touch of any bright item nearby. Warm blades can run from a rusty red brown up through peach and pink.
For a bright coloured blade, base it very pale and glaze a different colour in from each end, leaving a pale band in the middle.

When the blends are done, run pure white along both cutting edges and down the centre ridge with the side or flat of the brush, bracing your hands for one slow stroke. Add a few short flicks from the centre out to the edge, with a tiny dot where each meets the edge. Do not overdo the number.

guides.title: Painting animals
guides.summary: Warm filters in the fur shadows, a glossy nose and pink scars make horses, hounds and beasts feel alive.
body: Check reference photos of the real animal for markings, nose and lip colour and how the fur lies. Prop the picture where a glance is enough. Markings only need to read as the right animal, so treat them loosely, like weathering.

Many animals have a paler belly and chest than back. Paint the underside lighter, or sponge a mid brown down the back over a pale base and a darker strip along the spine, then wash the whole animal to tie it together.

Plain black or grey fur looks dull. Filter a very thin yellow-brown onto the lower side of each muscle and feather the edge. Paint short lines down the legs in the direction the hair grows, then a light drybrush picks out texture.
Long muzzles have a lot of surface facing up at the light. Keep that top plane bright all over and put the shadows on the sides and under the cheeks.
Noses and lips are damp, so add tiny dots of a pale colour along them for a glossy reflection. Eyes can be plain black with a tiny off white dot at the back.
For healed scars, trace a pinkish red along the cut, then a slightly lighter mix on its lower, upward-facing edge. Use the same pink for gums and for the skin of any rider so the model ties together.
On mounts, keep the animal simple so the rider stays the focus: a couple of brown drybrushes, black tack, pale hooves.

Vary horses across a unit so they do not look cloned: different coat colours, white face marks of different shapes, white socks from a thin band at the hoof to half the leg on one to four legs, and black, pink or body-coloured muzzles. Black manes and tails are quick and contrast well.

guides.title: Painting an army efficiently
guides.summary: Put effort on faces and focal areas, cut base coats to a minimum, and reuse every brushload before rinsing.
body: Do all building, priming and basing before the big painting sessions, so those are only paint on models. Base every model the same simple way. List every unit with columns for each stage and tick them off honestly.

Follow a written step list from a finished test model. Do, do not think. Work each stage across the whole batch rather than finishing one model at a time. Reuse a small set of elements on every model, such as one metal, one accent metal and one glow colour.

Brushed base coats are the biggest time sink. Use a sprayed main colour or a primer close to it, or one-coat paints over a light undercoat, and keep extra base colours few. Thin one-coat paints at a set ratio so results repeat. Group areas that share a wash, base them all, then wash them in one go.

Base in the shadow colour and go straight to highlights instead of base, wash and re-layer. If time is short, highlight only the colour that defines the army and shows on every figure, then the most eye-catching one.

Spend time on the face, head, shoulders, chest and any focal effect. Secondary areas get one coat and one highlight. Back-row models can stop at faces and weapons. A few muted colours spread around the troops, with one bright focal thing such as a shield, looks deliberate.
Before rinsing, scan the model for every other spot needing the colour already on the brush.

Use the biggest brush you can manage. Be neat only next to finished areas, and skip places nobody sees at table distance. Do the fiddly precise jobs while you are fresh and leave washes and drybrushing for when you are tired.

Decide early what standard you are aiming for. Rank-and-file models do not need perfection: paint ten and judge the unit, not one model. Give each a rough time budget, and save blending and glow effects for leaders and centrepieces so you avoid burnout.

guides.title: Painting bases with inks
guides.summary: Thin, strong inks over a black and white undercoat give rich, shaded bases quickly.
body: Prime black, then add a strong white from one side so the light and shade are already in place.
Inks are strong and thin, so the undercoat shows through as shading. Use darker colours where the black shows and brighter ones where it is white.
Inks stay wet longer than paint, so you can blend neighbouring colours with a clean damp brush.
Let the ink dry fully before painting over it or it can lift. A hair dryer helps.
For highlights, add a little ink to an opaque pale paint and pick out the top surfaces.

For a fast plain earth base, glue on a mix of sand and grit and let it dry. Drop two or three drops of earth brown ink round the base with a few drops of flow improver, and let it wick through the sand.
Inks can reactivate under wet glue, pastes and snow products. Give the base a matt varnish before adding tufts, flock or snow.

guides.title: Painting black armour
guides.summary: Black cannot be shaded, so build it up with cool grey highlights, fading from the top, plus soft reflections on curves.
body: Even over black primer, paint a thinned coat of your black paint. Blacks differ in sheen, and later touch-ups show as patches against bare primer.
A wash cannot darken black and can leave a patchy sheen, so work only with lighter colours. Pick out joints and undersuit in a different black or very dark grey so they read as another material.
Paint black mixed with a very dark blue-grey loosely where light will land. It barely shows but takes the harshness off.

Build up a chunky dark blue-grey highlight round the panels, then mid and lighter blue-greys inside it, then pale grey on top edges and sharpest corners with the side of the brush. Mix white into the blue-black rather than using pure white. Tidy wobbly or thick lines with black or the dark grey before the next step.

Make highlights strongest at the top of each part and fade them lower down. Keep them small and facing the same light direction across the whole model. Covering too much area is the usual mistake and turns the armour grey; starting small is easier than shrinking a patch.

On domes and curved plates, add soft patches of light too, not just edge lines: domes catch light in a spot, cylinders in a stripe. Mix the grey half and half with glaze medium, build it in two thin coats, then a smaller lighter patch inside. Thick coats leave hard bands.

Faster options: drybrush a dark then a mid grey, tidy streaks on flat panels with thinned black, and add one fine pale edge. Or base a very dark muted blue-grey and paint black into the middle of each panel, leaving the edges as the highlight. For worn black metal, drybrush dark steel very lightly instead.

Finish with tiny icy pale dots on the brightest corners. If the whole model now looks grey, glaze or wash very thin black over it, twice in the shadows. This pulls it back to black and also hides messy blends.

guides.title: Painting boils, pustules and pus
guides.summary: Bruised edges, swollen reds and a yellow pus tip with a pale dot make boils and pustules look ready to burst.
body: Finish the skin first. Then dab a lighter skin tone on each raised boil to separate it from the flesh around it.
Fade a very thin purple or deep burgundy glaze into the skin round the base of each boil, like bruising. A thinned red wash ringed round it makes the skin look inflamed.
Build a red to magenta towards the swollen part. Small dots and thin glazes, repeated, give a soft change rather than a hard ring.
Paint a thin mustard yellow in the centre, strongest in the middle, then glaze a thin cold yellow over the boil and the skin next to it to tie it together.
Thin a pale yellowish bone a lot, wipe most off on tissue, and touch it onto the very top of each boil. A tiny dot here is what makes it look tight and full.
For burst boils, fill the hole with a glossy green-yellow gloopy technical paint and let some trickle down. A second coat makes the drips stand out more.

guides.title: Painting bone and skulls
guides.summary: Build bone from a sandy base through bone and pale cream, shade the recesses brown, and dot white on the tips.
body: Base in a sandy beige or a medium bone that covers well, two thin coats, or spray a bone-coloured primer for a big horde. Going straight to a pale bone gives a patchy, chalky base.

Layer a bone colour over the larger areas, leaving the sand showing in the recesses. Highlight the raised areas with a pale yellow-cream and dot white on the highest points, such as tooth tips and the top of the skull.

Drop a shade only into the deepest recesses, around teeth and where bone meets skin. The shade sets the mood: warm brown looks natural, a thinned blue-grey run in as fine lines gives cold contrast against warm bone, and black gives the strongest contrast.

Your middle colour sets the mood too. A greenish tan gives grimy old bone, a warmer tan cleaner bone, a cool grey-white bleached bone. If the model already has a lot of yellow or tan, the grey-white stands out better. For a rough, aged look, lay each layer as fine scratchy strokes and keep plenty of midtone.

Quick skulls: over a bone base, brush a brown one-coat paint or a half and half shade and lift it off the tops with a clean damp brush or a fingertip before it dries, then highlight the crown. For tiny teeth, use very little paint and the flat of the brush, then tidy afterwards.

Old bone has dark, dirty eye sockets, cracks and streaks; fresh bone is paler and smoother. A light grey or green drybrush suggests mould in damp places. Keep bone matt, with gloss only where you want slime.

Whole skeleton units: paint the bone first, before armour and cloth, since drybrush and wash spill onto everything nearby. Bone paint can dry chalky and take a wash unevenly; a coat of satin varnish first lets it flow. A dark brown one-coat paint thinned with about ten parts medium makes a good all-over wash. Soak up pools with a clean brush.
Then give each bone one highlight, or a drybrush, from a few off-whites, brightest on the skull and darkest on the legs.

guides.title: Painting chainmail
guides.summary: Dry brush chainmail with downward strokes only so the top of each ring catches the light.
body: Block the mail in silver early and messily, or drybrush a dark gunmetal over a black primer, which fills the gaps between the links for free. Paint the cloth and leather around it afterwards, and work the silver well into the links so no primer shows.
Wash it with a dark brown or black. Poke the brush into the links as you go: air bubbles trapped there keep the wash out and leave bright spots. Soak up excess so the links do not clog.
Load the dry brush lightly with your metal mix and wipe most off on a tissue or your thumb. Stroke from top to bottom only, never back up. This catches the top of each ring as if lit from above.
Tilt the model so the brush reaches into the folds.
Repeat with a brighter mix, still on the downstroke only. Buffing in circles loses the lit-from-above look.
Finish with a single fine line of bright silver along the top edge of the mail coat and the rims of nearby helmets and blades.
For neglected mail, run a thinned rust orange into a few random links, around buckles and in low folds where water would sit.

guides.title: Painting chips and scratches
guides.summary: A small dark chip with a light line under it reads as paint knocked off; dab it on and keep it small and on edges.
body: Pick a dark colour close to your shade colour, or one that contrasts strongly with the armour. A very matt dark brown shows best on metallic armour, and a warm brown reads as rot on organic hulls. Pale schemes show chipping most.

Tear a small piece of foam so the edge is ragged, dab it in paint, then dab most off on a dry palette until it leaves only a faint speckle. Once most of the model is finished, a fine brush or an old splayed one is safer, as a sponge can splatter onto other colours.

Dab along panel edges, corners and exposed parts like knees, toe caps, hatches and helmet tops, with only a few on flats. Keep the spacing random, not an even pattern. Stop early; adding more is easy. Handled parts such as grips wear smooth rather than chipped.

With a fine brush and near undiluted paint, dot along edges with a slight wobble and join a few speckles into bigger chips with ragged outlines, like little islands on a map. Turn the brush so shapes vary. A wet palette or a drop of drying retarder keeps the paint flowing through hundreds of small touches.

Paint a fine line of the armour highlight colour along the lower edge of each chip. It reads as the lit lip of a dent. In larger chips, fill most of the dark with a dark metal, leaving a thin dark rim, and add a dot of bright silver at the lower edge.

Or work pale first: dot chips in the base colour lightened with white, then tuck a dark brown against or just overlapping each one, towards the top. Pale on its own reads as a shallow scratch in the top coat; dark reads as damage down to primer or bare metal.

Chips can stand in for edge highlights. Tap and scuff a broken edge along the panels instead of a clean line, add silver into some chips, and slips just read as more wear. It is often quicker than neat edging across an army.

Keep chips small and tight. Long harsh scratches make a big object look small. For subtle wear, scratch with your highlight colours instead; on black armour a few small light silver marks are enough. Dab the colour around transfers and stripes over them to wear them, and put most damage where knocks would land.

guides.title: Painting cloth folds
guides.summary: Shade the hollows and light the whole upward side of each fold, keeping soft transitions and sharp lines only at hems.
body: Do not just line the top ridge of each fold like an edge highlight. Cloth reads through broad shapes of light and dark.

Base coat with a larger brush, then glaze a slightly darker tone into the recesses and lower parts of each fold. Turning the model upside down shows which areas face down. Deepen in stages, ending with a precise dark line deep in the folds. A shadow shifted in hue, such as turquoise under sage green, is livelier, but keep it related: a yellow shaded dark red looks wrong.

Put lighter layers over the whole upward-facing side of each fold, leaving the hollows and downward sides dark. Let the light run right up to the shadow line and join across neighbouring folds, with strokes following the direction of the cloth.

Add a smaller, brighter step on the highest parts of the biggest folds. Blend it out softly where you can; cloth is soft. Keep real darkness only where cloth tucks under a fold, as small bumps low on a cloak still catch light.

Visible steps are fine. The pattern of light and dark is what reads as cloth. To soften a hard border, paint the thinned mid colour over it or stipple a very thin glaze across it. For rough linen, short crossing scratchy lines of the highlight replace blending altogether.

Large plain areas with few sculpted folds, such as the skirt of a long coat, look dead if left flat. Invent a few soft highlights where the cloth would bulge, or grade the whole garment from darker at the top to lightest at the hem with downward strokes, each layer starting a little lower.

Keep sharp lines only on real edges such as hems and seams, skipping parts that turn into deep shadow. For quick uniforms, line pocket edges and crease tops with one light tone, then retrace just the corners and peaks with a paler one.
For the last touch, use a warmer, brighter colour only where creases meet or catch the most light.

guides.title: Entering a painting competition
guides.summary: Judges look for clean basics, strong contrast and a clear focal point first, so pick your neatest model and check the rules.
body: Read the rules before you start. Most contests split entries by category, such as single figure, large model, group or unit, diorama, bust and sometimes a youth or first-timer class. Check base size limits, whether the model must be your own work, and whether it must be new.
Judges usually look at the whole piece from a normal viewing distance first. A model that reads clearly, with strong lights and darks and one obvious focal point, gets picked up for a closer look.

Up close, they check the basics: no mould lines or gaps, no bare primer, no fluff or dust in the paint, clean edges between colours and an even, deliberate finish. A missed mould line can sink an otherwise good model.

Next come the harder skills: smooth or controlled blends, believable light, crisp eyes and faces, convincing materials and any freehand. Difficulty counts, but a simple model done cleanly beats an ambitious one done badly.
The base and display matter. Keep the base in scale and in the same colours as the model, and do not let it hide the figure. A plain plinth with a neat rim is safer than a busy one.
Photograph the model under bright light before you hand it in. The photo shows flaws your eye skips, and you have a record if it gets knocked.
Carry it in a box with foam or a magnet tray. Many contests use open scoring, where every entry gets a grade, so ask the judges what held yours back. That advice is often worth more than the result.

guides.title: Painting cracks
guides.summary: A dark wandering line with a light line just under it, plus bright points on the raised peaks, reads as a real crack.
body: Paint a thin, wandering dark line for the crack. Let it branch and change direction.
Run a thin light line just below the dark one to show the lower edge catching the light.
Add tiny dots of a very light colour, even white, on the sharpest points where the edge sticks up.
Keep the bright points uneven so the cracks do not look like a printed pattern.

guides.title: Painting crystals
guides.summary: Crystals are dark at the top of each facet and bright at the bottom; glaze it smooth and finish with fine scratches and dots.
body: Use a light undercoat for glowing or see-through colours, as many greens and blues will not glow over black. Then base a deep, dark version of the colour; dark to light is easier to control.

Translucent crystal reverses normal lighting: dark at the top of each facet, bright at the bottom. Every dark area should sit next to a light one. Facets facing the light act like mirrors and can be almost white.
Smooth with thin glazes, each finishing a little nearer the bright end. Sweep off the end in one stroke so no blob is left. Glaze the darker colour back over any step that looks sudden.
On a crystal blade, run the light towards the tip on one face and towards the hilt on the other.
For a strong glow, glaze heavily thinned fluorescent colour over it all, pushing more into the shadows.

Finish with razor-thin pale blue-white scratch lines and an edge highlight on every edge and ridge, laid with the side of the brush; the edges hide earlier slips. Add one tiny bright dot where a facet sits in shadow, with a little gloss mixed into the white.

Quick version: undercoat white, hold the model upside down and wash the crystal so it pools on the faces that point down, repeat on a smaller area with a darker mix, then drybrush a bright tone. The drybrush also catches nearby edges as a free glow.

On clear plastic crystals, a satin varnish first gives the paint grip while the plastic stays see-through. Wash the colour on, glaze a lighter tone with a little gloss medium into the recesses, and catch the facet edges with a light metallic drybrush.

guides.title: Painting dark skin
guides.summary: Base a deep brown flesh, shade warm browns into the eyes, and build up through lighter flesh to yellowish highlights.
body: Base coat the skin in a deep brown flesh tone, two thin coats. Dark skin varies a lot, from deep tones leaning purple or umber to lighter ones leaning warm orange, so choose the base to suit.
Wash a warm mid brown around the eyes and into recesses, then a darker reddish brown only in the eye sockets.
Highlight the brow and raised areas with a mid flesh tone thinned half and half, then a lighter flesh. Focus on the forehead, brow, bridge of the nose, cheekbones, top lip and top of the chin.
Continue with a pale bone and then a pale yellow-cream over smaller areas. Yellow-tinted highlights look natural on skin, warmer and sunlit compared with plain ivory.
The size of the highlights decides how dark the skin reads. Broad highlights give a lighter tone; small tight ones, with more surface left dark, give a deeper one from the same paints.

Glaze thin warm browns over the steps to smooth them, and thin red into the lips, under the cheekbones and under the eyes so the face looks alive. Re-layer the small bright points and glaze again until smooth.

Finish with a little near white along the brow line and a few fine lines around the brow for expression. For a very dark, cool skin, build from black through a dark purple grey with a little blue in the highlights instead.

guides.title: Painting each material differently
guides.summary: How sharp the shine is and what shape your brush marks take tell the eye whether a surface is metal, silk, leather or cloth.
body: Do not just colour in. Ask what each surface is made of and how it catches light. Two parts given the same highlight in the same way start to look like the same stuff.

Shiny things get narrow, bright highlight bands with strong contrast and a few tiny bright points. Polished metal and gems can run from near white to near black in a small space. Wet or rubbery surfaces put bright reflections right next to near black, with few midtones.

Matt things like wool, skin and leather get broad, soft transitions. Matt cloth should never reach pure white or pure black, and rough surfaces such as bark take only weak highlights. Skin and hair sit in between: satin, with bright but softer highlights.

Brush marks carry texture: cross-hatching reads as coarse wool, fine parallel lines as satin, small dots as rough or felted cloth, irregular broken strokes as leather. Put the texture in the midtones too, not only the top layer.
Keep silk and armour smooth. Stipple hides, furs, coarse cloth and pitted metal. Streaky strokes suggest grain on horn.
A smooth surface next to a textured one makes both read better, even in similar colours. A thin dark line where two materials meet also sells the separation.
Gloss varnish does part of the work: on black claws, eyes or fresh blood it makes them read hard and wet without more painting.
Stippled texture fades at arm's length but rewards close viewing and photos.

guides.title: Painting eyes on faces
guides.summary: Dark socket, off-white eyeball leaving a dark rim, then a pupil or iris that touches the lids, and an optional tiny glint.
body: Use a size 0 or similar with a sharp point and short bristles; the point matters more than the size. Brace elbows on the desk and a finger against the model, and move only your fingertips.

Paint eyes once the face has its base and shade but before the highlights, so slips onto the cheeks get covered later and a bad attempt costs little. Some paint them before any skin at all, over the black primer, for the same reason.

Fill the socket with black mixed with a warm dark brown. It is softer than pure black, and it shows where each eye sits so you can check both match in size and angle. If the sculpt is vague, paint a small oval anyway.

Paint the eyeball in an ivory, light grey or off-white with a touch of skin colour, never pure white, leaving a thin dark rim all round. Turn the model sideways and stroke along the eye. Quick version: a white dot in each corner, leaving a black line between them as the pupil, the same width in both eyes.

Make the pupil a short dark line or iris that touches both lids, or let the upper lid cover part of it. A floating dot in white looks startled. Build it by touching the same spot a few times. Irises sit roughly above the corners of the mouth, and both eyes must look the same way; off centre makes the figure look somewhere.

Messy is fine: reshape the eye from the outside with the skin and shade colours, or a little brown wash with most taken off the brush, which also shrinks eyes that came out too big. Keep every paint thin so fixes do not build up. On rank and file, a shaded socket with no pupil is acceptable.

Cover any black left under the eye with skin, or it reads as goggles, but keep a fine dark line along the upper lid as the lashes. Paint eyebrows in a brown tinted with the skin colour so they sit in the face rather than looking drawn on.

On bigger faces, ring a bright saturated iris inside the dark, lighter on the side away from the light, then one tiny pale dot on the side facing the light, in the same place in both eyes. On busts, shade the eyeball like a small sphere with a touch of red in the inner corners. Gloss varnish on the eye alone makes it look wet.

guides.title: Painting faces
guides.summary: A warm base, a warm brown wash as a map, then thin layers on the raised areas build a believable face.
body: Base a warm mid skin tone in thin coats so no texture builds up; a grey or white undercoat makes this easier than black. Stroke along features, not across them. Then wash with a warm chestnut brown. A cold brown makes skin look dead. The wash shows where the shadows go.

Thin the mid skin until see-through, wipe most off the brush and paint the raised areas, avoiding the dark lines. Draw each stroke from the recess up to the high point, such as from under the cheek onto the cheekbone. A second coat on brow, cheekbones, nose and chin builds a soft gradient.

Highlight with a paler tone on the nose tip, brow, cheekbones, top lip and jaw, plus the folds from nose to mouth. Light comes from above, so the upper face is lighter than the lower; lighting one side slightly more looks livelier. Join the brow highlight into the forehead so only a small shadow stays above the nose.

For depth, glaze a thin muted dark blue under the cheekbones and on the jaw, which also reads as stubble, and a thin deep red brown on the cheeks and lower lip for warmth. Freckles are tiny dots of thinned brown ink in a narrow band across the nose and cheeks.
Alternate opaque layers on the high points with an all-over glaze of a darker mix, pulling from dark towards light, until smooth. Glaze the base back into the shadows if it looks flat.

Skin has a slight sheen, so push a few last points brighter with a pale warm yellow added. On bald heads, glaze highlights thinly rather than painting a hard line. Black out the helmet or hood round the face partway through; framing it makes it far easier to judge.

Match the contrast to the character. Fierce or muscular faces take deep shadows and near-white top points. Young or soft faces keep the wash only in the ears, under the brows and at the hairline, with a few small highlights.

The usual mistake is too much paint on the brush. Stop once the face looks right; fiddling muddies it and often leaves it too pale. About half an hour gets most of the result. Practise on spare heads glued to corks. If one side goes badly under a hood, paint it as deep cast shadow.

guides.title: Painting feathers and wings
guides.summary: Keep the base of each feather light and the tip dark, add thin hatched lines for texture, and darken the wing tips.
body: Drybrush or stipple a pale tinted colour, such as a pale blue, heavily over a dark undercoat. A colour with some hue looks richer than plain grey.

Thin a strong white into a wash with flow improver and run it into each overlap where one row of feathers sits on the next. The base of each feather is light, the tip dark. For crisp clean white wings instead, base pale grey and paint each feather in slightly thinned white, leaving grey between them; expect two coats.

Paint a line down each feather's spine and round its outer edge, then many thin hatched lines angled out towards the tip in a pale tinted colour, closer together near the base. Overlap the white without covering it. A nearly dry brush skimmed along the vanes picks out sculpted texture quickly.
Soften any hard white edge with a very thin white glaze. Line dark between the feathers where they need separating.

Drybrush a mid grey onto the outer wing tips with very little paint, then black on just the very ends, or glaze thin black over them so the feathers fade into darkness. A few thin lines where colours meet blend them.

For a coloured bird, do the same over white and glaze a yellow, pink or other ink over the bright centres. For a warm gradient, base yellow over white and build several thin orange-red glazes towards the tips. Thin washes of related colours vary the feathers without repainting.

Brown birds: base a dark brown-grey, drybrush mid brown then light tan, and add crisp pale tan edges by hand on the front feathers. Give the lower rows and tail a different tone, such as greys, so the rows separate. A thinned black wash between dark ends and lighter bases smooths the change.
Black feathers: skim a dark grey up the spine with the side of the brush, then along the side ridges, and finish with a light grey on the upper spine and outer edge only.

guides.title: Painting fire and flames
guides.summary: Paint flames from the inside out: white and pale yellow at the core and base, through orange, to near black at the tips.
body: Start from a white undercoat. It makes see-through yellows and oranges glow. Avoid high-coverage yellows early on; they are greyed and kill the glow. Fluorescent yellow and orange over the white add extra punch.

Fire is hottest at its base and core, so flip normal highlighting: lighter colours go in recesses and low down, darker ones on raised ridges and tips. When drybrushing, work backwards from light to dark, each step covering less, and start strokes at the cooler end.

Base in a pale clean yellow, then block in a warm egg-yolk yellow and orange as thin washes, pulled towards the base for yellows and towards the tips for oranges and reds. Always leave the previous colour in the creases. If a bright colour spreads too far early, push it back so the hottest point still stands out.

Stipple orange-red down from the tips, then barely catch the very ends with a red and black mix. Use a soft weak black; strong black wipes out the red. Watch the orange, which gets covered easily. If the recesses lose their glow, run thinned yellow back in. One part orange to three of glaze medium brushed over the steps softens them.
Add definition: thin dark lines along raised ridges and thin pale lines in the folds, following the flow. Invent a few lines on smooth areas.
Top up pure white deep at the base, add a little brownish grey smoke at the tips, and scatter a handful of tiny pale dots as sparks.

Glaze thin orange or red onto nearby metal or stone, strongest next to the flame, so it looks lit. Start with white on edges that face the flame, then the glow colour over it in several thin coats. If it looks like flat red paint, it is too thick; stop as soon as the glow reads.

Green, blue or purple flames work the same way: pale core, main colour through the middle, deep dark tips. Three greens wet blended together make fast magic fire. Use clean water; dirty water muddies bright colours.

guides.title: Painting from reference
guides.summary: Look up photos of the real material or effect before you paint it, and keep the picture in view while you work.
body: Before trying a new effect or material, find pictures of the real thing. Guessing usually goes wrong. Burnt wood and glowing coals for embers, real rust for rust, people standing by water at dusk for reflected light.

Study the picture before painting: where the light falls, what colour it is, how it fades, and how much of the area is dark, mid and bright. Get the lights and darks right first; the exact hue matters less. Reference often shows far more grey midtone, or a brighter source, than you would assume.

Gather everything before you start, in one folder built around the mood and main colours you want: photos, art, textures, and painted models you admire. Then add details such as fabrics and wear. Stopping to search mid-project breaks your flow. Check colours against more than one source.
For faces, collect many photos of one well-photographed person in different light, and copy where the shadows fall in the eye sockets, under the nose and below the lips.
Put the reference right behind the model on the desk, ideally printed, so checking it takes a glance and not an unlocked phone. Printed step notes from a guide work the same way.

When something looks off, compare the model with the reference and look for the difference in contrast, colour or where the light sits, then adjust. Showing photos at an in-between stage helps too; others spot flat areas you have stopped seeing.
For reflections on metal or glossy parts, photograph the primed model under a lamp and copy where the shine falls.
When following a new technique or reference, copy it exactly the first time. Adapt it and add your own ideas once you know how it behaves.

guides.title: Painting fur
guides.summary: Drybrush or wash fur first, then build tufts with lines or blends, keeping it darker on top and on the lower legs.
body: Plan the light before the texture. Treat the fur as a few big shapes, brighter where it faces the light and darker underneath, and keep the chest, under the arms, lower legs and feet duller than the back, face and shoulders.

Base coat textured fur with slightly thinner paint, applied slowly so it settles into the grooves instead of flooding the strands. Drybrush fur before any neat work so the overspill gets covered by later base coats.

Quick method: over a dark brown base, drybrush mid brown lightly all over, then a lighter brown even more lightly, then flick a pale colour onto just the most raised tips. Warm khaki or bone tones look more natural than plain light greys.

Line method for dark fur: darken the animal with a brown-black wash, then paint many thin lines along each tuft in dark brown with a little warm bone added, each lighter mix covering only the middle of the tuft.

On smooth sculpts, paint the fur on. Use thin paint and a brush with a good point, start moving before the tip lands and flick off so each stroke tapers. Go over an area two or three times with lines in slightly different places, following the way the hair grows.

Do not take every tuft to the brightest colour or the model goes flat. Soften harsh steps by thinning the previous colour to a glaze and stroking it over the join. For white fur, use greys tinted with purple, brown or blue rather than plain grey.

For a pelt or tail, wet blend pale to dark along the fur with all colours set out first. A quick grey pelt: grey at the edges and tan brown in the middle, a very thin black wash, then a pale blue-grey drybrush with the side of the brush.
Where skin meets fur, paint a few short lines into the fur instead of a hard edge, and look at photos of real pelts for colours.

guides.title: Painting gems
guides.summary: Paint a gem dark on the side facing the light and glowing on the far side, then put a crisp white dot towards the light.
body: Pick the light direction first and match the rest of the model. Light passes through the gem and comes out the far side, so that side glows and the light-facing side stays dark.

Place the glow by the model standing upright, not by the gem. A gem set at an angle on a hilt may end up with its bright side almost underneath, and that is correct. Keep every gem and lens on the model agreeing.
Paint the gem black or nearly black and keep a dark rim round it.

Build the colour towards the far side in two or three steps, each smaller and brighter. Start each stroke near the dark side and lift off at the bright side, where the paint gathers. On a tiny gem or lens, dark, one mid tone and a dot is enough.

Smooth with thin glazes, two to four coats per step; the first passes look messy, so keep them thin rather than fixing it in one heavy stroke. Shifting hue as you go, such as black to blue to pink, looks richer than one colour getting lighter. A last very thin glaze of a deep tone adds richness.

Finish with one crisp white or ivory dot on the light-facing side, inside the dark area rather than on the very edge. A faceted gem gets its whole light-facing facet bright. Trim a fat dot by pushing dark paint against it. On larger gems, add a short line running down from the dot.

Quick method: paint the gem a light tint over a pale base, then hold the model so the side you want darkest points down and brush a darker tint, thinned with medium, towards it. The paint pools there and dries as a gradient.

A gem that looks flat almost always lacks contrast: darken the dark side further, push the bright side brighter, and keep the dot small. Stick to one or two related gem colours per model. A matt finish keeps the painted light clean; for real shine, add thin gloss inside the gem edge last.

guides.title: Painting glass and clear parts
guides.summary: Paint glass as a strong dark to bright gradient with a crisp white glint, then gloss it so it shines.
body: Glass reads through contrast. Give each pane, vial or bulb a dark edge, a gradient from dark to bright across it, and a small sharp white glint near the opposite corner.
Clear window parts can be primed and painted. It saves painting the whole interior and a painted gradient often looks better than clear plastic.

For a canopy or window, base it in a very dark mix such as black with a deep red or blue. Build a broad L of bright colour into the lower corner in several thin glazes, each stopping a little shorter than the last, then blend the middle with halfway mixes. Re-line the bright L finely and dot white into the top opposite corner.

For a mirrored visor look, set a dark purple base, then build blue into one corner and red through orange to yellow into the opposite corner, each step finer, with a white dot in each brightest point.

For liquid in a vial, paint the liquid line level with the base rim whatever angle the vial sits at, and fill solid below it. Highlight the top of the liquid and one side of the glass, and dot small bubbles in lines.
For a glowing liquid, paint white where it is brightest and a mid tone elsewhere, then give it two thin coats of a fluorescent colour. Add a soft hint of the same glow on nearby surfaces.
Quick potions: paint the bottle white, wash a light colour in, touch a second colour into it while wet so they mix, then add a thin diagonal white streak down one side.
Finish with gloss varnish on the glass only. An airbrushed gradient on its own can look artificial, so break it up with a few brushed highlights.

guides.title: Painting gun barrels
guides.summary: A neat dot of matt black with a touch of brown makes an undrilled barrel end read as a hole.
body: Mix matt black with a touch of dark brown and thin it so it flows but still covers. Pure black draws attention to the cheat.

Start in the centre of the muzzle and work outwards to the rim, curving round it. Turn the model so your hand stays steady as you reach the edge. A blunt, dampened toothpick can dab the centre dot instead of a brush.
Run a thin dark wash round the muzzle to suggest its edge.
Highlight the top rim of the muzzle if you like.

guides.title: Painting hair
guides.summary: Hair has a sheen, so highlight it in a band round the crown and build texture with many thin, varied strands.
body: Picture a ring of light resting on the head. Put the highlights where it would touch, usually round the crown and on the side facing the light, and let them fall away fast as the hair turns down or tucks under.

Block each tone into its zone first with a bigger brush, leaving the dark base deep in the recesses. In the lit areas even the recesses should only reach a midtone; in the shadow areas the brightest strands should stop at a midtone. Mixing these up flattens the hair.

Build texture with sharp, thin lines that follow the flow, light into dark. Each lighter step covers less, but vary the strand lengths so a band never ends in a straight edge. Keep the brightest bands narrow; wide ones look chalky. Thin lines are translucent, so do two or three passes per colour, and smooth the joins with thin glazes.

Quick method for beards and plumes: wash so the strands have dark gaps, then skim the side of a lightly loaded brush along them, base colour first and a brighter colour more lightly. Dot the tops of the strands for the last step. Beards look natural with greys mixed in among the browns.

Blonde: avoid bright lemon or sun yellows, which look like mustard. Build from sepia, rusty brown and ochre, then jump to ivory or a pale cream. White hair: base in an off-white or mid grey, keep the grey shading light, and save pure white for the final strands.

Black hair: highlight in narrowing bands of blue-grey across the top, finish with a pale icy blue and a couple of tiny spots, then a thin glaze to tie it together. It is fine to go too bright and glaze back; keep roughly half the hair dark. Avoid pure white on dark hair.

Red hair: real red hair is mostly muted orange and auburn. Keep true red for the low midtones, use a warm flesh as the top highlight, and knock it back with a touch of teal. A thin glaze over finished hair can also shift its colour away from nearby cloth. Bright fantasy colours work the same way, such as pink shaded with a thin purple.

Do not line the hairline in black; it looks harsh. Where a sculpt has no sideburns, a small patch of hair colour in front of the ear adds them. Across a group, pick three or four natural hair tones in one-coat paints and share them out for variety at little extra work.

guides.title: Painting hands, arms and bare legs
guides.summary: Light the knuckles, fingertips, knees and the top of each muscle, darken between fingers, and ring the light round tiny limbs.
body: Hands and bare limbs take the same light as the face: from above, so the top of each form is brightest and the underside darkest. Base and shade them with the rest of the skin, then highlight.

On hands, put the highlights on the knuckles, the fingertips and the back of the hand where it faces up. Run a fine line of dark brown between the fingers so they read as separate rather than a mitten.
On bare arms and legs, light the upper part of each muscle and the top of the knee or elbow. Leave the lower part and the back of the limb in shade.

At small scale, folds on sleeves and the shape of a limb are hard to see. Paint the highlight as ring-shaped strokes wrapping round the limb, brightest towards the top of each ring, then join them with a stroke along its length so it does not look like stacked hoops.

Finish with a thin pale line on the upper edge of each ring or knuckle. Keep it short; a pale line down the whole finger flattens it. On larger models the sculpted folds and muscles guide you once the first highlights are in.

guides.title: Painting horns
guides.summary: Build horns with fine growth lines from a dark base, and think about which end is light to lead the eye.
body: Base in a very dark warm brown, two coats, then a mid warm brown over most of the horn.

With the brush tip, paint fine lines along the horn in a lighter orange-brown, pulling them out into the darker areas. They give horn its ridged texture. Keep them mostly on the lit upper side, where texture would show.
Repeat with lighter colours, yellow-brown, bone, pale cream and finally white, each inside the last set and closer to the lightest end.

Glaze a dark brown and black mix into cracks and onto the dark end. A pale streak along one edge adds a hint of shine. A coat of clear medium softens the scratchy look. For a banded horn, add thin stripes of thinned dark brown running from the root towards the tip.
