For a smooth fade without wet blending, base the horn bone and thin a see-through brown about half and half with medium. Coat two thirds of the horn from the root, then two more coats each stopping shorter. Let each dry first so the bands stay soft. The overlaps build the gradient.
Usually the tips are painted light for sharpness: strong contrast from a pale tip to a dark base, with a white dot on the point, makes spikes and claws look sharp.
Reversing it, light at the base and dark at the tip, pulls the eye to the face. Useful on helmets and plain faces.

Keep horns a different tone from nearby bone, such as a dark grey lifted to a pale grey-green, or a darker brown, so they read as a separate material. A small light dot where a curve bends away reads as a reflection, and gloss on dark horns makes them look hard and polished.

guides.title: Joints, cables and undersuits
guides.summary: Paint dark joints and cables after the armour, then edge highlight them in stacked blue-greys brightest on the outside.
body: Dark paint is strongly pigmented and hard to cover with pale colours, so paint joints after light armour and keep it off the plates.

Line the brush up with the length of each joint so the bristles follow the groove. Use two thin coats rather than one thick one, and stroke along the ribs, not across them, or the paint gets wiped into every groove.
Paint joints and cables black, then a fairly broad dark blue-grey highlight, leaving black in the recesses.

Add a thinner, shorter mid blue-grey, then a very fine pale grey, and optionally tiny pale dots in the centre of the highlights. Make the highlights finer and lighter towards the outer side of the limb, where light lands.

A round pipe or cable has no edge to follow. Skim one line along the side facing the light, usually the top. On ribbed joints, touch only the middle of each raised rib with the tip, leaving shade on both sides.
For glossy black cables, jump straight from the blue-grey line to a tight pale blue line with no step between. The hard jump reads as shine.
If ribbed highlights get messy, run very thin black into the recesses to clean up the lines.

For speed, leave joints black with one thin blue-grey line on the edges and ridges at elbows, knees and waist, or paint them metallic and wash them dark. Keep it to one subtle step; too much grey makes black look dusty, and a clean dark joint makes the armour round it look sharper.

guides.title: Painting lava and glowing cracks
guides.summary: Start bright over white, then lay dark cooled plates over it so the cracks between them glow from yellow to red.
body: Choose the look first: dark cooled plates with glowing cracks between them, or a surface glowing from inside, brightest in the middle and the recesses and charred at the edges. Either way keep the blending rough and the borders jagged. Real lava is never a smooth gradient or a neat line.

Work from bright to dark. Over a white undercoat, lay a yellow tint, then orange, then a transparent red, leaving yellow in the deepest recesses where it is hottest. Orange straight onto dark paint will not glow.
For cooled plates, paint black patches in rough five and six sided shapes. Start small and grow them, leaving wide cracks at first, then narrow the cracks so they thin out away from the heat.

To add cracks over a dark surface, draw thin, wandering lines of varied thickness in a pale ivory-yellow first. Then glaze orange over each line and a little to either side, so the dark next to it picks up a tint like spilled light.

Edge each plate broadly in deep red, then thinner bright red, then orange near the hottest cracks. Save pale yellow and a dot of white for the very hottest spots and the largest pools. If the glow looks cramped, push the orange and yellow further out; if it looks cool, pull thin yellow back in.

For glowing armour, dab thinned red patchily over the flat panels, leaving orange in the recesses, then a darker red closer to the edges. Stipple black onto the edges and tops for a charred look and tint it with a touch of the dark red. A final matt varnish evens out any satin patches in the dark paint.

For a lava base, add crackle paint thickly over gritty texture, prime white, tint yellow then orange, drybrush red over the raised crust and stipple black on top. Leave the glow showing round the feet, ring the heat with blackened ground and grey ash, and drybrush light grey on the highest rock edges.

For spitting lava, flick a few specks of orange or white near the pools. Raised splashes can be made from thin clear plastic softened over a flame and pulled into shape, pressed into putty and coated with thick water-effect gel before painting.

guides.title: Painting leather straps
guides.summary: Dark brown base, a black wash or glaze in the recesses, glazed khaki tones and sharp sand edges, plus tiny cracks.
body: Line all straps with thinned black, then base a dark cool brown, leaving a little black at the edges.

Shade with thinned black, or a glaze of half base and half black, into the recesses. Mixing a soft brown wash with a darker one also works: the soft one flows evenly and the dark one sinks into the creases.
Glaze the base mixed with a khaki brown along the middle of each strap, then khaki alone, drawing towards the centre.

Edge highlight with a sandy khaki, or the brown mixed with a warm flesh tone, then pure sand or pale bone on the sharpest edges, where real straps rub. A big jump is fine if the line is thin. A rough, broken edge makes leather look worn. A few dots on toe caps and corners finish boots and pouches.
For texture, add a few short diagonal strokes, tiny lines and dots of the sand colour as cracks and scuffs. Use a different texture from cloth so the materials look distinct.
If the blending looks patchy, pass one thin glaze of a mid brown over the whole area to pull the tones together, then add the fine scratches on top to hide what is left.

Shiny leather is different: light gathers in folds, so paint thin bright lines down the recesses as well as soft broad highlights on the fold tops. For matt black leather, add a little rose or pink to black in one or two small thin passes; more turns it grey. For glossy black, finish with gloss varnish.

For speed, prime in a mid brown and dust a lighter brown over the top, so straps come pre-shaded. Thin the same brown for a stained strap, or base boots darker and edge them with it. Mix two or three leathers across a unit, and highlight each pouch's edges and flap so neighbours do not merge.

guides.title: Painting leaves and foliage
guides.summary: Rough colour patches on each leaf and thin dark lines between overlaps make sculpted foliage read clearly.
body: Base the leaves in a mid green, or a warm brown or orange for autumn, then wash a darker tone over them so the overlaps and gaps go dark.
Dab a darker or warmer colour into the middle of each leaf in a rough, hashed pattern. Outline the rest of the leaf in a pale opaque colour, letting a few dots stray into the centre.
Cover the pale outline with a bright yellow green. The pale colour underneath keeps it bright.
Paint thin lines of a deep purple or very dark green between overlapping leaves and in the recesses. It separates each leaf from the next.

Work a little of the main green into the edges of the bright colour to calm it and tie the colours together. Rough and scratchy strokes look right, so a steady hand is not needed. Vary the colour slightly from leaf to leaf.
For pink blossom, prime white and wash a bright pink one-coat paint, thinned half and half with medium, over the leaves. Then drybrush a pale pink with a little near-white in it.

guides.title: Painting marble
guides.summary: Stipple lighter colours through a stretched wipe or paint fine wandering veins, then gloss it so it reads as polished.
body: Base a mid-dark colour, keeping the paint thin next to trim. Stipple in a related dark for variation. Look at one real marble first to see whether its veins are cloudy, bubbly or crack-like.

Wipe method: stretch a baby wipe in every direction to open the holes more than seems right, wrap it tight over the panel and tape it. With a big firm brush, stipple progressively lighter colours, more towards the biggest openings. Dry each layer fully.
Paint past the edges as if the panel were cut from a larger block. Peel the wipe slowly, as damp wipes tear, and stipple a darker mix and pure white to boost contrast.

With an airbrush, base in the dark vein colour, wrap the stretched wipe snugly, and spray the light stone colour straight down at low pressure from a fair distance. Angled spray blurs the veins, and high pressure lifts the wipe.

Vein method for pale marble: buff a pale bone and then ivory over the surface, then thin a grey or khaki until inky. Black is too stark. Drag a fine brush across while wagging or slowly twisting it, so the line wanders and tapers. Let some veins split into branches, follow the main flow, and avoid criss-crossing.

Go over the middle of each vein again so it is strongest in the centre and fades at the edges. Start fresh veins on each separate block; they should not run smoothly across a join. If a vein comes out too bold, work thinned base colour in from its sides to narrow and soften it.

Do not judge it until the trim is painted and lined with a dark wash. Too light or too dark? Glaze back and stipple or line again. A very faint glaze of a cool green or other mineral tint adds realism; outdoor marble can also take brown dirt or green lichen glazes.
Marble is polished, so finish with a gloss or satin varnish, in thin coats so it does not pool.

guides.title: Shading and highlighting muscles
guides.summary: Shade only where forms face down and join neighbouring muscles with shared highlights, so the body reads as one shape.
body: The usual mistake is ringing every muscle with the same dark outline. Each one then looks like a separate island, and the skin reads as armour plates or a starved body.

Pick the light direction first; a zenithal undercoat from that side helps. Anything facing up catches light, even right next to a recess. Only surfaces facing down, such as under the arms, under the chest and the lower body, get the deepest shadow.
Gaps between muscles that face up should hold the midtone, not the darkest shade. Think of the skin as a sheet draped over the muscles rather than the muscles themselves.

Run the first highlight layers across the tops of neighbouring muscles, even over small recesses, so they join up. Only the last one or two, brightest steps pick out single muscles. Push each highlight right to the top of its form.

A wash pools in every recess equally and ignores the light. Use layers to place shadows, or steer the wash only into recesses that should be dark. Quicker route: wash the skin in two thin coats, paint the base back onto the muscles, then soften the hard edges with a half and half mix of base and a lighter tone.

On big smooth muscles, thin a slightly darker skin tone until runny and paint it on the undersides. Put a matching wash only in the deepest spots: armpits, between fingers, under the brow. A thinned lighter tone on the tops then fades in without true blending.

If the shadows are too strong, shrink them to a thin line instead of a wide band, or use a less dark colour. Covering an overdone patch with a low midtone, or glazing a mid step over it, reconnects the forms.
Keep shadows darker low on the body and lighter higher up, so the eye goes to the chest and face. Warm, slightly saturated browns in the shadows stop the skin looking grey.

guides.title: Painting white and cream cloth
guides.summary: Shade pale cloth with soft light washes and tiny steps, never a dark brown wash, and save pure white for last.
body: Pale colours show every flaw. Build a smooth base with quick thin coats and good drying time between; thick white goes chalky and hard edged. Over a black undercoat, many thin scratchy layers on the lit areas will get there, with the black showing through as shadow.

A dark brown wash over off-white turns it muddy. Paint the white first, then shade it with a soft wash of a darker ivory mixed with about four parts clear medium, or with glazes of sandy beige. A bone one-coat paint mixed half and half with medium also works: brush it into the folds and leave it alone while wet, as overworking it blotches.
Deepen with a khaki brown mixed with the sandy tone, and use khaki with dark brown only in the deepest folds.

Or work up from below: base a cream or sand for worn, aged white, or a light grey for crisp white, add a touch of darker colour on the downward faces and fold insides, then build up. If the base is very dark, the jump to white looks harsh.

Tinted greys make a livelier white: a warm reddish grey for shadows and a cool pale green-grey for highlights, or blue shadows with yellowish highlights. Snow has bluish shadows; cloth usually has yellowish or brownish ones. Next to dark, strong colours, quite a grey tone reads as white.
Keep each new layer only a little paler than the last, each over a smaller area. Small jumps hide mistakes, and pale cloth usually needs less contrast than you expect.
Use a size 4 or larger brush. It stays wet longer and can cover a whole cloak with one load. Add a little water in warm weather; pale paints dry fast and go grainy.

Save the brightest tone for last, sparingly, on creases and hems. An ivory looks warmer and less harsh than pure white over a whole garment. Going to white too early is the usual mistake. Wash the other colours afterwards, keeping it off the white.

guides.title: Painting rope
guides.summary: Base rope light, wash it brown, then highlight back along each twist with a finer pale top.
body: Base the rope in a light sandy beige so the wash has something to darken. A mid brown base also works if you want darker rope.
Wash with a brown shade so it runs into the twists.
Highlight back with the base colour in short dashes that follow each twist along the rope.
Add a finer highlight of pale yellow-cream on just the top of each twist.
Rope is a good job to do while another area dries, and it can share its colours with teeth or wood to save opening new paints.

guides.title: Building up rust
guides.summary: Build rust in shrinking glazes or dabs from dark brown to bright orange, on edges, rivets and wherever water sits.
body: Put rust where water would sit or run: pits, rivets, seams, inside corners, under overhangs and in streaks below fittings. Keep it mostly in shadowed areas, lightest on rubbed edges, leave some patches clean, and start small. Adding more is easy; taking it off is not.

Finish the metal first, or base a dark steel and scratch on a little silver. Then glaze a thin dark brown from plate edges and round rivets, pulling it the way water would run, and lift the brush straight up so it stops where you planned. Shrink the area with each layer, moving through mid brown to a low-coverage bright orange.

Quick weathering: thin an orange-brown with about five parts water. It looks strong wet and dries much softer, so build it in layers and add a brighter orange in the centre of the patches once dry. Round a rivet, blob the colour on and wipe the top clean with a fingertip.

For rough, pitted rust, stipple in patches, keeping deep brown showing, with tiny black flecks for pits and the odd white dot in them for bare metal. A scrap of sponge held in tweezers, dabbed almost dry, gives fine speckles. Use two or three tones; real rust is never one colour.

Rust texture paints give a crust. Stir well and stipple with an old brush, thin over fine detail. After about five minutes, rub raised areas gently with a sponge; too early removes too much, too late and it will not shift. Most reactivate with water. Bring back shine with a light metal drybrush on edges only.

Acidic rust reactor liquids keep working for hours. Wear gloves and eye protection and use an old brush. Flick it from a stiff brush pulled back with a toothpick for scattered spots, never with bare fingers; brushing it all over usually overdoes it. Judge the result the next day.

Rust should be dead matt; mix a little matt medium into a colour that dries with a sheen. Powdered rust pigment at about three parts powder to seven of water gives a subtle finish. Rust beside spotless paint looks fake, so haze the paint round heavy patches with a little pigment or a very thin brown filter.

On painted panels, put red-brown then orange inside chips, leaving a dark rim, and drag fine orange streaks down from a few. Finish by tapping bright silver along edges where the metal would rub clean, and a touch of bright orange on a few rivets. Next to blue or green, orange rust pops.

guides.title: Painting scales and scaly hide
guides.summary: Drybrush scales up in lighter, gentler steps with pale tips, and keep the gaps dark or dusty so each scale stands out.
body: Plan the light first. Upper surfaces catch the most light and thin parts of wings glow brighter. Lay out any pattern, such as dark markings over a blue, before highlighting, then highlight each colour in its own tones. Stipple the first lighter colour softly into the middle of the brightest areas.

Drybrush the base colour fairly generously to restore it on the raised scales, then a much lighter tone with a lighter touch, then lighter again. Finish with a very light flick of the palest tone on the scale tips. Use a clean, fully dry brush for each colour.

Start with a circular overbrush so raised areas take paint from every angle. To pick out particular ridges, brush across them, not along them. After a wash, do not press hard or you push paint back into the recesses.

Drybrush scales before neat work on the areas next to them, so any dust gets tidied later, and keep a small gap from spines and trim so the joins stay dark. Turn the model after each step; missed patches hide inside legs and under the belly.

Fast version over a black primer: airbrush light grey then off-white from above over the scaled top surfaces, leaving tail and feet dark. Lay the colour over it, then flood a black one-coat paint thinned half and half with medium across the hide. The primer light does the highlighting.

For dusty gaps, keep each scale mostly dark with only its tip lit, then run a pale enamel wash or liquid pigment between the scales. Wipe it off the raised tops with a sponge dampened with thinner so it stays only in the gaps.
Where a smooth belly meets the scales, glaze many very thin coats of a pinkish flesh along the join. Several weak coats give a soft change where one strong coat leaves a hard line.

For glossy scales on a display piece, treat each scale as a small polished stone: one side light, the other dark, with a sharp change between them. Edge highlight only the most exposed corners, with tiny bright dots on the sharpest. Painting a few scales in a different hue adds interest.

guides.title: Painting scars
guides.summary: Make a sculpted or painted scar read with a dark cut down the middle and pale, slightly pink raised edges.
body: Finish the skin first, including its highlights. A scar is a detail added on top of a finished face.

Run a very thin dark red into the cut. Once dry, mix a touch of black into that red and paint it into the deepest part of the line so it reads as a groove. A simpler version: mix the skin base about half and half with a dull red, thin it and paint it along the scar.
Highlight the raised lips either side of the cut with a paler skin tone with a little pink in it. On a big scar, the lower lip alone is often enough.

No sculpted scar? Paint a thin, narrow diamond of mid skin mixed with a little pinkish red, then a fine pale line along its centre. Or scratch a scar line into the plastic with a hobby knife before priming.

A faint red or purple-pink glaze around the scar, softened at its edge with a damp brush, makes it look fresh and tender. Keep it thin so it tints the skin rather than covering it. Leave it out for an old, healed one.
If the scar crosses an eye, leave the pupil off and paint the eye plain off-white so it looks blinded.
Keep the skin highlights around it. If you paint over them, the scar looks like a line drawn on rather than damaged skin.

guides.title: Painting sci-fi terrain
guides.summary: Paint dark sci-fi walls and interiors fast with a black primer, heavy drybrushing, washes and a few glowing screens.
body: Prime black. On busy terrain, any corner you miss just reads as shadow.

Apply the main colour with a big drybrush loaded quite heavily, worked in rough circles. Two passes act as a base coat but leave black in the deepest corners. For big walls, a strong colour sprayed straight from a can over near-black is just as quick.
Pick out vents, boxes and trims in a dark metal with a large brush, then smaller bits such as cables. Light silver on the worn edges of frames and fittings is enough.
Wash the lot with a slightly thinned brown wash and give it an hour. A second wash on the lower part of each wall makes it sit down into the board.
Drybrush the main colour again, then a lighter tone, and finish with a very light all over drybrush of pale bone to tie it together.

For interiors, drybrush a warm dark metal all over, build up lighter metal passes, and add coloured washes in a few recesses for grime and variety. If the inside is the star, keep the outside simple so the two do not compete.
Keep each terrain type to a short set of colours so a whole board can be batch painted. One strong accent, such as a rich yellow on crates and hazard props, ties the board together.
Block in where each light colour goes before detailing so you can check the balance. Paint the screens, then add tiny white lines as readouts.

guides.title: Painting scratches
guides.summary: Paint believable scratches as a thin pale line catching the light with a darker line along one side.
body: Use a sharp fine brush and paint thinned so it flows. Roll the tip to a point on the palette and test a stroke beside the model. Each scratch should be one quick stroke.

Mix a highlight a step lighter than the surface, or use bright silver for bare metal showing through. Paint short lines where things get knocked: edges, corners and lower areas. A photo of real scratched paint beside you gives more natural shapes than inventing them.

Mix a dark brown with a touch of the base colour and paint a thinner line tight against the pale one. The dark line is the shadow inside the gouge. Keep it on the upper side of the pale one; below, the scratch reads as raised. On bright reds, yellows and oranges, use a very dark version of the colour; black looks harsh.

For a nick across an edge, paint a small dark mark, then a thin pale line on its lit side and a tiny bright dot on each corner. Start edge scratches on the panel and run them off the edge, so the brush leaves the model safely.

Keep the direction similar across one part, as if from the same blows, and let a few run across several plates as one strike. Vary the length and size. Avoid pairs and even spacing, which look planned. Fewer scratches usually look better than many.

Match the light around them: a darker scratch with a softer highlight in shadowed areas, a paler one in lit areas. On metal, a few bright scratches also hide rough blending. A very thin red-brown filter, about ten parts water, then ages the metal; on brass a turquoise tint suggests corrosion.
On a painted stripe or panel, scratch it with the colour underneath as if it has worn back, then add a smaller dark line inside each one. Do this after transfers so they look worn too.
If a scratch looks wrong or too wide, paint the surrounding colour back over it and try again elsewhere.

guides.title: Painting sheer cloth
guides.summary: Paint see-through fabric by painting the skin underneath first, then glazing the cloth colour thinly over it.
body: Paint the skin and anything else under the cloth as if it were bare. Build the layers in the order they exist in real life.
Paint the cloth solid wherever it is thick, folded over, pulled away from the body or hanging free.
On folds lying against the skin, shade the underside and highlight the top, letting the highlight run a little past the sculpted fold.
Glaze very thin cloth colour over the covered skin, drying between passes. By airbrush, mask the rest and use light bursts of heavily thinned paint.
The number of passes sets how sheer it looks. Build more next to the solid folds and in shadows so it fades from opaque to see-through.
Gone too dark? Mix the skin highlight with a tiny bit of cloth colour, repaint the strongest lights such as cheekbones and collarbones, then glaze once more.
For a tattoo or freckles running under the cloth, paint them on the bare skin, then add the cloth colour to the same paint for the covered part.

guides.title: Painting shields
guides.summary: Paint shields off the model, layer rings of light towards the rim, and outline metal rims and bosses before painting them.
body: Paint shields off the model where you can: stick each to a pot lid or cork with tack putty, prime black and leave the back for last. A black primer saves outlining at small scale, though bright colours need more coats.

Start with the colour that covers most of the face. Over black, a bright colour goes on far faster over a darker related base: a red-brown under red, or the blue mixed about two to one with black under blue.
On a round shield, layer the highlights in rings, each lighter ring nearer the rim, so the light gathers towards the edge. A few small light touches where two colours meet raise the contrast.
With no metal rim, highlight the edge itself: add white to blues and yellow to greens. Lay the final light line along the rim with the brush held flat.

For metal rims and bosses, run a fine line of watery black along every metal part first, then paint inside it. Iron: silver, then darken the recesses with thin black lines. Bronze: gold and brown mixed evenly, a brown ink wash, then silver added to the mix for one or two highlights.
Tidy any black that strayed onto the face of the shield, paint the back, such as brown with wood grain, then glue the shield on.

guides.title: Eyes on small models
guides.summary: Simple eyes for tabletop scale: a dark line or socket with soft off-white, never stark black and white.
body: Make sure the area around the eye is already dark, from shading or a thin line of dark brown or black run into the socket. Sockets left skin coloured look blank and odd. When you base the skin, leave a thin dark line round the eye; it frames it and hides small wobbles.

The quickest option: skip the eyeball. A dark warm brown in the socket reads as eyes in shadow, and slightly wrong eyes look worse than none. Under a helmet, one thin dark line per eye is plenty. Or fill the eye with one flat colour: off-white for people, red or yellow for monsters.
For painted eyes, fill the eye with an off-white or light grey rather than pure white, using near-black instead of pure black. Softer contrast reads better at this size.

Ways to place the pupil: paint the white across the socket and add a short upright dark line touching top and bottom; or dot off-white either side of a dark line; or paint the socket white, let very thin black, about one to four with water, flow into the recess round it, then dot the pupils with thicker black.

Avoid a round dot floating in the middle of the white. It makes the figure look startled. Check both eyes look the same way from several angles, as the sculpt can mislead; if one looks sideways, make the other match.
On a larger face, one tiny pure white dot on the same side of each eye adds a reflection. A vertical slit pupil makes a creature look beastly.

Thin the paint to an inky flow, test it on your thumb, brace both hands and come in from the side. Paint heads before gluing if you can. If it goes wrong, repaint with the socket colour once dry and try again.

guides.title: Painting smoke
guides.summary: Paint smoke in tinted greys with each puff lit on top, and add white then fluorescent colour if it glows from inside.
body: Avoid plain black and white greys. Base the smoke in a near-black or a dark grey with a purple tint, in a couple of thin coats.

Shape every puff. Highlight the top of each billow with a cool blue-grey or warm reddish grey, using the tip or side of the brush, and leave the recesses dark. That contrast makes it read as a rolling plume.

Keep the brightest layers towards the far end of the plume. Thin smoke lets more light through, so it reads paler away from the source. Glaze back and forth to smooth; for plain smoke you can stop there.
Where smoke rises from something hot, leave a small gap at the join so a little of the glow colour still shows.

For smoke lit from inside, darken it first, then paint near white into the deepest creases under each puff and inside the source. Cover the white and a little beyond with a thin fluorescent colour. Over grey or black the fluorescent loses its punch.
Each glowing puff should run from bright at the bottom, to darkest across its middle, to the normal grey light on top. Keep glow off the tops so it looks lit from within.

Blend with many thin glazes of mixes of the glow, dark and grey. Intensify the core with repeated small dots of white then fluorescent, each smaller than the last, and glaze a similar ink where the glow meets the smoke.
For quick ghostly smoke or spirits, wash grey over the area, run a dull and a bright green into the deepest parts, and pick out the raised parts in white. Purple works the same way.

guides.title: Soft, youthful and feminine faces
guides.summary: Keep shading and highlights subtle and thin on soft faces, or they quickly start to look harsh and older.
body: Soft faces are sculpted with few lines beyond the eyes, nose and mouth. Heavy shadows and bright highlights make them look harsh.
Paint the head separately if you can, over a white, grey or bone primer, so you start pale.
Apply a pale, slightly pink flesh in two very thin coats. Thick paint clogs the subtle sculpting, and the colour dries a little darker than it looks wet.

Shade with a few warm flesh tones, each darker than the last and thinned to a wash, used in smaller amounts each time: hairline, around the eyes, beside the nose and mouth, and a touch under the cheek. Still define the key borders: between the lips, under the nose and below the lower lip.
Work back and forth: shade a little, highlight a little, then repeat. It stops the face drifting too dark or too light. Rounder faces have few recesses, so the smoothness of the glazes matters more.

Highlight with thin glazes of pale flesh mixed with a pale yellow, then a cream, and only a very thin white on the highest points. White alone dulls skin; yellow keeps it lively. No hard lines anywhere. On small heads, one soft highlight is often enough; strong highlights age a face.

Light one side of the face a little more than the other. Keep the jawline softer than the forehead and brighten the chin only slightly. Glaze the lower lip with a thinned reddish tone in several coats. Judge it at arm's length; close-up photos make highlights look harsher than they are.
For large, cartoon-style faces, keep features soft and simple. Sketch the eye shapes lightly first so they are level, then fill them with a small gradient and a bright white dot.

guides.title: Painting stitching
guides.summary: Pick out stitches on leather and cloth with a dark line around them, a light sandy colour and a tiny highlight.
body: Run a thinned black or dark brown around the stitches to separate them from the leather or cloth.
Paint the stitches a sandy, light khaki or bone colour. Touch each stitch with the brush tip rather than dragging a line along them.
Add white to that colour and dot the top of each stitch. Do it with your other final highlights.
If a stitch smudges, tidy it with the dark line colour once dry rather than painting over the whole row.

To paint stitches where none are sculpted, such as stitched skin, draw a dark seam line, then short dark bars across it with a dot at each end, a little wider than seems right. Paint a thin pale line down the middle of each bar, reloading every few stitches.
Trim a wobbly pale line back with the dark colour. A tiny lighter mark just below each hole makes it look punched in, and a touch of deep red where the thread enters suits stitched wounds.

guides.title: Painting stone and rock
guides.summary: Paint stone walls and rock quickly with a base spray, drybrushing in two tones and stippling for texture.
body: A fast start: spray the building a mid green, then while wet dust grey over it from one angle. The green left in the recesses looks like moss and age. A plain grey or brown base works too.

Avoid a plain neutral grey. Real stone holds browns, greens, purples and reds, so mix grey with a dark brown, or lighten a deep red brown with a pale green. For desert stone, use warm pinkish greys and bone.

For rocks on a base, base, wash and drybrush. A brown wash makes grey stone look natural, a black wash makes it read as rubble, and a green wash suggests moss. On buildings, a dark brown pin wash in the mortar lines over satin varnish, cleaned back with a damp brush, adds depth.

Drybrush all the stonework a sandy brown, heavier in some places than others, then catch the edges and sticking-out stones with a bone colour. Start with a fully dry brush and go lightly with pale tones, or the stone turns chalky.

For speckled natural rock, load a large brush, wipe most of the paint off, then stab straight down rather than dragging. Alternate rounds: stipple a lighter colour, darken with a thin wash, stipple again. Each round adds depth.

Add colour shifts: a very thin cool blue-grey glaze over the midtones between warm shadows and highlights, a little red pigment in low spots for iron staining, and green where moss would start. Too pale? Glaze the dark mix back over.

Even surfaces look like plastic. Thin the stone colour so it covers a little unevenly, then dab lighter and darker mixes onto random stones, or glaze a few scattered bricks in a warm tone and dab each with tissue. Keep it to a small, spread-out share, with no repeating pattern, or the wall looks spotty.

Big areas of one colour still look dull. Break them up with moss, pigment, stains, scorching or a few stones in a different tone. Lower walls can take a darker drybrush and a little earth or black pigment as grime.

guides.title: Painting tank tracks
guides.summary: Give tracks a dull, grimy cast iron look with a rough dark metal base, a brown wash, worn edges and dust.
body: Treat tracks like basing: choose colours that suit the model and the ground it stands on rather than one fixed recipe. Paint them before fitting if the kit allows.

Stipple on a thick mix of dark silver and a flat brown with an old drybrush. Two coats give solid colour and a slightly rough, cast surface. A quicker start is a brown base or a deep brown one-coat stain, then a light dark silver drybrush over the raised links so the brown still shows in places.

Wash the whole track in a dark or red-brown wash. An enamel or oil wash gives more working time; let the acrylic dry fully, ideally overnight, and a gloss varnish first helps the wash flow and clean back.
When an enamel or oil wash is touch dry, wipe the flat areas with a dense make-up sponge dampened with white spirit. The base colour comes back and the grime stays in the recesses.
Rub soft pencil graphite onto the raised links and edges with a fingertip for a dull, worn sheen. Save bright silver for the sharpest edges, where fresh wear would show.

For dust, mix pigments to match the soil, thin them with white spirit to about skim milk and brush over the tracks and lower wheels. Once dry, clean the raised parts with a cotton bud. Or give tracks and wheels a very light drybrush of pale bone or earth to tie them to the hull and base.

For heavy grime, dab earth or mud texture paste onto tracks, wheels and the lower hull; it also hides print lines. Flick on a little dark, wet-looking mud last. Hold back: overdone weathering looks fake.

guides.title: Painting tartan and plaid
guides.summary: Space guide lines evenly round the cloth, paint crossing stripes between them, then shade the whole pattern as one.
body: Base the cloth in two or three thin coats, spreading each coat around so no texture builds up. Leave the shading wash until the pattern is done.

Space the pattern before you start. Paint one upright line at the front, one at the back and one on each side, then add lines halfway between them, and halve again for a finer check. The pattern then closes up evenly with no odd gap.

Keep stripes about a millimetre wide and a couple of millimetres apart, in a darker shade or a thin contrasting colour. On a curved cloak, let the gaps widen slightly towards the hem so the lines follow the folds.
Add a second colour beside or between the first lines, then the cross lines. Paint the first one parallel to the hem and work upwards, following the curve of the cloth.
Where lines cross, a small square of a third colour sells the weave. Tidy wobbles with the colour underneath.
Shade and highlight the whole cloth over the finished pattern to tie it together. Aim for the impression of tartan at arm's length; folds hide a lot of wobble.

guides.title: Painting tattoos
guides.summary: Mix tattoo ink from blue, a touch of black and some skin colour so the design sits under the skin.
body: Finish the skin first. Pick a smooth area such as a forearm, chest or the side of a shaved head.

Mix a mid blue with a little black and some of the skin colour. The blue gives the faded look of real ink, and the skin tone stops it sitting on top like fresh paint. On dark or green skin, go much darker or paler so it shows. A drop of flow improver helps it run.
Thin the mix and paint the core of each shape first, smaller and thinner than the final size, then build it out. Starting too big means cutting back with skin colour, which is much harder.
Keep the design simple: bands, dots, zigzags or a simple symbol read well at this scale. Run it right up to the edge of a sleeve or strap so it looks like it carries on underneath.

Let it dry fully, or seal it with varnish, then glaze a thin skin mix over it so it sits in the skin. A thin highlight mix over the parts facing the light fades it further; a stronger glaze makes it look old. Skip the glaze for a crisp, fresh design.

War paint is different: it sits on top of the skin and can look stark. The quickest way is a bright one-coat paint over the finished, highlighted skin, so the highlights show through it. Face camouflage works as broad stripes of a very dark green, then a mid green.

guides.title: Painting teeth
guides.summary: Paint teeth from a sandy brown at the root up to off-white at the tips, so they look set into the gums.
body: Base the teeth a warm sandy brown, or a dark brown or grey-brown for dirtier, older teeth. A dark gum line or mouth around them helps them stand out.
Mix in a bone colour and paint the upper two thirds of each tooth, leaving the root darker. Keep the paint thin so the earlier layer shows through and adds depth.
Add white to that mix and paint the tips only. The darker roots make them look set into the gums.
On fangs and big teeth, paint a few lines from root to tip as growth lines, paler ones nearer the tip, and finish with an ivory dot on the point.
Tiny teeth have no room for shading, so start brighter with a light sand, go straight to bone and finish with a dot of white on each tip.
Avoid pure white all over. It looks like plastic and draws the eye in the wrong way. Make teeth further back in the mouth darker, and use the same dark shadow colour inside the mouth as in the skin.

Paint the inside of the mouth, the tongue and gums before the final tooth layers so you do not spoil the teeth, then line round them with a dark colour if they need separating. For glassy, alien teeth, work up from a very dark grey to white instead.

guides.title: Brush painting vehicles and large kits
guides.summary: Paint vehicles and big kits by brush, panel by panel: prime, shade, layer up, edge highlight and chip.
body: You do not need an airbrush. Spray prime in the main colour first, which saves a lot of brush time on big areas. Over a light-from-above zenithal primer, the main colour thinned to a glaze keeps recesses darker and edges bright; without one, use two thin opaque coats.
Shade each panel slightly darker towards one end, and run a recess shade into the joins between panels.

Layer back up with lighter tones, working one panel at a time with a large brush so the coats stay smooth. Soft drybrushing in several steps also works: start each colour in the panel centres and fade towards the edges, brighter on top and darker low down.

Quick hull: run a wash into recesses and round rivets, then drybrush the base colour in small circles over everything to soften any harsh wash marks. Flick a paler tone over the edges and a pale bone very lightly on the sharpest corners.

Finish with crisp edge highlights in the brightest tone along the top edges, and pick out rivets in a slightly lighter mix. Repaint a hatch or access panel a little lighter so it stands out. If a highlight looks stark, mix in some base colour and go over it.

Paint metallics last, with a cool metal such as steel on tracks and a warm one such as copper on exhausts. Paint tools, cans and stowage off the model where you can, then run a dark brown wash round them and pass the hull's pale drybrush over everything so it all looks dusty together.

Add chipping and weathering on edges, corners and low areas where it would get knocked or muddy. A sponge covers big areas quickly; use the brush only where the sponge cannot reach. Weather stowage by different amounts so some looks newer.

Break up big flat areas with markings, a second colour or weathering so they do not look plain. Keep the main colours muted and place a few bright accents with care. Use rivets and panel lines as guides for stripes rather than freehanding straight lines.

guides.title: Painting verdigris
guides.summary: Build patchy turquoise corrosion on brass, bronze and copper, thickest where water would sit.
body: Finish the metal first, including its shade and highlights; a dark brown-black wash over brass is a good start. Iron rusts orange, but brass, bronze and copper turn blue-green. Look at photos of real verdigris: it is random, patchy and thickest around rivets, dents, holes and recesses.

Thin a deep jade or mid green to a wash, about four parts water to one of paint. Touch it into recesses and the shadowed side so it flows in by itself, starting each stroke outside the recess and ending in its deepest part. Dry and repeat where you want it stronger.
Go over part of those patches with a brighter turquoise, letting some of the first green show. Leave any tide marks; they read as water staining.

Dab a little pale blue-green into the deepest spots or onto rivet tops only; a touch of light flesh tone in the mix gives a chalky crust. Do not weather evenly everywhere. Even an ultra-thin turquoise glaze in the deepest shadows alone makes copper read as copper.
For heavy corrosion, darken the metal first with a dark metallic or dull brown-grey stippled where water collects, then stipple greens from deep to pale over smaller areas each time.
Quick version: base a dark metallic brown, brush a dark turquoise one-coat paint over it unthinned, then pick out rivets and edges in a bright old brass.

Verdigris effect and patina texture paints: shake hard and use an old brush. Slightly diluted they dry to a natural minty crust; neat they look flat. Work one small area at a time, mostly in recesses, and wipe raised areas back with a damp cotton bud. Make sure any enamel underneath is fully dry first.

Re-brighten raised details with bright metal or silver so they stand clear of the green, keeping verdigris off spots that would be rubbed clean. For realism, pull thin pale streaks straight down from rivets and cracks as runoff, always working top to bottom.

guides.title: Getting children into painting
guides.summary: Give a child a big, simple, expressive model and keep the first sessions about fun and their own choices, not technique.
body: Small, detailed armoured figures are a poor first model for a child. Tiny lenses and fine trim make it easy to feel they have failed. Pick something large with a big face, big eyes and a fun pose; a primed plastic toy works too.
Start with a few minutes of talk about how colours tell a story, such as what a red creature with yellow eyes says about where it lives. Do not dwell on how small the model is.
Let them colour in a line drawing of the model first. It is a safe way to plan colours and practise staying in the lines.
When they paint, teach only two things: how to load the brush and how to rinse between colours. Set out a few colours, a water pot and old clothes, and let the rest wait.
Ask about the figure's name and story and praise their choices rather than the neatness.
Do not rush. Painting one part, like the face, is a good session, and they can finish another day. Never push a shy child to show their work.

guides.title: Painting clubs and painting with others
guides.summary: Painting nights, clubs and online groups give feedback, motivation and new ideas, and need only a small travel kit.
body: Painting with other people speeds up learning. You see how someone holds a brush, thins paint or picks colours, which is hard to learn from photos alone.
Look for hobby clubs, gaming groups, library or community centre craft nights and local hobby venues that run painting evenings. Many welcome complete beginners and people who only paint.
Online groups and forums help when there is nothing nearby. Share work in progress, join a monthly painting challenge, or paint along with friends on a call.
Take a small kit: a few brushes, the paints for one model, a water pot with a lid, a palette, paper towel, a lamp and a mat to protect the table. Clean up fully before you leave.
Bring one model and a modest goal. Busy rooms are better for base coats, washes and talking than for your most delicate blending.
Ask questions and offer help. Most painters are happy to show a trick. Share paints or tools only if you are happy to lend them.
A group project, such as each person painting one model for a shared scene or a club board, keeps people coming back and finishes things no one would do alone.

guides.title: Painting wood grain
guides.summary: Paint wood grain with loose broad lines, then finer, lighter wobbly lines and a pale edge.
body: Base all the wood a dark brown in a few thin coats, then wash with thinned black or dark brown to fill the recesses. Using the same wood colour across a model ties it together. Check it still contrasts with nearby bone and leather.
With the base brown slightly thinned, paint broad loose lines along the length of the wood, letting them run together and leaving dark gaps.

Paint finer lines inside the first ones with a lighter brown mix, then lighter again. Let them wobble, merge and split, and add the odd knot. Do each lighter step in two thin passes and never retrace every earlier line.

On smooth parts with no sculpted grain, such as small barrels, pull long, slightly wavy lines of inky dark brown along each plank instead, breaking some off. Skip this where grain is sculpted, as painted lines over real texture look busy.

Gather the brightest lines near edges, ends and breaks, where wood is driest. A few tiny dots stippled over the surface suggest rough, pitted timber. On small weapon stocks, two sets of thin lines in a warmer red or orange brown are enough.
Finish with a pale grey-brown edge highlight using the side of the brush, and a few small chips in the light mix on handles for wear. A fine black line where wood meets metal separates them.

Old, weathered wood turns grey and silvery. Start from a grey-green or grey-brown and glaze brown over it, or paint grey and ivory grain and warm it with an even sepia wash, which tints the lines and keeps the texture.

Do not highlight every line or it looks harsh. For variety across planks, filter a few chosen ones with a reddish, greenish or yellowish paint thinned about one to ten, wiping most off first. Look at a photo of real wood for the pattern.

guides.title: Shading armour panels
guides.summary: Darken the lower part of each armour plate with a quick wet blend, then line the deepest recesses.
body: Work one panel at a time. Paint most of it in the main colour, leaving the bottom edge.
While it is still wet, add a little black or a dark shade at the bottom and brush back and forth to pull it up into the colour.
Let it dry and repeat to smooth streaks. Move on to another panel while each one dries.

Glaze method: make a very thin darker tone, about half and half with glaze medium, dab most of it off and paint the lower part of the panel. It dries in seconds, so add a second coat ending a little lower and a third right at the bottom. A lighter glaze from the top down to halfway adds more depth.
Wash method: after the recess wash, push extra wash towards the bottom of each plate and let it dry fully. Two or three passes give a smooth fade.
Thin black to an inky flow and run it into the deepest lines with a fine brush.

Highlight in stages: a broad edge line in a mid mix, softened on large curves with the base colour while wet, then thinner, brighter lines, then tiny spots on the sharpest points. Skip edge highlights where heavy weathering will go.

Harsh steps mean too big a jump between tones; add an in-between mix and thin the paint more. Weathering darkens a model, so aim a little brighter than you want. On big flat panels a simple light-to-dark fade from top to bottom reads well.

guides.title: Panel lining
guides.summary: Run a dark wash, ink or thinned one-coat paint neatly into panel lines so edges and plates stand apart.
body: Pick a liquid that stays dark when thin: ink and contrast-style paints hold a fine point, while thinned black acrylic tends to come out grey. Tint it with a touch of the dark base colour to match the scheme; on pale armour, black with a brown wash looks less harsh. When unsure, go darker.
A gloss varnish first lets the wash flow along the groove. Water-based washes run least well, thinned contrast-style paints better, and enamel or oil washes best of all.

On a matt surface, brush clean water into the line first and wait a few seconds so the flats start to dry while the groove stays wet. Then touch the tip of a lightly loaded brush into it and the wash runs along the water instead of flooding the panel.
Keep the model level so the wash does not run up the groove, and go twice for darker lines. Touch and let it run rather than dragging the brush across raised panels. Wipe excess off the brush first.

Spills: on gloss, wipe wet wash off the flats with a dry cotton bud, and lift dried oil or enamel with a bud just damp with its thinner. Adding plenty of medium keeps an acrylic mix wet long enough to wipe. Dried water-based wash on matt paint will not come off.

Enamel pin wash on vehicles: over varnish, run the wash into recesses and round rivets, leave it 30 to 60 minutes, then clean the excess with a brush damp with white spirit. Stroke downward on vertical faces to leave faint streaks. Patch missed lines with thinned dark acrylic.

Watercolour also works: paint dark watercolour, mixed to a runny paste, messily into every line over the finished acrylic, which should be a little brighter than wanted. Let it dry matt, then dab the flats with a damp clean brush to lift it, wiping the brush between passes.
Do it before edge highlights. A bright edge looks brighter next to a dark line, and the highlights tidy any slips.

guides.title: Parchment and scrolls
guides.summary: Paint parchment strips and scrolls in a warm or cool pale tone, aged with a sepia wash and fake text.
body: Choose warm or cool to suit the model. A pale sand works for most, but next to lots of warm cream or bone, use a cool light grey so the parchment stands apart. On a dark, muted model, keep the paper muted too, and match its shadows to the model's warm or cool shadows.
Base a sandy tan or the cool grey in two coats, then layer a paler bone or grey over everything except the creases between pages. Strokes running across the strip read as paper texture if they show.
Highlight the raised folds with a pale cream, painting across the strip in the direction of the folds. Add a smaller, whiter highlight on the highest folds.
Age it with a thin orange-brown sepia at the top edge, down the creases and in any nicks. On cool parchment, shade with a thin blue-grey instead.
Run thinned white along the outer edges and curled ends with the side of the brush.
Paint the writing last. Use tiny thin squiggles, dots and dashes in a dark brown, which looks softer and more natural than pure black. At this scale they read as text.
If the writing looks stuck on, pass a thin glaze of the parchment colour over it in places so it sits in the surface. Glaze a little brown back into the folds if you lose the shading.
Quick version for a squad: base a pale brown, highlight the raised parts and curled edges with a pale cream, then wash the whole strip brown so it ages and settles into the folds.

guides.title: Pearl and shell sheen
guides.summary: Shade a pale grey towards purple-blue and highlight it towards green-yellow for a pearly shimmer.
body: Start from a soft mid grey or silver grey as the middle tone.
Shade towards a cool purple-blue rather than black or plain grey.
Highlight towards a pale green-yellow rather than plain white, keeping the very top point near white.
Keep the changes between these tints smooth with thin glazes. The shifting colour is what sells the pearl look.
The same idea on dark armour plates gives a mussel-shell style metal, with blue-purple and green hints in a near-black.

guides.title: Porcelain and doll-like faces
guides.summary: Porcelain faces are pale, smooth and glossy, with soft cool shadows, flat painted features and a crack or two.
body: Porcelain has very little shading. Base the face in a pale off-white, #eee8de, and keep the shadows soft, light and cool, such as a pale blue grey, #b9bfc8.
Blend with thin glazes. Every rough step shows on a pale surface. Keep shadow to the eye sockets, under the nose and along the jaw.
Paint features the way a doll is painted: flat and stylised. Round rosy cheeks as a soft glaze of pink, #e3a1a6, thin dark lashes, and small crisp lips in a deep rose, #a3384a.
Make the eyes glassy and a little large. Paint the iris, a black pupil and a white dot, then gloss the eye alone so it looks like glass.
Cracks sell the material. Paint a thin dark grey line, #4a4a50, that wanders and branches. Run a fine pale line along one side, as if light catches the broken edge.
A chip shows the dull ceramic under the glaze. Paint a small patch of matt warm off-white, #e2d8c6, with a fine dark line around it.
Finish with gloss varnish on the face and hands only, and keep clothes and hair matt. The difference in shine is what makes it read as porcelain.

guides.title: Pre-highlighting
guides.summary: Paint or drybrush light areas before a wash or see-through paint so the highlights show through it.
body: Pre-highlighting means putting the light in first. A pale layer underneath makes thin or see-through colours over it look brighter and ready-shaded.

Quick version: over a light primer, drybrush a pale sand all over, heavier where you want it to stay light, then apply thinned colour, about half paint and half water. Over black, drybrush a mid grey then white on the highest points; the model looks black and white, and that map of light is the point. It suits shaky hands.
Precise version: paint a pale colour only on the areas you will highlight and on small raised details, let it dry, then go over with the main colour.

A flesh colour drybrushed heavily over grey primer bases the skin in one step and lights the cloth for tints. Give faces and hands extra attention. The drybrush also shows up small details you might miss.

After the colour goes on, soak up any that pools on flat areas with a dry brush. Paint black undersuits back in, since the tint stains them. Clean the brush well between steps and restore any panel lines you covered.
On black or brown items, paint quick lighter highlights first, then one wash over the top pulls it together.

For smooth panels without an airbrush, stipple white with a soft domed brush onto the middle of each panel over a dark undercoat, then smear several very thin coats of a see-through colour over it. With an airbrush, spray thin white only where the light lands, then a brighter colour over it.
It is not only for the start. At any stage you can paint white back where you want brightness and glaze colour over it. Add a second thin coat of colour only where you want it darker.

guides.title: Pressing chainmail, scales and rivets into putty
guides.summary: Let putty firm up a little, keep tools wet, and press repeating patterns in rows with simple tubes, nibs and mesh.
body: After mixing, let the putty firm up for 20 to 40 minutes so it holds a mark but no longer sticks. Too soft and the pattern smears. Too hard and it cracks at the edges.
Keep tools and fingers wet with water, or a thin smear of petroleum jelly, so the putty does not grab. Press straight down and lift straight up.

Chainmail: press rows of rings with the end of a thin hollow tube, such as fine brass tube or an empty pen refill. Offset each row by half a ring. Fine metal mesh pressed in gives a quicker mail texture.
Scales: press the end of a cut tube or a pen nib at a slight angle. Work from the bottom up so each row overlaps the one below, and make the scales smaller near joints and edges.
Rivets: press a thin tube for a ring, or roll tiny balls of putty and press them on with a wet tool. Space them evenly using a strip of tape marked at regular steps.

For lots of repeating detail, sculpt one good strip, press it into reusable mould putty, and use the mould as a stamp. Texture rollers on a flat sheet of putty also work; cut the sheet to shape once it firms.
Blend the edges of the textured patch into the model before it cures, then leave it at least a day before priming.

guides.title: Quartered and split designs
guides.summary: Paint halved and quartered shields or uniforms with a clean dividing line by working one colour up to the other.
body: Decide the layout first: halves, quarters, or one main colour with accents. Moving colours around is easy at base coat stage and hard later. Do metals and small details before the split so you are not painting round them afterwards.
Paint the darker colour first. A pale colour like yellow can then go up to it without the dark one spoiling the join.

Find the centre from a seam, emblem or inner detail on the panel rather than the whole outline. Small dots in a cross shape help on flat shields. On armour and clothing, most splits can follow natural lines such as a belt or the edge of a chest plate.
Fill most of the area quickly, then slow down near the line and pull the brush downwards in one smooth motion, creeping closer each pass. Turn the model so every stroke runs the same comfortable way.
For a split straight down a leg or across a flat shield, mask one side with thin tape, paint up to it and peel it once dry. Tidy any paint that crept under the edge.
Bring the second colour up to meet the first, then cut back into each colour with the other to straighten any wobbles. Later chipping and weathering hide small ones too.
Repeat the split on smaller shields and cloth, and alternate the two colours around trim and pennants so the pattern carries across the whole model.
Shade and highlight each colour as normal afterwards so the marking matches the rest of the model.

guides.title: Quick faces for tabletop
guides.summary: Fast faces for small models: midtone skin, an all-over wash, a couple of highlights and simple eyes.
body: Keep small faces to a few colours and set them all out on the palette before you start. Too many tones on a tiny face quickly look messy. A hair dryer speeds up drying between layers.
Base coat a midtone skin in two or three thin coats, then wash the whole face so the recesses fill. Lift any wash that pools on flat areas with a clean, damp brush.

Layer the midtone back over the raised parts: brow, nose, cheeks and chin. On small models one lighter step, made by adding a pale ivory, is often enough. Thin it more than feels right so it sits smoothly over the wash.
Keep the eye sockets dark. On most tabletop heads, solid dark eyes look fine. If you want more, paint a near-white eye with a dark rim and a dark pupil.
Paint teeth in an ivory or off-white, never pure white, which looks false. Check the ears, which are easy to miss.

Leave the darker base showing as thin lines around the features to define them. Use brown for skin shadows and lines, as black looks unreal. If you cover a line, paint it back with a fine brush. If the face looks flat, run a little warm brown wash into the eye sockets and under the nose.
For a warmer look, block the cheeks, mouth and lower face in a red-brown first, then build flesh highlights on the raised planes.
For big batches, one coat of a one-coat skin paint over a light primer and a light dry brush of a matching skin tone is enough. Do not add a second coat just because it looks pale.

guides.title: Quick highlights for speed painting
guides.summary: Add a few fast lines and dots on upward edges and the head to make a speed paint look finished.
body: Highlight only the edges that face up: head, shoulders, knees, feet and the top of any pack. That may be enough.

Mix each highlight from the colour already in use plus your palest colour, such as an ivory, rather than opening new pots. Start with the face and the main colour, and stop whenever you like. On a big army those two are often enough, and the step can wait until the models are table ready.
Paint a single thin line, not a thick line then a thin one. It is faster and more forgiving.
Use the side of the bristles on long edges and weapon edges. A familiar brush that holds its shape matters more than a new one.
For a second step, put a lighter colour on only a short section of the first line, where your lamp actually hits.
Another fast way: paint one bold, very pale highlight, then glaze heavily thinned base colour over the area. The glaze tints the line, ties it in and hides wobbles, so you need not fix each line.
Spend most of the time around the head and any unique details. Keep the recesses dark so the contrast stays strong. Everything else can stay rough.
Set out every colour for the group before you start. Aim for about a minute of highlights per model.

guides.title: Quick minor materials
guides.summary: Fast tricks for small leather, cloth, gold and metal details so they look done without much time.
body: Small details matter less than the main areas. Two quick routes: a clean base coat, a wash of a thinned darker colour and one bright highlight, or one coat of a one-coat paint and one edge highlight.
Leather: a light tan one-coat paint, dry, then a dark brown one-coat over it. Or warm brown with short hatched strokes of a highlight for texture.
Cloth: base a grey and add one highlight colour in about three thin passes, each smaller than the last.
Gold: a strong single-coat gold shaded with a warm brown wash that dries slightly glossy. If it looks too bright, mix in a little dark metal for an old, tarnished look.

Steel: a very dark metallic, or a dark metal mixed half and half with black, then hatched lines of steel and bright silver on the edges. Over black primer, a dry brush of light grey and a dark wash is faster. A touch of very thin green in a few spots suggests old patina.
Bone: a cream bone base and a dark grey or brown wash. Gems: deep red on the lower part with black left at the top corner, an orange-red highlight, then a white dot.
Buckles: paint the whole buckle and strap end metal, then drop the strap colour into the middle. It is faster than painting round the buckle.
Run thinned black where materials meet, such as a strap on cloth. Stipple brown pigment up over the boots to tie the model to its base.

guides.title: Base, wash and tidy method
guides.summary: The fast routine for tabletop troops, board game pieces and rpg heroes: base coat, wash, tidy or drybrush, then highlights.
body: Prime white or light grey so colours go on bright in one or two coats.

Block in every colour, including small details and markings, before any wash. Go a little lighter than you want, because the wash darkens it. Neatness matters less than coverage, and slips are easiest to fix now while every colour is still flat.

Wash the whole model a couple of areas at a time. Pick the wash by colour: black for very dark colours and steel, brown for mid tones, leather and gold, a light brown or grey for pale colours and white. Lift pools on flat areas such as cloth so it does not dry blotchy, and let it dry fully. Skin often looks better with its own warm wash.
Wash once only. A second wash darkens everything again and means more highlighting to win the colour back. On a leader, a second wash in just the deepest spots is fine.

Tidy: thin each base colour a little and repaint it on the raised and flat areas, skipping every recess. Leave a very thin coat on narrow trims so a hint of shade shows. The model is now ready for the table, and boots, belts and pouches often need nothing more.
On smooth armour, a heavy soft drybrush of the base colour can replace the tidy step, followed by a very light drybrush of a lighter colour on the edges.

Optional: a lighter highlight on the top edges where light lands, and thinned black in deep recesses to restore lines between colours. Very dark areas can skip the wash and go straight to an edge highlight.
Paint details after any drybrushing so overspill does not matter. Reuse one area's base colour as another's highlight where it suits. Each stage stands alone, so you can stop and come back later.

guides.title: Recess shading and lining
guides.summary: Put a dark shade only into recesses by hand, for a cleaner finish than an all-over wash.
body: An all-over wash dulls bright colours and stains flat areas, and you then spend time painting them back. Recess shading puts the shade only into creases, joins and panel lines. Keep all-over washes for textured parts like fur, mail and rough cloth.

Use a small brush that holds a sharp point. Thin a wash or a darker version of the base colour well, around one part paint to four of water. Wipe off the excess, touch the tip into the recess and let the paint run along the line. Clean any spill straight away while it is wet.
You need not line every gap. Start where definition matters most: around the face, knees, feet and pack, and the joins between plates.
For a gentler step, first glaze a thinned mid-dark shade around the recess, then run the fine dark line only into the deepest gaps. It stops a panel jumping straight from base colour to near black.
Where a sculpted line is shallow, paint the dark line in with the same care as an edge highlight. Highlights either side make it look deep.
Shade where two surfaces meet with each surface's own darkest tone, not a black line, which looks like a cartoon outline. Shade by depth: deep creases get more, shallow dips less.
Make lines a little lighter near bright highlights and darker low down, with most shade on undersides away from the light. Fix slips once dry with the neighbouring colour.
Alternatives: gloss varnish, an oil or enamel wash wiped back, then matt varnish. On a large vehicle, a soft drybrush of the base colour afterwards hides smudges and softens the lines.

guides.title: Writing down your painting recipe
guides.summary: Write every paint, mix and step down in order, so a scheme can be repeated across an army or done in short sessions.
body: Once a scheme works on a test model, write the steps down in order: the area, the colour, the paint you used, how thin it was and the technique, such as base coat, wash or edge highlight.
Keep it short. Note what changes the result, not every stroke. Most schemes need a modest set of paints, with the rest mixed, so record the mix ratios as well as the pots.

Include the checks that are easy to forget, such as the primer colour, which wash went on which area and the order of steps. Skipping one can mean redoing work or a model that does not match the rest.
With the list in front of you there is nothing to decide. Sit down for twenty minutes, do one step across a batch and put it away. It keeps a project moving on tired days.
Follow your own notes on every later model so the whole army matches, and update the recipe when you find a better step.

Keep all your recipes in one place with a photo of the finished test model. A photo of the pots lined up in order, a searchable notes app or a notebook with a dab of each colour beside its name all work. Date each entry and note what went wrong, such as a colour looking too pale over black.

guides.title: Red armour over black
guides.summary: Paint rich red armour over black that stays deep red rather than turning orange or pink.
body: Prime black. Base a strong mid red with thin paint and fast strokes; expect three or four coats for smooth, solid colour. A light spray of white from above first makes the red brighter in fewer coats. Another start is two gentle dry brushes of a dark red-brown, leaving black in the deepest recesses.
Shade with a slightly darker red thinned to a wash. Drop it into the panel lines, then glaze it down each plate, lifting off at the lower edge.

Shade again with a darker mix over a smaller area, and use very thin black or a dark brown only in the deepest lines. Clear dark joins between plates mean fewer highlight stages, which keeps the red from drifting pink.

Highlight with redder, brighter reds rather than adding white or yellow, which turn it pink or orange. Glaze each up the upper surfaces, then use it a little thicker as an edge line. If you want a lighter edge mix, add a warm flesh tone rather than white.

Each lighter step covers less area and only the top edges facing the light. Build edges with thin lines and dots so they do not grow too big too fast, then flick tiny touches of orange only on points, corners and knuckles.
Work around the whole model and come back once dry, rather than finishing one part at a time.
For a smoother finish, wet blend pure red on the top of each plate down into a red and black mix, in two passes, then edge highlight as above.
For a wet, glossy look, sponge a thinned brighter red over the plates, dot in the strongest speckles, and gloss varnish the red only.

guides.title: Reflected and bounce light
guides.summary: Add a weak second highlight on undersides, as if light bounces up from the ground, for solid, shiny shapes.
body: Shiny surfaces pick up colour from what is below them as well as the light above. Surfaces near a strong colour, such as a mossy base, also bounce a little of it back into their shadows.
Finish the normal shading and highlights first. Bounce light is a last step.
Thin the base colour, or a slightly lighter muted tone, to a glaze and run it along the undersides of each part, following the curve. Keep it muted, not bright.
Make it strongest on parts nearest the ground. Check from the main viewing angle: it should be just visible, not obvious. Build it slowly, then add a slightly stronger touch over a smaller area.

To pick up the surroundings, mix a muted version of the nearby colour, such as an olive green over a mossy base, into the shadow side. Use the same tint under weapons and horns so the light is consistent.
A warm glow on downward edges suggests fire or lava below. Keep cool highlights on the top ridges so the two lights contrast.
With an airbrush, spray white from above, then a coloured tint from below, and leave it in the shadows. Washes and one-coat paints cover it, so build the rest by layering.

On dark weapons: a main highlight on top, a dark band below it, then a weaker highlight on the parts facing down. For a polished, gem-like look, reverse the gradient on a panel: dark at the top and light at the bottom.

guides.title: Worn paint on edges
guides.summary: Show paint rubbed back from edges by stopping the colour short of the edge or dragging half-dry grey along it.
body: Paint wears off edges, corners and raised parts first. Plan the wear there.

Over metal: finish the metal first, then paint the coloured panel but stop just short of the edges, so the metal left around the rim looks like worn paint and doubles as a highlight. Vary the gap so it does not look like an even border. Smudge a few edges with a fingertip while wet.

The same works on vehicles and scenery: a dark metal base, a black wash and a light drybrush of steel, then two coats of the panel colour kept off the edges. Slightly patchy coverage reads as faded paint.
On rusty terrain: paint thinned colour into the recesses and pits and away from the edges in two or three rough coats, then add a little rust wash back where it covered too much.
For scuffed paint: mix a grey with a little brown and run it along the edges. As it starts to dry on the brush, drag and rub it across nearby surfaces to leave specks.

For worn raised detail such as tread plate, add a few drops of drying retarder to the top colour, paint a small section and rub the raised parts with a damp, worn brush while still soft. Keep old brushes for this.
Over varnish, thinned dust or grime on the lower legs can be rubbed off the raised edges with a damp finger, leaving dirt in the recesses.
Start lightly and build up. Add a few silver scratches and pick out rivets in silver for more wear.

guides.title: Painting scale mail
guides.summary: Make rows of armour scales read as metal with dark gaps, bright lower edges and a tiny dot on top of each scale.
body: Base the scales in metal and wash them so the gaps between scales go dark. Keep those gaps dark through every later step. Dark right beside bright is what makes the scales look shiny.
Layer the base metal back onto the raised middle of each scale, or simply dot it there, leaving the gaps alone.

Turn the model so you paint downwards along the lower edge of each row, and flick a thin, brighter line along each scale in one short stroke. Find a comfortable hand position and keep a rhythm; it goes faster than you expect.

The usual mistake is highlighting every scale the same way, which flattens the effect. Light the whole panel first as if it were flat: one broad bright area, a shadow area and a weak bounce area near the ground.

Then shape the scales inside that light. Each brighter step covers fewer scales and less of each one, so the brightest tone ends up on a few scales in the centre. In the bounce area, highlight each scale from the bottom instead of the top.
Finish with a tiny dot of the brightest tone at the top centre of each scale, where it tucks under the next row. In the shadow areas, tone the dot down with the base colour so it is not glaring.
If an edge line comes out too thick, trim it back by painting the shadow colour up to it. Narrow trim beside the scales needs only a fine highlight, not full layering.

guides.title: Selective base coating
guides.summary: Leave the dark undercoat showing in the recesses instead of base coating everything and washing.
body: Prime black or a dark colour, such as a dark drab that can act as the shadow for every area. Base coat each area but stop short of the deepest recesses so the undercoat stays there as shadow.
It gives cleaner definition than base plus wash, in fewer steps, and colours stay bright.
Do not chase full, neat coverage. Paint the raised details and the larger upward faces and let the brush miss the deep parts. Anything left unpainted still reads as shadow, not as unfinished.
Use paint thin enough to flow but strong enough to cover in two coats. Ideally the only time you go back over an area is to add a brighter highlight.

For a rough blend, thin the next colour about half and half with water, pull each stroke towards where the highlight should be, then do a second, smaller pass. Work round several areas so each is dry when you come back.
If paint fills a recess, a dab of the dark undercoat colour fixes it.
A see-through brown one-coat paint over a varied undercoat looks like natural wood and leather.

guides.title: Gloss, satin and matt finishes
guides.summary: Brush gloss on gems, eyes and wet or damp areas and matt elsewhere so materials read differently, even in the same colour.
body: Finish is how shiny a surface is, which is separate from what it is made of. Varnish the whole model matt first if you want an even base, then add sheens on top.

Gloss makes things look wet or polished: gems, lenses, glass, water, fresh blood, slime, eyes, open mouths and tongues, shiny boots, lacquered armour. It also deepens the colour under it. A thick blob of gloss on a black eye stays put and shines sharply.

Satin gives a soft sheen that suits leather belts, worn jackets, slightly polished armour and a touch on skin. Matt black leather looks like cloth until satin goes over it. A medium that dries with a slight sheen can stand in.
Matt kills unwanted shine on cloth, skin, fur and anywhere a wash has dried shiny. Dead matt rust next to glossy puddles makes both effects more convincing.

Thin gloss with a little water so it is not goopy or streaky; thick gloss can dry cloudy or tinted. Brush it only on the parts that need it, as the very last step, so no later matt coat dulls it. Brushed varnish comes out shinier than sprayed. To preview, brush plain water over the area and look while it is wet.
Keep it deliberate: gloss a few chosen parts, such as helmets and boots, and leave gloves and pads matt. It takes very little time, so it suits fast batches too.

Finishes can be swapped later. If varnish fills the recesses and they lose definition, drop a little wash back in. Paint grips varnish poorly, so a slip on top can be wiped off with a damp cotton bud. Blow dust off first, because varnish fixes it in place.
If a model looks wrong but you cannot say why, mismatched sheen is often the cause. Gloss also shows lamp glare in photos.

guides.title: Shading metallic paint
guides.summary: Darken metallics with washes, ink glazes or mixed-in dark paint, then put the shine back on raised parts.
body: Start bright. A smooth base of bright metal in one or two thin coats keeps the midtones lively once shading darkens it. Base over a matching colour: a warm brown under gold, black under silver.

Pick the method by surface. Washes suit textured metal such as mail, where they settle into every gap. On large smooth plates and blades they bead or dry patchy, so thin matt paint works better there. Shades that dry slightly glossy keep more shine than very matt ones.

Quickest: a wash in the recesses. Keep a thinned and a full-strength version on the palette, build up slowly and stop it pooling. For clean metal with no tide marks, brush a dark wash over one section, then scrub it off the raised areas with a clean dry brush while wet.

For more control, mix a dark ordinary paint or black into the metallic, up to half and half, for the shadows and blend it while wet. Mix enough for the session, as the ratio is hard to match again. Recesses end up darker and duller while pure metal on top is brighter. Then run the dark colour alone, thinned to an ink, into the deepest corners.
