If a hard line shows where shadow meets metal, mix in-between tones, from about three parts shadow to one part metal up to half and half, and paint each along the line. Stippling a little metal across it instead gives a worn, brushed look.

How far the dark spreads sets the look. Thin, soft shading with the darkest only round rivets gives clean, bright metal; darker shading over larger areas gives old, grim metal. Keep the shadow on the same side of every shape across the model.

Anything non-metallic laid over metal robs its shine. Re-layer the original metallic, slightly thinned, on the raised parts only, then finish with one sharp edge highlight of bright silver, and on round parts a small spot rather than a line.

Warm brown shades suit gold and copper. A little copper mixed into gold makes a warm shadow, and after a brown wash, a thin purple in only the deepest gold recesses adds richness. Blue-black suits steel. A hint of turquoise around rivets suggests old corrosion. A little colour in the first wash tints the metal towards the rest of the scheme.

guides.title: Shading metallics with ink
guides.summary: Mix or glaze black or coloured ink into metallics to shade them without losing the shine or leaving tide marks.
body: Black paint mixed into a metallic dilutes the shiny flakes and goes dull. Ink darkens it while keeping the sheen, and unlike most washes it mixes straight into metallic paint.
Keep the metal base smooth: no more than two thin coats. Rough metallic shows badly under ink.
Mix a range on the palette from mostly ink to pure metallic. Cover the area in the darkest mix, then layer lighter mixes where reflections should be, and finish edges in pure metallic.

Or work the other way: add a little ink to the metal and paint it into the recesses and lower part of each panel, raising the share of ink with each pass and keeping each pass lower. It builds a smooth gradient but is slow.
Or glaze heavily thinned ink over the finished metal in several thin coats, like a wash. It dries a little glossier than a normal wash, and a dash of matt medium takes off some of that.
Keep it to the recesses and stop it pooling on flat areas, which leaves tide marks. Ink can lift again when wet, so do not scrub water or wet paint over it afterwards.
Pick the ink by metal: a bluish black for silver, a warm reddish brown for gold and copper. Thin browns and oranges in the shadows make it look older. Dot pure silver where light reflects most.
Strong dark and bright zones on one panel are what make metal look reflective. Exaggerate the dark areas you see when you hold the model under the lamp.

guides.title: Shading with one-coat paints
guides.summary: Use a contrast-style one-coat paint as a guided wash or tint over a base colour or metal for smooth, fast shading.
body: Base each area in its midtone, over a primer that makes that quick. A white primer keeps bright colours strong.

Test a new colour on a spare piece first. A good one dries lighter on raised areas and darker in recesses. Some barely change and act like an ink; those need highlights and a dark recess line added on top.
Cover the whole area with the one-coat paint. Covering everything avoids the rings a thin wash leaves.

Push the liquid so it settles in recesses and on downward faces. End each stroke in a recess and lift off there, because pigment collects where the brush stops. Wipe areas you want bright with a brush dipped in pure medium.
Over metal, pick a light, weak tone so it tints rather than covers: warm flesh over gold, grey over silver. It stains textured areas evenly.

Thinned with its medium, about two parts paint to one, it shades more softly and can shift the hue: brown over green gives a drab khaki. Using the same shade on every fleshy part ties a model together.

For more depth, sandwich: one-coat paint, layer the lighter colour back on the raised areas, then a second thinner coat over the top. Or stack a darker one-coat paint of the same colour family under a brighter one; the recesses keep the darker tone.

Soak up pools with a dry brush, and lay the model on its side while it dries so the paint does not run down and pool at hems. If a result looks like a dirty wash rather than soft shading, use more medium next time. If the colour you want does not exist, mix a normal paint with contrast medium.

guides.title: Shading without a wash
guides.summary: Shade by glazing or layering a darker paint into the folds by hand, or start dark and only build up.
body: Washes make most sense for speed painting and heavy texture. For cleaner colour, shade by hand. Thinned ordinary paint leaves no tide marks and gives more control. Smooth rounded shapes and wide flat areas such as cloaks do not hold a wash well anyway; it dries in patches and rings.
Pick a light direction and shade the side facing away from it, plus anywhere light would not reach. A photo of a zenithal undercoat shows where the shadows naturally fall.

On a light base, shade first and highlight after. Thin a darker colour, such as a darker mix of the base or the base plus brown, wick most of it off the brush, and glaze it into the recesses and folds in several thin coats, each dry first. A little matt medium keeps the glaze where you put it instead of running into every recess.

For skin and muscles, glaze a soft shade along every recess, then a fine darker line in only the deepest ones. The base stays as your midtone, so you can go straight to highlighting. On a big batch, keep just the dark line.

Or paint a darker layer into the recesses and glaze over its edge to blend it. On a showpiece, wet blend instead: a slightly darker mix in the deepest part of a crease, the base colour beside it, stroked together while wet.
To stipple shadows, use a small brush with little paint and angle it steeply so it hits only one side of each feature, much like an airbrush would.

Shading a bright red with a vivid violet, or a warm colour with a cool blue, gives richer shadows than black. Paint will stray onto the raised areas, so thin the base colour slightly and paint it back over the stained spots.

Or skip shading entirely: base in a dark tone and build the light up, leaving the dark in the recesses. Over black primer, leave the deepest recesses unpainted and keep some darker colour at the base of each fold or strand.

guides.title: Silk and satin
guides.summary: Paint shiny fabric like polished metal: strong contrast from dark to near-white, built from fine parallel lines.
body: Base the cloth in a very dark version of its colour. Shiny fabric needs a big jump from dark to light.
Build up with many very thin parallel hatched lines along the folds rather than smooth strokes, much like brushed steel.
Each lighter step covers a smaller area than the last, like tiles on a roof.
Push the top highlight almost to white mixed with a little of the midtone, using the same pale tint as highlights elsewhere.
Line up the brightest points with those on nearby surfaces so they all follow one light.

guides.title: Simplifying a method for squads
guides.summary: Cut stages from a display method so it works across many models: keep the shade and the edge highlights.
body: A display method with every stage can take a couple of days per model. Save it for leaders and centrepieces.
Write down the full sequence from your first model, then decide which steps to drop for the rest. The middle layers between the shade and the highlight usually go first.
Get the base colour down fast with a spray, airbrush or a light primer.
Keep one shade, usually as a recess line or wash rather than a set of glazes, and skip the subtle first glaze. A black wash on metal and small details often needs no highlight afterwards.

Keep the edge highlights. They do most of the work at arm's length. Swap blended highlights for one or two clean edge lines, and only on the upward edges of the top half: head, shoulders, knees. Use a paint that gives a crisp line in one coat.
On metal, quick scratchy highlights replace careful edge lines and look suitably worn. Models in the back ranks can skip a highlight stage, and fine dots belong only on faces and focal points.
Merge steps: instead of dark, mid and light grey, use dark grey, a half and half mix of the two middle tones, then light grey.
Alternate a slow, fiddly step with a quick, mindless one, such as a wash on the next batch, to keep your energy up. Use the same colours as your detailed models so the squad still matches them.

guides.title: Gritty, sketchy style
guides.summary: Build highlights from thin scratchy lines over a coloured primer that stays showing as the deepest shadow.
body: Prime in a warm dark colour or black, then add see-through accent colours from one consistent angle.
Never fully cover the primer. Leave it in the shadows and paint around it. It unifies the model and saves shading.
Highlight with many thin lines and scratches instead of smooth blends, placed where light would hit each shape. Follow the form of each surface with the strokes so the volume reads.
Thin the paint a little more than usual and barely graze the surface with the tip of the brush. Semi-transparent paint means no single stroke can ruin it, so work fast and loose.
Repeat with a lighter colour over a smaller area. Stacked layers of scratches act as an easy blend and read as worn, battered surfaces. Make bold jumps in brightness; rough is fine, messy is not.

Use a brush one size bigger than feels comfortable, or hold it further back on the handle, for looser strokes. Turn the model so strokes can go in every direction without awkward hand angles, and let the brush marks show.

Vary the marks by material: small stippled dots for cloth, bolder strokes for bone or metal. On black weapons, build gradients from broken lines and dots, then soften them with two thin coats of a dark brown wash.
For a grimier mood, layer brown, rust and dust washes over a simple base and highlight, and keep metals high contrast. A time limit, such as one afternoon, stops you polishing the roughness away.

guides.title: What to learn next: a skill roadmap
guides.summary: A rough order for learning painting skills, from tidy base coats to display work, with one new skill per model.
body: Stage one, first models: remove mould lines, prime evenly, thin your paint, base coat neatly, then one wash and one drybrush. Aim for tidy and finished. A dozen models done this way teach more than one fussed over.
Stage two, the basics: one layered highlight on raised areas, tidy edge highlights, simple eyes and faces, and neat bases with painted rims. Learn to look after a brush tip and use a wet palette.
Stage three, control: two or three highlight steps with smoother changes, glazing to soften them, colour schemes with one accent, and checking value so the model reads from arm's length.

Stage four, depth: wet blending, stippling, stronger contrast, one clear light direction with darker lower halves, simple freehand and weathering. Try a small light source, such as a glowing eye or lamp.
Stage five, display work: light cast from glowing objects, metal painted without metallic paint, texture effects, scenic bases and planning a whole model around one focal point.
Move on when the current stage feels routine, not when it feels perfect. Most people hop between stages, and that is fine.
Add one new skill per model and try it on one area first. A test model or spare part keeps the mistakes off the good figure.

guides.title: Freckles, age spots and blemishes
guides.summary: Dot freckles, pores and age spots onto finished skin in mixed sizes and spacing so they look natural, not patterned.
body: Finish the skin first. Blemishes are a last step that adds texture, because real skin is never perfectly even.
For freckles and age spots, mix a soft dark: a dark brown, or a dark blue with a little black, eased back with some skin tone. Test a dot on the palette and soften it further if it looks harsh.
Dot spots of different sizes with a fine point. Let some overlap and leave gaps of varying width. Your hand will try to space them evenly, so dot quickly without thinking hard about each one.
Give a few spots a slightly lighter centre or a darker partner, so they seem to sit at different depths in the skin.
For pores and fine texture, dab tiny dots of a pale skin highlight, mostly on the lit areas. They catch the light like small bumps and imperfections.
Finish with a thin glaze of the skin tone over the area to blend the spots in. If any part still looks like a pattern, break it up with a few more random dots.

guides.title: Painting skin by layering
guides.summary: Build skin up from a dark base with lighter mixes on smaller raised areas, then glaze in a little colour.
body: Use a wet palette. Base the skin in a warm mid brown or your darkest skin tone in a few thin coats. Brown is kinder than black: a missed spot by an eye or ear reads as shadow, not a harsh line. It also covers black primer far better than a flesh tone does.

Starting dark lets you choose where shadows stay. A wash over light skin runs into every recess whether you want it or not. Lay your mixes out in a row from dark to light so you can step back if needed.

Mix half base and half mid skin, judging halfway by brightness, thin it, and paint most of the face. Leave the base showing in the deepest recesses: around the eyes, nose and mouth, at the hairline and the collar. Keep the first layers broad. Narrow early highlights make skin look shiny and leave no room to build.

Step lighter with each new mix, on smaller areas where light lands from above, ending on the brow, nose ridge, cheekbones, upper lip and chin. Lighter mixes cover worse, so two thin coats are normal. Test each new mix on the nose tip, which will be bright anyway.

Highlight towards a pale yellow-cream rather than pink for a natural look, finishing with near-white only on the highest points. Mix the top tones from your flesh plus white or ivory rather than a separate pale pot, so the set stays related. Stop short of pure white, which looks bleached. Judge colours dry.

Skin is not shiny, so smoothness matters more than contrast. Too light or too stark? Glaze the previous stage back over it. Alternate highlights and glazes, but do not stack glazes with no highlight between, or the face flattens out.

Run a thin dark brown into the mouth line, eyes and ears. Glaze a little purple under the cheekbones and a little pink on the cheeks and lower lip. If a deep shadow side looks unpainted up close, add a few faint, still dark highlights there.

On small figures, push highlights onto raised forms such as knuckles, elbows, knees, nose and brow; it reads better than strict top light. For rank and file, cut this down to a couple of shades and a couple of highlights.

guides.title: Many skin tones from one undercoat
guides.summary: Get pale, olive or dark skin from one flesh undercoat and a drybrush by choosing a different wash or one-coat paint.
body: Prime a mid flesh tone in two light coats, or prime white or grey and base coat flesh.
Drybrush a light flesh, then a pale bony flesh, over the skin. It also pre-highlights straps and fur.

Wash with a warm flesh shade for a standard skin tone. Two thin coats of a tint settle more softly than one heavy coat. Some flesh washes are much darker than they look; if one swamps the skin, layer the drybrush tone back over the raised areas.
Use an ochre one-coat paint for olive skin, or a brown one built up in more coats for darker skin.
Every skin recipe is a base, a tint, a tidy-up and a highlight, and any one step can be swapped. Put one recipe's highlight over another's base to get more tones from the same paints.
The same drybrushed base under a red one-coat paint gives rich red cloth with the highlights already in place.

guides.title: Dripping slime and goo
guides.summary: Paint drips thickly with an unthinned glossy slime effect paint over a pale base so they look wet.
body: Paint the drips and blobs pale first, such as a light bone. A pale base lets the translucent slime colour glow.
Use a glossy, translucent green effect paint made for slime and ooze. Do not thin it.
Apply it generously so it builds up thick on the drips and stays shiny. The thickness and the gloss are what sell the wet look.
Let it dry fully, then add a second coat on the fattest drips and the lowest point of each, where goo would gather.
Keep the surrounding areas matt. The contrast in sheen makes the goo look even wetter.

For a hanging drip from a mouth or claw, fix a fine thread or wire from the source to where the drip ends. Brush gloss varnish along it in thin layers, drying each one, like dipping a candle. The bottom grows fatter, which looks natural.

For a pool, fill a hollow on the base with white glue, paint it, and add several coats of gloss. To suggest a glow, glaze thinned green over nearby metal and touch the edges closest to the slime with green plus a little ivory.

guides.title: Smooth gradients on big areas without an airbrush
guides.summary: Get airbrush-like fades on big areas by brush using a larger brush, wet blending or many soft drybrush passes.
body: Switch to a larger brush. Small brushes leave streaks on big surfaces whether you glaze or wet blend.
Lay each layer first without worrying about the blend. Stop each one short of the last so some of the darker colour stays as a transition.
Wet blending is the most direct way to blend big panels and cloaks. Work one area at a time while the paint is wet, and expect to go over a blend more than once.

To soften a hard line, put a little paint down, wipe the brush on a tissue, then fan the damp brush out from it while wet. Paint lands where the brush lifts off, so stroke towards the highlight, or towards the shadow when darkening.
For a soft glow, use a big soft drybrush and build colour gradually over many very light passes.

Scratchy strokes or stippling also blur a step, and a blend need not be perfect to read well. To save time, jump straight to the brightest colour on a small area, then feather its edge into the layer below.
On large flat areas of skin, soft blends look better than line work. Where a rounded shape meets a hard edge, such as a shoulder blade, mark it with one distinct line.
Finish with a couple of glazes over the joins to smooth any steps. Light hands and many thin applications matter more than tools.

guides.title: Smoother layering
guides.summary: Hide layer lines with more, smaller steps, each covering a little less, and glazed joins.
body: Mix more in-between tones so each jump in value is small. Base and light mixed at about 3 to 1, 2 to 1, 1 to 1 and 1 to 2 give an even set. Test each mix with a dot beside the last layer; if the jump looks big, add some of the previous colour back. Strong pale paints shift a mix fast, so add them a little at a time.
Each layer covers a little less than the one before, like roof tiles. If every pass covers the same area, you get a hard line instead of a blend.
Start each stroke in the darker area and pull towards the light. Most pigment lands where the brush lifts off. For a highlight in the middle of a panel, stroke in from both sides towards it.
Thin paint, but not to a watery glaze. A drop of water is enough, and touch excess off on a tissue before each stroke. Very watery glazes dry with pigment ringed at the edges.
Pale mixes hold more white and cover more strongly, so lines show most at the light end. Thin each lighter step a little more and make the steps smaller as you go up. Dark steps forgive bigger jumps.
You need not mix a new colour for every step. The same thin mix applied twice, the second time on a smaller area, builds a soft step by itself. Feather the edge of each pass outwards as you lay it.

Work broad and thick first, then smaller and thinner. Painting whole volumes before details keeps the shape readable. Alternate a little shade and a little highlight so the colour does not drift too dark or too light.

To fix a visible step, mix a colour halfway between the two layers and paint it only along the join. Repeat a few times. A last very thin glaze of the top tone over the highlighted area also pulls the steps together. If you lose the darks, paint the shade back into the recesses.

guides.title: Snow and whitewash on models
guides.summary: Sponge or stipple off-white onto boots, kit and armour for clinging snow or a patchy winter whitewash.
body: For snow on boots and kit, roll a small piece of packing foam into a tight stub or hold it in tweezers. Load it with an off-white or very pale grey, which looks more natural than pure white, and dab most of it off on the palette.
Stab it lightly around the boots, coat hems and calves, where snow clumps first, then on top of shoulders, helmets and packs where it would settle.
Too thick? Dab again with a clean sponge, wipe with a finger, or repaint and try again.
For a whitewash camo, stab white onto armour with a small soft round drybrush that is almost dry, building an uneven speckle. Do it before layering cloth, as some will stray.

For a worn whitewashed helmet, base it off-white with a light brown wash and edge it in white. Then sponge fine near-black speckles on the edges and front, and join a few into bigger chips and a scratch or two with a fine brush.

For worn whitewash on a vehicle or helmet, seal the base colour with satin varnish, then apply a thin, uneven coat of a water-washable white. Once dry, wet a small area and rub with a damp brush; a stiff brush or toothpick takes more off and scratches. Vary the wear and clear it off markings. If too much comes off, paint small irregular white spots back.
Paint the base off-white with a snow texture paste and push the feet into it slightly.
Grey gloves and cold blue-grey tones elsewhere sell the winter look.

guides.title: Soot and scorch marks
guides.summary: Make barrel tips and exhausts look burnt with thin brown then black, a dry brush, or black pigment.
body: Thin a warm brown heavily and paint it on the end of the barrel or vent. It looks strong wet but tones down as it dries. For a heat-stained exhaust, base dark steel and give it three coats of a strong brown wash, then one of dark grey.

Once dry, add thinned black over the very tip, fading back a little way. With an airbrush, spray many light layers of a dark wash, drying each, then a touch of thinned matt black right at the end. Heavy coats streak.

Or use a small soft drybrush with very little off-black in soft circles at exhaust tips and vents. Smoke rises, so carry the marks upward above the opening, heaviest at the source and fading away. Stiff bristles leave streaks instead of a haze. On terrain, do the same above windows and fireplaces.

With black pigment powder, dab most off on tissue, stipple it around the muzzle and build slowly. Fix it with a pigment fixer touched on with an old brush. Pick out the rim of the nozzle with a dot of bright silver so the detail still reads. Dry light grey pigment brushed onto charred wood, unfixed, looks like ash.
For blast marks on shields and armour, stab a brush fairly loaded with black straight onto the surface in small, broken clusters, on the front where hits would land.

For burn holes in cloth, stipple a reddish brown round each hole and glaze more coats closer to it. Paint a brown-black tight to the edge, pure black in the centre, and a tiny touch of thin orange for heat.
Black thinned with far too much water breaks into tiny specks as it dries. Usually that is a mistake, but brushed above a burn it looks like ash caught in cloth.
For charred skin, sponge or dot a dark grey over blistered texture, then run a deep dried-blood red into the cracks so it looks raw.

guides.title: Speed painting
guides.summary: Paint a model in about half an hour by limiting colours, using one-coat paints and working while things dry.
body: Pick about three main areas, such as armour, skin and base. Put the paints out first; around five colours is plenty, with one very dark and one very bright for quick contrast. One colour can do several jobs, such as a drybrush colour that also picks out bone, rope and teeth.

Prime dark, then dust white or grey lightly from above. The dark left in recesses is free shading and the light gives a head start on highlights. Or spray a primer close to the main colour, so every gap you miss already looks right.
Use one-coat paints over that primer, or drybrushing on big textured models. Both shade and highlight in one go. Soak up pools at hems and low points before they dry as dark rings.
Paint the big, slow-drying areas first, then block in other parts while they dry. Use the largest brush you can control. A hair dryer on low heat, held well back, speeds up drying between coats.

Do not base coat everything. One pass of colour on raised volumes, with primer left in the recesses, is enough on most of the model. Small parts need a base and maybe one edge highlight. Sponging, scratches and stippled chips hide rough blending and look deliberate.
Spend the saved time on the head, shoulders and chest. If the focal areas look good, the eye assumes the rest does too. With so few steps, each one carries more of the look, so do those few neatly.
Finish with eyes, a few details and a neat base rim so it looks complete.
On a big batch, stop rank and file once they are table ready and take only leaders further. Do each step on every model before the next; time per model drops a lot.
keywords: how long to paint a model

guides.title: Spending time where it shows
guides.summary: Put most effort on the head, hands, chest and weapons and keep low or hidden parts simple.
body: People look at the head first, then weapons, hands and chest. Almost nobody inspects the feet. Also ask what the model is about, such as a red cloak and blood on a battle mage: those themed parts get your best work.
Spend less time on each area as you work down and away from the face. Let the highlights build towards the head: one from the feet up, a second from the knees up, a third from the waist up.
The main colour matters most. If the armour or skin that covers most of the model looks good, the whole model does, so it can take half or more of your time.

Low and hidden areas get one coat and done. Fine work deep in recesses adds little. Parts in deep shadow can stay very dark or plain black, and the back can often keep its base colours. If you have to turn the model upside down to find a spot, leave it.
Keep minor parts plain: cables black, one or two metals rather than many, and belts and pouches in one or two neutral colours with a thin wash.
A small detail near the face, such as a simple freehand pattern on an edge or glowing eyes as the only bright colour, adds a lot for little time.
When smoothing, only work a little paint where two colours meet instead of glazing the whole area.
Rush the early steps if you like, but not the finish. A last pass touching up rubs and slips makes the whole piece look done.

guides.title: Sponge chipping
guides.summary: Dab chips on fast with a torn bit of sponge with most of the paint removed, then refine a few by brush.
body: Tear a small piece of firm foam with medium holes, such as packing foam, from the middle so the surface is ragged. Dense makeup sponge gives a flat speckle and very open foam gives blotches. Hold it in reverse grip tweezers, or push it into a brush cap for tight areas.

Load it with the chip colour, then dab most off on a towel or dry palette. Thin the paint only slightly: runny paint soaks into the foam and floods. How much is left and how hard you press set the chip size. Too much gives blobs, too little faint specks. Test on the back of the model first.
Press straight down lightly on edges and corners where wear happens first. Do not drag it, or you get smears. Build up over a few light passes rather than one heavy one.

Do the edges first, then decide how much flat surface to scuff. Keep chips small and random, as even or symmetrical spacing looks fake. Lower and front parts wear most, tops least. On armour crowded with trim, keep heavy wear to big plates such as legs and shoulders. Chip after decals so they wear too.

Chip colours: a very dark brown on coloured armour, plain brown on black parts, bright silver on dark metal for fine scratches. For layered chips, sponge a lighter shade of the armour colour first, then dark brown into the middle of some.

Use the sponge marks as a map. With a brush, join some into bigger, jagged chips and broken, dotted scratches, and vary the sizes a lot. Put the biggest damage where water gathers or hits land: panel bottoms, rivets, overlapping plates.

Paint a thin line of the area's highlight colour along the lower edge of the bigger chips, so they look cut into the paint. On green, a cream rim shows better than pale green. Pick out a few of the largest chips in silver for bare metal showing through.

Chipping also hides wobbly lines, tape bleed and overspray along edges. If you overdo it, tidy back with the colour underneath. No sponge to hand? Wipe a stiff old brush nearly dry and stab it at the surface.

guides.title: Gradients with a makeup sponge
guides.summary: Dab smooth gradients and fades with a fine makeup sponge as a cheap alternative to an airbrush.
body: Use a fine-pored cone makeup sponge. It leaves a very soft stipple, where coarse packing foam leaves an obvious speckle. Prime with a tough primer, as dabbing is rough on the surface.
Cover the model in the shadow colour, then dab the main colour on from above so the shadow stays low.
Touch the sponge to a little water before loading and thin the paint slightly. Colours close in brightness blend most smoothly.
Let each layer dry before the next, as the sponge lifts wet paint. Each lighter layer covers a smaller area, until only the most exposed parts get the brightest colour.
Cover the planned brightest areas solidly and keep speckle out of them. Light paint dabbed over dark specks looks dull and busy.
For tight spots, cut off the rounded tip and slice it in half for small triangular points.
Rinse the sponge in water after each colour, and often in between. Dried paint clogs it and leaves chalky flecks.

Finish edges by brush. The slight texture suits old, worn or stone-like surfaces, and boxy shapes are easiest. On curvy, intricate models an airbrush is faster and smoother, but brings overspray and masking.

guides.title: Sponging texture and quick coverage
guides.summary: Dab paint with a scrap of foam for mottled skin, speckled texture and fast shaded metal over black primer.
body: Make a tool: twist a small piece of packing foam into a plastic brush sleeve or cap so a little sticks out. A narrow sleeve gives smaller, more controlled marks. Tweezers holding a torn scrap also work.
Load a little paint and dab most of it off on a towel, as with drybrushing. Thin the paint slightly so it is not thick and goopy.
For mottled skin, dab the skin tone gently over the area. Raised parts pick up more and read as highlights, and the dabs leave a rough, natural texture.
Follow with a thin glaze of the same colour to blend the dabs into what is underneath.

For quick metal, prime black and sponge a darker silver fairly heavily, leaving some black showing. Then sponge a brighter silver more lightly on raised areas. The sponge cannot reach recesses, so they stay dark with no wash.
For worn, industrial metal, finish with sponged browns and oranges for rust. The same tool dabbed on armour edges makes chips.

Rock, worn leather and battered armour take the same treatment, with two or three colours for depth over a dark base. Stippling with an old brush tip gives a similar texture with more control over where it lands.

guides.title: Painting a spotlit model
guides.summary: Light only a small area, as under a narrow spotlight: a hard, bright pool that falls fast into deep dark.
body: A spotlight effect lights a small area, usually the head and shoulders, and lets the rest drop into darkness. It is a stronger, more dramatic version of light from straight above.
Choose the centre of the pool first, usually the face or chest. Put a small dot of white there as a reminder while you paint.
Prime black, then spray or drybrush white only around that centre, from a narrow angle above. Let it fall off quickly. This value sketch is your map.
Paint the lit area with your full range of colour steps. Outside it, use only the darkest two or three, so the colour is close to black by the feet.
The edge of the pool sells the effect. Keep the change from lit to dark short and fairly hard, over a few millimetres, not a long soft fade.
Keep highlights inside the pool. A bright edge highlight on the boots breaks the effect. Dark areas can take a faint cold rim of colour, like a dull blue, #2c3440, so the shape still reads.
Check it in greyscale with a phone photo. If the brightest point is not where you want the eye to go, glaze everything else darker.

guides.title: Spots, stripes and creature markings
guides.summary: Paint uneven spots, stripes and blotches on creature skin, hide and fur so they look natural, not stencilled.
body: Look at real animals for ideas, such as frogs, big cats, geckos, fish and birds. Use them as inspiration rather than copying.

Make the pattern random: blotches of different sizes and shapes, some broken apart, with stray dots near the main patches. Even spacing looks artificial, so do not overplan. Larger, overlapping spots near the spine or plates and smaller, sparser ones further away make it fade naturally.
Follow the body. Narrow the markings where ribs or plates pinch together. Keep the first coat rough so you can rearrange the layout, then give a second coat once it looks right.

For a bright colour over a different skin, mark the pattern out in a pale neutral first so the bright colour goes on crisp. Build each marking with a deep tone, then a smaller, lighter blotch inside it, leaving the deep colour round the outside.
Shade and highlight the pattern with the same light as the skin under it, so it looks part of the skin rather than stuck on. A thin glaze of the skin shade over the top ties it in.
For ring spots like a big cat's, dot irregular blobs of thin dark paint, wait about half a minute, then touch a clean, dry brush to the middle of each. The edge dries darker than the centre.

Under a bright one-coat paint, paint bold, jagged markings in a deep thinned colour over a light undercoat and let them dry. The one-coat paint goes over everything and the markings show through darker. Subtle marks vanish.
For stripes on fur, paint them in a thinned dark one-coat paint over the finished fur, then drybrush the whole area again so both read as one material. For armies, sponge or flick spots on.

guides.title: Stacking edge highlights in stages
guides.summary: Make the first edge highlight wide, then paint each finer, brighter stage inside the last.
body: Line the recesses first if you want sharper edges, with the base colour darkened and thinned.

For the first stage, mix the base and the highlight colour about half and half so the step is not harsh. Make it about twice the width of your final line: run a thin line, then widen it on a second pass. Keep the width even around the model.
Paint each later stage within the one before, so a sliver of every earlier stage still shows. Each stage is a little less thinned, finer and covers less, so each goes faster than the last.

Load only the tip of the brush and thin edge paint a little less than layers: just a touch of water. Skim the side of the brush along raised edges at about 45 degrees, and use the tip in a pull towards you on inner edges. End each stroke where the brightest point should be.

Take the early stages round every edge. Keep the later, brighter stages for the top edges facing the light, or do every edge for a very crisp look. Edges that catch lots of light can skip the first stage. On leaders, a last stage on corners, knuckles and the brow lifts them. Troops can stop after one stage; make that one a little brighter.

Desaturate the final mix slightly so bright colours do not look acidic, and finish with pale dots where two edges meet at a corner. On a curved surface, use a very short line where light hits instead of a dot.
Keep stages on soft edges, such as cloth folds, more muted. A bright line there looks odd.

Fix slips by painting back over them with the earlier stage, and trim a line that is too thick with the base colour. If a jump in brightness is too big, glaze a thin version of the first colour along it, or drag slightly thinned paint from the brighter line towards the darker one.

guides.title: Stamping designs onto models
guides.summary: Print rings, emblems and heraldry onto shields and armour with a silicone stamp, an etched plate or a brush cover.
body: Stamping kits made for nail art or hobby use have etched plates, a flat scraper and a soft silicone stamp. A clear stamp lets you see where the design will land.
Paint the area first and let it dry. Spread a little paint over the etched design, such as a white acrylic or an enamel, then scrape the surplus off so paint stays only in the grooves.
Press or roll the stamp onto the plate to pick up the design, then press it straight onto the model. Work fast, because acrylic dries on the stamp within seconds.
Fill any gaps by hand with a fine brush and tidy the edges with the base colour. A white print can then be painted over with a bright one-coat colour, such as yellow, for a strong emblem.

For quick rings, dip the end of a clear plastic brush cover in paint and press it on. The curved end may print only part of a ring, so turn it and press again. Different covers give different sizes. Thin a ring that is too thick with the background colour.
To blend the design in, sponge a textured base colour onto the shield first and re-sponge over any smudges. A thin khaki glaze at the end makes it look stained rather than freshly printed.

guides.title: Stippling texture
guides.summary: Dab a nearly dry brush onto the surface so many tiny dots build rough, grainy texture on cloth, leather and stone.
body: Use an old brush with splayed or trimmed bristles; stippling wears brushes out fast. A split tip makes many dots at once. Re-splay the bristles as they pull back together. For tight areas, a small drybrush with a narrow front edge is more accurate. On large cloaks, a scrap of sponge dabbed the same way is quicker.

Load the brush and wipe most of the paint off, then tap the side of the tip straight down, never dragging. Each tap leaves a cluster of dots. Turn the brush between dabs and break up the spacing so the eye does not spot repeats.

Paint consistency sets the look. Thin paint builds slowly and smoothly; thicker paint leaves grain that suits leather, rough fabric and stone. Keep bright highlight dots a little thicker, as very thin paint spreads into big dots.

Block in rough shading and highlights first as a guide, then stipple lighter colours over smaller areas, leaving gaps. On robes, let more shadow show towards the bottom and stipple more solidly near the top.
With a firm drybrush you can stipple even the base coat and first highlight over black instead of airbrushing. There is no overspray and the gritty texture is there from the start.
Stipple darks back into folds and recesses, and finish with a sparse, light stipple of a pale colour on the sharpest edges. Dots rather than lines along edges give a rough, worn look.
For battered iron, stipple a weak silver over dark, washed metal until it looks pitted and hammered, then flick a few bright scratches across it.

Stippling hides blending mistakes and keeps light colours out of recesses better than drybrushing. Vary dot size and avoid patterns. Keep it off surfaces that should look smooth and shiny. If an area turns too bright or busy, stipple the previous colour back over it, or glaze thin base colour across to pull it together.

guides.title: Stippling to blend
guides.summary: Build smooth gradients or hide rough steps by dabbing many tiny dots of thin paint instead of brush strokes.
body: Stippling is a motion: touch the brush tip to the surface over and over, leaving small dots. Packed close together, the eye blends them into a smooth fade.
Thin the paint slightly or to a glaze, then wick most of it off on a tissue so each dab leaves only a little see-through colour and many dabs build it up.
Mix a range of small steps between your colours. Small steps hide mistakes. Dab most densely where each colour should be strongest and space the dots out towards the previous one.
Each lighter mix covers a smaller area. Move to a smaller, sharper brush as you go. Or paint the brightest colour first and stipple midtones over its edge.
To soften a border, add a touch of water to the brush and stipple lightly along it. Let each pass dry before going over it again: touching it while wet is the most common mistake.
Overdone a light colour? Stipple the previous mix back over it until the step looks right.
Faster version: paint simple hard bands of colour first, then stipple each colour into its neighbour from both sides, densest near its own band and sparser as it crosses. The dots disguise the lines.
It is not as smooth as careful glazing but takes far less time and leaves no brush strokes. Leave small gaps between dots on cloth for a velvet look, or finish with thin glazes for a seamless result.

guides.title: Rust and grime streaks
guides.summary: Pull thin browns or rust washes down from holes, rivets and trim as vertical streaks, feathered at the end.
body: Think where water would run: down from rivets, bolts, vents, pipes, chips and the undersides of trim. Rain runs straight down, so keep streaks straight and parallel. On flat upward faces water pools, so use stain patches there instead.

Thin a dark warm brown until inky, or mix it with about the same amount of glaze medium so it stays see-through. Paint a ring round the fitting, pull a line straight down, and soften the end with a clean damp brush.

Build streaks in several thin passes. Let each dry, then add more, slightly offset, longer or shorter. Keep the strongest colour at the source and let it fade. For oil leaks, start below the source and drag up towards it, as paint gathers where the brush stops. Paint that is not thinned enough leaves thick, overdone drips.

Once dry, go over corners and drip points with a thinner orange-brown, then tiny ochre dots only in the deepest spots for fresh rust. Match streaks to the base so they show: lighter grime or whitish dust on dark green or red, darker reddish or greenish tones on sand yellow.
Keep it irregular. Vary length and strength, and rinse the brush often so it stays clean for feathering. Fan or chisel brushes streak fast but look uniform; a soft single brush gives more variety.

Enamel or oil streaking paints give more working time: dot a little on, wait a few minutes, then drag it down with a brush damp with odourless thinner. Build in layers and leave a few streaks sharp for contrast. Some rust washes soften again with water: dot, let dry, then stroke down with a damp brush.
For contrast in finish, keep old stains matt and add a few thin, dark, glossy drips running from seams so they look wet.

Gone wrong? Water-based effects can usually be scrubbed off with warm water and a soft toothbrush. A reddish rust stands out well on green or blue. Real rust products with an activator look natural but are random, so practise first.

guides.title: Streaky, rotten textures
guides.summary: Wet blend a few drab colours in streaks along a part so armour or cloth looks rotting or water-stained.
body: Base coat a mid olive or green. Thin it, a lighter olive and a grey-brown, and keep them wet on a wet palette.
Work one small area at a time. Lay a thin coat of the base, then pull streaks of the other colours through it while wet.
Always streak along the length of the part: up and down on legs, cloaks and shields, across on arms.
Go back and forth so there are no hard jumps. Add a darker olive in places for contrast.
Highlight edges, rips and the strongest streaks with the light olive mixed with bone. Line deeper streaks and recesses with thin dark brown.
Finish cloth with a thin yellow-brown wash dragged down from the top and a little dark brown stippled at the hem.

guides.title: Stringy gore and drool
guides.summary: Pull strands of blood or drool between teeth and blades with a stringy gel or a tinted glue mix.
body: Finish painting the mouth or blade and everything near it first. The strands are fragile, so touch the area as little as possible afterwards. Dust the model with a soft brush or a blast of air so no fluff gets caught in them.

Use a thick stringy blood gel, or mix clear gloss red with a little dark brown ink and some clear glue until it pulls strings like a thick sauce. Mix on an old lid with a cocktail stick, as glue ruins brushes. Black, brown or blue shifts the blood tone. For clear drool, use plain stringy contact glue or craft glue.
Take a blob on a cocktail stick, pin or needle tool, touch one anchor point, pull away and touch the next. Dab each anchor two or three times so it holds.
In a mouth, spit gathers deep inside and at the corners of the jaw. Work from the back outwards, tongue to palate and gum to gum, as strands deep inside are awkward to add last.
Work fast. Glue thickens within about half a minute, so swap to a fresh blob and tool when it gets heavy. Warming a gel pot in warm water gives thinner strands.
Let it dry fully, then pick off stray threads with tweezers. Pulling them while wet unravels the lot. Very fine strands vanish at arm's length, so make a few thicker ones on gaming pieces.
Gloss the inside of the mouth, not the teeth all over, so it looks wet against matt skin. A dab of gloss on a thick strand forms a hanging drop. If a blood mix dries matt, brush gloss blood over it.
Add a little splatter around the mouth or blade too, and stop early. It is easy to overdo. Carry these models on magnets so the strands are not knocked off.

guides.title: Stubble and expression lines
guides.summary: Glaze a grey and flesh mix for stubble, and add fine pale lines for wrinkles and expression.
body: Finish the skin first, including the main highlights. Stubble and fine lines go on top.

Mix the skin colour with a little blue-grey, about four parts skin to one grey, and thin it to a glaze. Mixing grey with flesh keeps stubble looking like part of the skin rather than grey paint. Plain dark grey, dark brown or blue-black heavily thinned also works.
Wick the brush almost dry on tissue, then brush it over where hair would grow: chin, jaw, cheeks up to the sideburns and the top lip, or a shaved scalp. Keep it off the cheekbones and nose.
The first coat barely shows. Let it dry and repeat, usually two or three coats. Several thin coats look far more natural than one strong one, so stop before it goes solid grey.
Quick option: brush on thinned black ink and dab it with a fingertip before it dries, leaving a faint shadow with a soft edge.

Re-highlight the raised areas over the stubble afterwards, especially round the mouth, and glaze a little red back on the lower lip if it lost colour. A very thin dark red on the nose and cheeks adds a weathered, ruddy look.

For wrinkles, use the final pale highlight to paint fine lines at the outer corners of the eyes, a few across the forehead, and beside the mouth. Keep the contrast gentle: soft shifts, not hard lines.

guides.title: Faded and sun-bleached paint
guides.summary: Fade a whole paint job by lightening and greying each colour, most on top surfaces, then tie it in with a filter.
body: Sun fades paint where it hits most. Tops and upper edges go lighter and greyer; undersides and sheltered recesses keep more of the first colour.
Start the scheme slightly dull. Add a touch of grey or pale sand, #c8bc9f, to each colour before painting, so nothing looks fresh.
Then fade the tops. Glaze or drybrush a pale warm grey, #bdb5a6, over upward-facing surfaces, building it slowly. On big flat panels, dots of pale oil paint dragged downwards work well.
Each colour fades its own way. Reds turn pinkish, blues and greens go grey and chalky, and black becomes a dusty grey. Plan the faded colour, not just a lighter one.
Unify with a thin filter. A pale sand or dusty grey filter over the whole model mutes everything together.
Add a few sharp, newer chips and scratches. Bright fresh metal against faded paint sells the age.
Finish matt. Sun-bleached paint is never shiny.

guides.title: Tabletop standard versus display level
guides.summary: Tabletop means every area painted, shaded, highlighted and based; display adds smooth blends, crisp detail and a story base.
body: A tabletop standard model has no primer, bare plastic or bare metal showing anywhere, and each main area, such as skin, cloth and armour, has its own clear colour.
It has basic depth: a wash or ink in the recesses, then a dry brush or a simple highlight on the raised areas. The aim is a model that reads well at arm's length.
The base is finished too: paint plus a texture such as sand, grit, grass or slate, and a neat painted rim.
Display level adds blends that make the light look believable. They need not be perfectly smooth, but steps should not jump out up close.

Small details hold up close to: crisp buckles, eyes, faces and hair texture. Freehand, transfers or texture effects are common, with transfers painted over so they look painted on rather than stuck on.
A display base is built or sculpted to give the model context, and painted with the same care as the figure.
Check display work in a sharp, close photo, which shows missed spots and flaws the eye skips. Size sets a limit: a very small figure cannot carry as much detail as a large monster.
Tabletop is not a dead end. You can come back to any finished model later and add more shadows, highlights and details.

guides.title: Painting tentacles and suckers
guides.summary: Fade tentacles from a dark root to a pale tip, then pick out the suckers in a lighter, contrasting colour.
body: Decide the direction first. Most look best dark at the root, where they join the body, and pale or bright at the tip. Reverse it for glowing or poisonous tips.
Base the whole tentacle in the darkest colour, such as a deep purple, #3d2342. Then work towards the tip in two or three lighter steps, each covering less of the length.
Smooth the steps with thin glazes, or wet blend while the paint is wet. On many tentacles, a drybrush or airbrush from the tip end gives quick, even fades.
Highlight along the top of each curve, not the whole tentacle. The underside, where the suckers sit, can be a paler, different colour, like a soft pink, #d9a0a8.
Pick out each sucker with a light rim and a darker centre. Paint the rim in the pale colour, then drop a thin wash or a dark dot into the middle.
Spots, stripes or a colour shift along the length, such as purple to pink to cream, suit sea creatures.
Finish with gloss varnish or a gloss glaze to make them look wet and slimy. Keep it on the tentacles, not the whole model.

guides.title: Texture marks as highlights
guides.summary: Use lighter scratches, lines and dots as both wear and highlight, so you build texture and light in one go.
body: Texture only shows where light catches it. Put the marks where highlights belong and keep the shadows smooth and plain, so the busy lit areas stand out. Lighter, denser marks read as brighter; sparse ones read as darker.

Start the texture with the first layer after the base coat. Added only at the end it looks stuck on. Each lighter step uses smaller marks over a smaller area, and a glaze towards the light between steps ties them together.

Leather: drag the brush tip loosely across areas you want lighter, mix in some stippling and add a few crack lines. Cloth: draw many short thin lines along the folds, letting some jump higher so the edge is uneven.

Straps and brushed metal: paint very thin parallel lines, glaze over them to knock them back, then add more on top. Horn and bone: paint lines that follow the shape, getting lighter and smaller towards the tips.
Worn edges should not be one even line. Dab broken, uneven marks and vary the thickness, letting it thin out where there is less wear. This is also forgiving if long clean edge lines wobble for you.

For see-through colours like red, trace the marks in a brighter, more opaque mix, then glaze the proper colour over them. If the highlights climb too far, glaze the base back over or rework with an earlier midtone.
Mixing different textures across a model adds contrast and a lived-in look. Keep a few smooth areas so the textured ones have something to stand against.

guides.title: Keeping texture in scale
guides.summary: Keep scratches, stipple and texture fine, getting finer each stage, or the model starts to look small.
body: Chunky scratches and texture make a model look like a toy. Aim for marks fine enough to suit its size.
The first texture stage can be slightly chunky, mostly towards the edges.
Each lighter stage goes inside the last, finer and closer to the edge, leaving some of the earlier stage showing.
Use a fine point, good light and a firm brace: rest your little finger on your other hand to lock your grip.
Step back to arm's length now and then to check the scale reads.

guides.title: Thinning washes with medium
guides.summary: Thin a wash with clear medium or flow improver so it shades recesses without staining the raised areas.
body: Mix roughly equal parts wash and clear medium on the palette and stir well with a large brush. If unsure, add a little more medium; you can always add a second coat. A gloss medium helps the wash pull into recesses and leaves flat areas cleaner, which is handy on gold.

Water is fine up to about half and half. Past that it breaks the paint and leaves pale, crusty rings in the recesses. Medium thins the colour without breaking it. The same goes for one-coat contrast-style paints.
Brush it on one panel at a time, pushing it outward from one spot. It still settles in recesses, but the raised areas stay lighter, so there is less to paint back.
If it beads up or sits on raised areas, a tiny drop of washing-up liquid or a few drops of airbrush thinner break the surface tension. Use very little or it can foam.
Keep a second pot of pure medium. Dip a clean brush in it to pull away any puddles left on flat areas. Leave the wash 30 to 45 minutes before painting over it.

On pale colours like bone, a warm flesh or purple wash thinned this way gives soft definition without looking dirty. Hide small blotches afterwards with a light drybrush of a lighter tone in the middle of each area.

guides.title: Tinted or candy metallics
guides.summary: Get coloured shiny metal by putting a thin coloured one-coat paint, ink or glaze over a metallic base.
body: Base the area smoothly in silver, gold or a coloured metallic, then drybrush a brighter metal over the raised areas. The shinier the base, the more it glows through. Any roughness also shows through the tint.
Over a spray metallic, still brush a coat of metal on top. Spray metallics are so smooth that washes and one-coat paints slide off them.

Thin a deep one-coat paint or ink with a little water or medium and apply it one panel at a time, like colouring in, then leave it alone. Going back into a drying panel tears it and leaves blotches. If that happens, re-base the panel and redo it.
Let it dry and add a second coat the same way for a richer, darker colour. Some metal must still show through or the metal look is lost.

Silver under a warm tint gives copper, bronze or gold with highlights already in place; under blue, red or green it gives a candy finish. Gold under red gives a warmer metallic red. One silver can serve every metal on the model this way.

Shade with a thin wash that matches the colour, not black, and a dark ink for the deepest shadows. Bring shine back with a very dry stipple, light drybrush or edge highlight of bright metal on the top surfaces and edges.

With an airbrush, spray dark metal all over, bright chrome from above and any edge highlights, then build the clear colour in many light, dry passes. Wet coats pool. Thin clear paints with care: too little thinner clogs, too much weakens the colour. If a part goes wrong, spray silver over it and start again. Wear a mask with filters.

Quick alternative: mix a little ink into the metallic. Purple ink pushes bright gold towards copper or bronze; blue or brown in silver gives cooler or warmer steel. Ink keeps the sparkle, while ordinary flat paint dulls it, which suits iron. Test mixes on a spare part. A thinned gloss varnish on top gives a wet, glassy look.

guides.title: Tiny bright shine points
guides.summary: A few very small, very bright dots and lines on eyes, blades and armour make them read as shiny.
body: Shine comes from contrast, not area. Shiny things have few midtones: the jump from dark to light is sudden. Keep your brightest colour to very small spots, with a dark colour right beside them.
Put a tiny bright dot in eyes, lenses, gems and slime, usually on the side facing the light. For a lens that pops, paint it white first, then a strong colour over it, then a white dot in one corner.
On blades and armour, add short thin bright lines and dots on the corners and edges where light would catch. On barrels, one thin scratchy line along the top suggests a reflection.
Instead of a full final edge line everywhere, place a tiny dot of the brightest colour just where edges meet or change angle. It raises contrast with almost no time or risk.
After weathering, a few dots of bright metal on random points bring back the shine on metal parts.
Use near-white or pure white only here, and only a few. Too many spots and nothing reads as the brightest. Do it last.

guides.title: Torn and worn cloth
guides.summary: Paint rips, holes and frayed hems with dark shapes, a light lip under each, and broken edge highlights.
body: Mix dark brown with a little black and paint a few small irregular holes and tears, mostly near the bottom edge where cloth wears most.
Vary sizes and shapes, and do not take them too far up the cloth. Treat any sculpted holes the same way.
Paint a small line of light highlight just under each dark mark. The light lip makes a flat dark shape look like a hole with depth.
For a frayed hem, highlight the edge in a lighter cloth colour with random small nicks in it, then paint a few short lines running into the fabric from the edge for loose threads.
For general wear, dab short, jagged strokes of the lighter colour along the existing highlights instead of a clean line. It is easier than a neat highlight and suits used gear.
Fine crosshatched strokes of a well-thinned light colour suggest worn weave. Put each stroke down in one pass so it stays thin, and use them to hide small mistakes too.

guides.title: Upgrading an old paint job
guides.summary: Refresh second-hand or early models with touch-ups, a wash and new highlights instead of stripping them.
body: Check the model first. If paint is so thick that detail is lost, stripping may be worth it. Otherwise paint over it.

Repair before painting: pull off loose parts, clean the old glue off both faces and reglue so they sit tight. Fill chips and gaps with putty. Primer or paint evens out tiny scratches, so do not chase every mark.

Work out what bothers you. Common faults: everything too dark, no clear main colour, one effect drowning the rest, and sloppy, undefined edges. List the fixes and do the ones with the biggest effect for the least time first.
Scrape off mould lines or nubs with a hobby knife, right through the paint. A coat or two covers the bare spots without priming. Brush off dust and shavings with a big soft brush.
Touch up the main colour with the nearest match you have rather than re-basing the whole model.
Paint the underlying colour first, then the trim and details over it, a touch brighter than you want.
Wash to tie old and new paint together, then add fresh highlights. Contrast is what lifts it: if everything is dark, nothing reads as dark.

On a whole army, upgrade a step or two at a time and keep a list for later. The biggest gains are usually more contrast on the figures and more detail on the bases; keep base details that still work. If figures are glued down, do not fight to reach hidden spots. It is far more achievable than repainting everything.

guides.title: Classic toy soldier style
guides.summary: Simple bright reds, blues, black and white with only gentle highlights give a clean, classic toy soldier look.
body: Pick a few strong, simple colours: a clear red coat (#b01f24), blue cuffs and facings (#1f3f8a), black hat and boots, and white belts and straps.
Base each colour neatly and fully. Clean edges between colours matter more here than any shading.
Shade lightly, then layer a slightly brighter red and blue over the raised areas. Keep highlights subtle so the colours stay bold and flat.
Highlight black with a dark grey, mixed from black and a little white, on edges only.
Warm the faces with a light blush of thinned red on cheeks, nose and lips.
Swap the coat and cuff colours to make an opposing side with no extra planning. A gloss varnish at the end adds to the old toy look if you want it.

guides.title: Metallic paint placed like painted metal
guides.summary: Place light and dark metallic mixes as reflections, as you would for painted metal, for a high-contrast shine.
body: Real polished steel shows near-white highlights right next to very deep shadows. Copy that contrast; pure black is fine in the deepest recesses of metal.
Base a matt dark colour, or a smooth mid steel. Metallics grip poorly on gloss, and the dark gives the shadows.
Mix steel with matt black for fixed shadows: bands of light and dark running along cylinders like legs, the lower part of round shapes. Let it dry before judging, as wet paint still shines.
Washes kill the shine. Shade by glazing the dark mix back in from each side instead. Leave the very bottom slightly lighter for reflected light from the ground.

Stipple a half and half steel and dark mix as the first light, wiping most off the brush. The texture reads as brushed steel. Then stipple steel and bright silver on the upper areas, with the brightest dot on a tip or corner.
Avoid jumping straight from brightest to darkest. Keep a midtone, such as half steel and half silver, between them, or glaze a thinned mid mix over a hard line.

Edge only the most prominent upward edges with a light touch, and run a thin dark line into panel lines and between plates. On plates or scales, put the light end of one beside the dark end of the next. The contrast makes the metal sparkle.

Plain steel is dull in colour. Add interest with a bold rust or verdigris, or faint glazes of blue, purple or warm yellow on the highlights of polished metal. On gold, if silver-heavy top highlights look too white, warm them back with a thin brown glaze in plenty of medium.

guides.title: Painting two light sources
guides.summary: Light one model from two sources, one clearly stronger, with a band of shadow left between them.
body: Start from a colour true to the material, such as a sickly green skin. It changes how each coloured light looks on it.
Place the two lights at clearly different angles, roughly opposite each other: for example cool moonlight from low right and firelight from high left.
Decide which light dominates and make it noticeably brighter, so they do not compete. A fire close by overwhelms everything; dying embers give only a faint warm tint.
Do one light at a time. Mix each light colour into the base and step up in brightness over smaller and smaller areas. Sharp jumps over small areas look more dramatic.
Each light makes its own shadow. Keep a dark band where the two shadows meet. Without it the lights merge into mush and neither looks real.
Fast version over black primer: spray or paint a warm colour from one side only and a dark sea blue (#1e4a5a) over the other, then build each side up, covering less with each lighter step.
If one side looks flat, glaze a related colour from its highlight down into the shadow, keeping the two sides distinct.

guides.title: Building colour in thin coats
guides.summary: Two or three thin coats give even colour, sharp detail and no streaks or brush marks, where one thick coat does not.
body: The first thin coat looks patchy with primer showing. That is normal. Let each coat dry fully before the next.
Strong colours may cover in two coats; weak ones like yellow and white often need three or more.

Thin to suit the paint: dense paints need more water, many go on almost from the pot if spread well. A drop of water to three or four of paint is a safe start. Test a stroke before touching the model.

Thin coats flow into recesses without filling them, so fine detail stays sharp. Wipe the excess off the brush every time: too much paint on the brush drowns detail. Streaks, clumps and lost detail almost always mean the paint is too thick.
Thicker paint is fine if spread evenly. The problem is paint pooling at the bottom of a fold or a base rim and drying as a ridge. Pull excess away with a damp brush before it dries.
Every later layer and highlight needs the same care. A highlight that is not fully opaque never reaches its full brightness, which is why colours fail to pop. Give each new colour two or three coats.
Trick for neat edges: make the first coat thinner so it runs to the edges itself, then lay the second coat in the middle only.
It is a guideline, not a law. Over-thinned paint runs into recesses and fills detail too. If you build many layers, start with thicker opaque coats and go thinner as you refine.

guides.title: Filters: very thin all-over tints
guides.summary: A filter is a near-clear tint brushed or sprayed over a whole surface to unify and tone colours; unlike a wash, it must not pool.
body: A filter is paint thinned to about one part paint to nine or ten parts thinner. It barely covers and only shifts the tone of the whole surface. A wash is much stronger, around half and half, and is meant to pool in recesses.

Use a filter to tie patchy colours or camouflage together, tone down harsh highlights or modulation, bring back colour that went too pale, or add a dusty or grimy cast, such as a dark brown over green.
Seal the paint with satin varnish first, ideally left overnight. Enamel and oil filters can lift unsealed acrylic, and the satin lets them spread evenly.
By brush: load a flat brush, blot most of it off on paper, then stroke lightly in one direction, top to bottom, so any faint runs look natural. Never flood the surface.
By airbrush: spray thin, light coats without wetting the surface. Acrylic filters dry fast and show brush marks, so they suit spraying. Brush solvent filters instead, as their spray mist is toxic.
Build strength in layers. Wait 15 to 30 minutes between enamel passes, or the next lifts the first. Each pass adds tint and cuts contrast, so two thin coats are usually plenty; more just looks dirty.
Fix brush marks in wet enamel with another light stroke or a brush damp with thinner. Let the last coat dry fully, ideally overnight, before a pin wash or streaks.
On wood, give different planks different faint filters, such as red, yellow, green or blue, to mimic natural variation. If you use filters and washes together, filter first and wash after.

guides.title: Painting with stencils
guides.summary: Cut a simple stencil from masking film or vinyl, spray or dab thin coats, and let it set before lifting it.
body: Keep the design simple and bold. Cut it from thin masking film or removable vinyl with a sharp knife or a cutting machine, or use a ready-made mask. A round stencil gives a clean circle that is hard to paint freehand.
Line it up against a short strip of tape as a straight guide. Press every edge down firmly, pushing it into panel lines and curves with a pick or soft tool. Fuzzy edges mean it was not flat.
Spray or dab thin coats, with paint only a little thinned. Very runny paint creeps under the edge in spidery lines. Light coverage looks worn or grimy; heavy coverage looks stamped on.
No airbrush? Wipe a sponge or stiff brush almost dry and dab through the stencil while holding it flat. Never wipe across it. Use the stencil for the main shapes and finish small parts freehand.
Light colours over black take many coats. Put a white base inside the stencil first, then the yellow or other light colour over it.
Let the paint set fully before peeling. Lift too soon and paint pulls up and smears onto the dark area around it.
To wear the symbol later, put a thin layer of chipping medium or masking fluid under the stencil, not on top of it. Too much medium makes the paint stick to the stencil and tear away, so test first.

Medium underneath also lets you wipe off paint that leaked past the mask with a damp brush. No medium gives the crispest edges. Very small designs may be easier freehand, and on bumpy surfaces or symbols with two or more colours a decal is usually easier.

guides.title: Painting very small models
guides.summary: Paint tiny-scale figures with bold colour blocking and few layers, picking out what reads at arm's length.
body: Prep carefully. At tiny scales every mould line shows, and one heavy cut can take off a limb, so shave nubs in slivers. Prime in short, light bursts and check between them; too much primer drowns detail fast.
Nobody sees fine blends or small straps at arm's length. Pick out shields, cloaks, plumes, faces and spear tips. Choose a brighter version of each colour than usual so the shape reads at all.
Spray each strip or batch the colour that covers most of it, then drybrush that colour and block in the rest roughly.
Wash everything with a brown shade. It fills the gaps you skipped. Thin washes and one-coat paints more than usual: one blob covers a big share of a tiny model and floods grills and tracks.

Use fewer steps with bigger jumps. Push strong contrast between light and dark, and between neighbouring parts: dark metal on a bright vehicle, light metal on a dark one. Line between parts with thinned black, or paint all webbing and kit solid black first and leave a sliver showing at the edges when you colour it.
Tidy the brightest areas with their base colour and add a few highlights on heads and shoulders. Edge highlights help small parts read. A dusty drybrush round the feet makes a unit look finished.

Every layer adds thickness, so plan steps, use thin paint, and use an old fine brush worn to a needle tip. One mixed step between shade and base softens the jump. Leave part of each layer showing, or the gradient is lost.
On bases, use fine texture paste instead of sand, which looks like boulders, and only the smallest tufts. A light neutral base colour makes dark figures stand out.

guides.title: Vignette bases
guides.summary: Fade a base from dark at the rim to light under the feet so the eye is pulled onto the model.
body: Build the base and check the model sits on it before painting.
Paint the outer area very dark so it blends into a black rim.
Work lighter tones in towards the centre, under the model's feet.
Put the strongest highlights only on the tops of details near the middle.
Match the base colours to the model: cool tones for a cool figure, a warm glow for a warm one.

guides.title: Volumetric highlights
guides.summary: Highlight whole raised shapes by their form and direction, not just their edges, so the model looks solid.
body: A flat panel with a shaded recess and a lit edge can look flat up close. Decide where the light comes from and paint light and shadow across each surface instead: skin, armour, cloth and even metal.
A wash follows gravity, not light. One side of a groove faces up and should be brighter; the other faces down.

Think of each part as a simple shape: shoulders as spheres, legs and arms as cylinders, plates as boxes. Light it as that shape. A cylinder catches light as a line along its length; parts facing down or sitting low go darker.
Cover the top of each bulging shape, such as a muscle, cheek or plate, with an opaque lighter layer, leaving grooves and undersides dark.
Treat small shapes as part of bigger ones. A head is a sphere, so features nearer its top get more light.
Then add smaller, brighter highlights on the highest points.
Placement matters more than smoothness. Rough highlights in the right places already look convincing.

guides.title: Wash or glaze
guides.summary: A wash is meant to run into recesses; a glaze is meant to stay on the surface and tint it.
body: Both are mostly water and can share the same ratio of paint to water. The difference is how you apply them.
For a wash, apply straight from a loaded brush so it breaks surface tension and runs into cracks.
For a glaze, wick most of the liquid off first so it sits on the surface instead of running.
Very thin glazes act as filters that shift the colour underneath. They tint rather than hide, so use them to nudge a colour, change it or smooth a rough blend. Build them up in several passes.
A clear medium helps a glaze hold together and stay put, but many layers of medium can build a visible clear film.

Pick a glaze when a wash would spoil the finish. Washes can dry matt and dusty, and too much on metal dulls it: gold goes flat yellow and steel goes grey. A heavily thinned black glaze gives cleaner dark shading than a black wash.
One wash can do both jobs. Thin it about three parts medium to one part wash and glaze it over the parts that sit in shadow. Once dry, run the same wash neat into the recesses only.

guides.title: Watercolour and gouache washes
guides.summary: Over gloss varnish, a runny gouache or watercolour wash stays in the lines and wipes off the surface, so mistakes are easy to undo.
body: Seal the finished paint with gloss varnish first, by airbrush or spray can. The smooth gloss protects the paint and lets the wash wipe clean off the raised areas.
Water down black or dark brown gouache until runny. Opaque gouache gives stronger lines than clear watercolour, though watercolour works for a softer tint.
Brush it into almost every recess: panel lines, gaps between plates and joins. It does not need to be neat.
Let it dry fully, then rub the surface with a clean damp brush, a cotton bud or a wet finger. The recesses stay dark and the raised areas come clean.
Nothing is fixed at this stage. Water wakes the paint up again, so you can wipe off and redo anything you dislike.
When you are happy, seal it with a sprayed varnish before more painting. Brushing wet paint, a wash or varnish over it can lift it again.

guides.title: Wax seals
guides.summary: Paint glossy wax seals with a deep red or plum base, dotted highlights and a small shine point.
body: Base the wax in a deep red, a burgundy, or a pinkish purple that stands out on most models. Two coats, avoiding the centre detail.
Wash with a dark brown-black just to define the stamped centre, drawing off the excess. Or skip the wash by mixing a little black into the red for the base and leaving it in the recesses.
Highlight with a brighter red or pink, leaving shade round the centre. Skim it round the rim with the side of the brush and dot it onto the raised blobs and emblem.

Highlight again with that colour mixed half and half with a pale bone, on the detail and the tops of the blobs. On a dark burgundy, a little pale blue-grey in the mix gives a cooler, dusty highlight. On purple wax, lighten with a light grey rather than white so it does not drift pink.
Add a tiny dot of pale bone at the top as a reflection. Small, sharp highlights are what make wax look glossy.
Glaze a thin red or purple over the whole seal to bring the colour back, and gloss varnish it if the rest is matt.

guides.title: Weathered chrome
guides.summary: Spray a mirror chrome over a vehicle, keep some panels clean, and grime the rest down with one-coat paints.
body: Lay down a smooth gloss black base, or gloss varnish over black. The smoother and glossier it is, the more mirror-like the chrome.

Airbrush a mirror-finish chrome over the whole vehicle. It gives every metal part you need. Brushing a liquid chrome on with an old brush gives the shiniest finish but goes tacky fast, so work quickly.
Spraying chrome inks may need a lacquer thinner, as acrylic thinner can make them clump. Clean brushes and airbrush with the same thinner at once, and wear a mask.
Leave the chrome to cure fully, often around two days, before touching or masking it. It stays soft for a long time.
Decide which panels should stay bright chrome and keep paint off them. Chrome is slippery: most paints need two thin coats to grip, so build coloured details carefully.
Over the rest of the metal, layer black and then warm brown one-coat paints to build grime and depth. Add thinned red-brown rust round rivets and where moisture would collect.
Pick out a few parts in copper or bronze to break up the metal.

guides.title: Weathering basics
guides.summary: Weathering shows age and use with wear, rust, grime and dust, while battle damage shows hits, each placed where it would really happen.
body: Weathering shows time and exposure: faded paint, rust, green corrosion on copper and brass, worn leather, grime, dust and mud. Battle damage shows impacts: chips, gouges, scratches, holes and scorch marks.
Decide the model's story first. Something that never fights gets only weathering, something fresh from a fight gets damage, and a veteran gets both. Think about sun, rain, mud and hard use.
Put wear where it would really happen: edges, corners, feet, hands, hatches and other spots that get touched or knocked. Logical placement matters more than quantity.
The main kinds: chips and scratches in the paint, rust and streaks running down from rivets, vents and edges, dark grime in recesses and low areas, and dust and mud on lower legs, tracks and bases.
Thin washes, oils or enamel-style products make streaks and grime. Dry pigment powder gives dust and mud; fix it with a drop of solvent or matt varnish so it does not rub off.
Choose one level, subtle or heavy, and keep it the same across a group of models so they look as if they have been through the same things.
Build up a little at a time and check from arm's length. Weathering is easy to add and hard to take away. Aim for what looks good rather than strict realism.

guides.title: Weathering buildings and terrain
guides.summary: Age walls and roofs with damp stains, moss, tone shifts, soot and dust, placed where weather would really leave them.
body: Think about where weather hits: rain runs down from roof edges, sills and gutters, damp rises from the ground, and dust and mud gather low down and in corners.

Shift the tone first. Dot slightly darker or lighter oils where you want more or less shadow, then blend them out with a brush damp with white spirit. Seal acrylic paint with satin varnish first so the spirit cannot harm it.
For damp and growth, add a green oil low on stone walls, at the foot of corners and on roof tiles. A thin green filter near the ground does the same more softly.
Age tiles and lower walls with a wash of light and dark brown pigments mixed into white spirit. Leave it a couple of hours, then lift the excess off raised areas with a cotton bud.
Run thin dark streaks down from sills, gutters and broken edges for rain stains, and drybrush or airbrush soot above windows, doors and chimneys.
If walls look flat afterwards, run a light highlight along the edges and dust a few tiles and stones with green pigment for moss.

guides.title: Order of weathering
