guides.summary: Weather in order: chips and scratches first, then streaks and grime, then soot and dust, and stop early.
body: Apply transfers before any weathering so they get chipped and dirtied with the rest. Look at real reference first: real wear is uneven and patchy.

Chips and scratches first, as damage in the paint itself. Sponge them on corners and worn areas, chip transfers with the colour underneath, and join chips with a fine brush. These marks then guide where rust and stains go. Some painters put rust round rivets and recesses before the chips; either order works.
Liquid effects next, as dirt sitting on top of the paint: rust streaks pulled down from fittings and big chips, oil stains, grime washes.
Run brown or olive washes where walls or hulls meet the ground and feather them upwards with a damp brush. Wood near metal gets green stains and moss rather than rust.
Atmosphere last: soot round exhausts and muzzles, then dust rising from the ground, such as a light drybrush or pigment of dusty brown above the feet or tracks, fading upwards.
Weather the model and its base to tell the same story. If the metal is rusty, the wood, hems and ground around it should look worn too. Mix a few kinds of grime rather than one effect everywhere.
Paint add-ons such as stowage separately, then weather them with the same products, especially dust, so they sit with the model. Leave a few newer items and often-serviced weapons a little cleaner.
Weathering is easy to add and hard to remove. Check from arm's length often and stop when you are happy, before it buries the paintwork.

guides.title: Weathering pencils
guides.summary: Draw rust, chips and dust with damp watercolour pencils, then shape or remove it with a damp brush.
body: Dampen the pencil tip first, ideally by touching it with a wet brush rather than dipping it. Used dry, it leaves dusty, patchy lines, though a sharp dry point is fine for small markings.
Wet, it becomes a thick paste that goes on boldly. Draw on rust, chips, verdigris or dust, or drag a dark brown down surfaces for oily grime.
Use a clean damp brush to streak, fade or shape it. Several rust tones can be blended together on the surface.
It stays workable when wet again, so you can lift off overdone areas like an eraser. Varnish to fix it if the piece will be handled a lot.
Pale dusty colours show best on black items. Pure black works for scorch marks. Avoid a pale pencil over red, which turns it pink.

Quick edge highlights: run a broad, blunt pale pencil along a panel line so it catches both raised edges at once. Over a gloss coat, the side of a white pencil drawn along hard edges gives highlights you can feather or wipe off with a damp brush. Seal with another gloss coat when happy.

guides.title: Weathering pigments
guides.summary: Use dry pigment powders, dry or as a wet paste, for dust, mud, rust and dirt in treads, then fix them.
body: Finish all painting first, as powder gets into anything painted afterwards. Use an old brush kept only for pigment, tip a little onto a tissue as a palette, and keep it in a sealed bag. Mix two or three earth shades; they stay separate and look more natural than one tone. Wear a dust mask and use pigments meant for hobby use.
Dry: work a little pigment into the brush, dab most off, and stipple it on lower legs, tracks and edges, heavier near the ground. Pick a colour close to your base, and start with less than you think.

Wet: mix pigment with water to a paste, or with white spirit or enamel thinner to a milky wash, and brush it into recesses, tracks, wheels and lower hulls. It looks dark and harsh while wet and dries back close to its colour, so wait until it is powdery again before judging or wiping off the excess.

For dirt in treads or base cracks, dab pigment on and sweep a brush of clean water over it so it settles into the grooves and leaves the tops clean. Isopropyl alcohol flows even better and dries fairly tough, which suits rust round rivets.

Wipe pigment off raised areas with a damp cotton bud to bring back the colour underneath. Drag downward lightly for streaks. For thick crusty rust, stir pigment into brown paint so it needs no fixing.

Do wet work before dry, and seal sand bases first, as liquid can lift them. One flat dry layer looks lifeless. For textured mud, sprinkle a thin layer, touch fixer to it drop by drop without dragging, then sprinkle more until it looks gritty. A wash over pigment dulls it, so add a light dusting once dry.

Loose pigment rubs off. Touch fixer, thinner or alcohol next to it so it wicks in; brushing it smears. Fixer and varnish darken pigment and weaken the effect, so put on a little more than you want and add a light dusting if it fades. Never brush varnish over it, and spray only a light mist at low pressure.

On small figures, pigment can flatten the contrast they need to read on the table. Skip it if they already carry painted dust, and save it for vehicles, terrain and big bases. Bases that are never handled may not need fixing. Ground soft chalk pastels make a cheap substitute.

guides.title: Weathering transfers
guides.summary: Chip, scratch and dirty transfers along with the surface around them so they look painted on, not stuck on.
body: A clean transfer on a battered surface looks stuck on. Put transfers on before any weathering so they pick up the same grime. Let each settle fully and dry crisp, and varnish over it if you will brush over it a lot.

Paint small chips and scratches into its edges and across it with the colour underneath, thinned and with a sharp brush. Keep it sparse and let your hand wobble a little. A broken outline reads as worn paint. A sponge dabbed nearly dry with the background colour chips a transfer or freehand symbol fast.
Or scrape small nicks off the dry transfer with a wooden toothpick, a fine needle or the tip of a sharp blade. Go gently so you do not dig into the paint below.
Damage the surrounding surface the same way and line up scratch directions across both. Carry panel chips into the marking, and add a little metal inside bigger chips if the panel has it.

Shade, glaze and filter over the transfer as you did the panel around it, then rub shade off the upward faces. A thin reddish brown glaze tones down a marking that is too bright; a brown wash stops white ones looking pure white.
Drag the same grime washes and stains across it, and add your usual contrasting chips and highlights over both marking and panel. A thin dark glaze can fade it towards the bottom with the rest.

On cloth banners, gloss first, apply the transfers, then brush a thinned very matt dark wash over them. It hides the film and makes the banner look dirty. Paint notches into the edges so the design looks torn with the fabric.

guides.title: Wet blending
guides.summary: Lay two colours side by side on the model and mix the join while both are still wet for a fast gradient.
body: Base coat the area solidly first in a tone of the colour. Blending onto bare primer or black looks spotty.

Set up a palette, clean water and a damp towel. Use creamy, well-pigmented paint at about base coat consistency. Extra water speeds drying and breaks the paint up, so add a little retarder or glaze medium instead. On a wet palette paint grows thinner within half an hour; a dry palette gives more control.

Paint the first colour up to the middle, then paint the second colour up to meet it. Painting both first with a crisp border marks where the blend goes. Work one small area at a time. Or cover the whole area in one colour and work the second in from where it should be strongest.

Wipe the brush on the damp towel instead of rinsing, then work the join with quick strokes along it, using the belly of the brush, until it softens. A brush with a slightly worn or flat tip pushes paint better than a needle point.
Dark colours overpower light ones. If one colour creeps too far, drop in a touch of the other and push it back.
Once the paint starts to drag, stop. Overworking leaves texture. Let it dry and repeat: two or three passes usually give a smooth result, and each one strengthens the colours.

Neighbouring colours like red and orange blend easiest; very different ones take more patience. White, yellow and orange are hard to wet blend, so layer those. Very thick paints go lumpy and pre-thinned airbrush paints are too runny. Metallics blend too, and you can use two brushes, one per colour.

Treat the wet blend as a quick first pass for light and shadow, then refine it with layers or glazes. It suits cloaks, cloth and skin; on small, fiddly areas layering is easier. Practise on primed pebbles or spare parts first.

guides.title: Wet blending one-coat paints
guides.summary: Blend two or three contrast-style one-coat paints wet on the model for quick gradients, even across a batch.
body: Prime pale, or zenithal prime black with white from above, so the colours stay bright. Pure white gives the brightest result; cream or light grey is duller.
One-coat paints dry slowly, so they blend well. Line the colours up in order on the palette with medium beside them. Strong colours used neat can turn muddy, so thin them.

Paint the first colour over part of the area and stop about halfway. Rinse, take the second colour and paint from the other end, brushing back and forth where they meet. Often they bleed together by themselves.
Work from light into dark where you can: dark creeps into light easily, but not the other way round. A middle mix of the two helps on long areas.
If one colour gets too strong, add a little of the other while still wet. Do not keep working one spot too long or it lifts. A large brush with a big belly mops up pools quickly.

On small details like feathers, place the dark colour only at the root and push it down, then glaze a well-thinned lighter colour over the whole length. Where they cross you get a middle tone for free.
For a fade into the paint below, use clear medium as the second colour, for example towards the tips of claws.
On a batch, go darker at the feet and brighter towards the head. Once dry, glaze over areas that need more depth, and add a light highlight over both colours to tie them together.

guides.title: Wet blending large areas
guides.summary: Blend cloaks, big cloth and skin quickly with a large brush, a mid tone and a shadow and highlight pulled in wet.
body: Use a large, full-bellied brush, size 8 or even a flat, and lay it close to flat to blend with its side. A tiny pointed brush cuts through the paint and leaves streaks. Satin primer helps, as a matt one soaks up water.
Base the area in a strong, smooth mid tone first. Mix a few steps towards a shadow colour and a highlight colour on a wet palette.
Look at where your lamp catches the model and mark those raised areas roughly first.

Paint the mid tone beside a recess, put the shadow colour into the recess while wet, and brush it along the fold into the mid tone. Do the reverse for highlights on the raised folds: a broad lighter stripe down the crest, with the base pulled along each side.
Use the paint barely thinned. The damp in the brush is enough, and thicker paint stays wet longer. Work one section at a time, quickly.
The first pass often looks streaky. Let it dry fully, a hair dryer is fine, and repeat on top rather than chasing smoothness. Get the values and shapes right first; hard lines at this stage are fine.

Finish with layered highlights or a fine line on the sharpest creases and hems. Glazes of the main colour, thinned about one part paint to three of water, smooth and unify the whole area; three to five usually soften a hard edge. On army pieces, a few wear scratches hide rough spots.
A shadow with a touch of blue gives a cool shade against warm highlights.

guides.title: Wet-in-wet blending
guides.summary: Wet an area with water or medium, then touch in thin paint and let it spread and soften on its own.
body: Wet-in-wet differs from ordinary wet blending. Instead of pushing two wet paints together, you wet the surface first and let thin paint diffuse into it, as in watercolour.
Wet the area with clean water, with a little medium or retarder if you like, so it is evenly wet but not running or pooling.
Touch slightly thinned paint into the wet area with the brush tip. The pigment spreads and softens by itself; thinner paint travels further.
Guide the spread with the tip of a clean damp brush. Watch the edge of the wet area, where the paint stops and can dry as a hard line.
Work one section at a time and let it dry before wetting the next one beside it.
If it goes wrong, let it dry and start again rather than adding more paint, which only muddies it. Partly done work looks messy, so judge it once the area is finished.
It suits soft shadows where parts meet, soft dark lining and loose colour shifts, and can be quicker than many glazes. Learn ordinary wet blending first.

guides.title: Where chips and scratches go
guides.summary: Place wear on edges, corners and parts that get hit or move, mostly small chips with a few larger ones.
body: Look at photos of worn vehicles, farm machines and tools first. Your eye already knows what real wear looks like.
Paint wears first on edges, corners and anything sticking out. The highest point of a curve counts as an edge. Hatches, doors, hinges and metal rubbing on metal wear too.
Concentrate damage where things get knocked: lower legs, hands, feet, knees, forward-facing plates, weapon heads, shoulder edges. Leading edges low at the front take more than the top at the back.

Leave quiet areas, such as inner legs and backs of shoulders, with little or no damage. The contrast makes worn parts stand out. Keep the amount even across the model: if one panel is heavily worn, the rest should match.

Start with small fine chips roughly following each edge, then add a few larger ones. Keep most small so the model stays in scale. On a big clean panel add one or two, step back and judge before adding more.
Moving parts and fronts get parallel scratches from scraping past things. On flat panels, keep scratch direction the same so it reads as a scrape, with the odd diagonal across.

Mix fine lines and dots of different sizes. Shallow damage shows a pale undercoat or a lighter tone of the area's colour. Deep damage shows dark material below: paint a dark chip inside some of the light ones, but not all. On a rusty part, chip with a lighter rust tone.
Match the amount to the subject: a parade-neat piece gets little, a scrappy vehicle gets lots, and a vehicle more than its rider. It is far easier to add damage than to take it away.

guides.title: Clean white armour
guides.summary: Paint clean white armour with an off-white base, neat warm recess shading, cleanup and sharp pure white edges.
body: Most of what reads as white is really greys and off-whites, and it looks whitest next to a strong colour. Save pure, opaque white for the final edges.
Prime white or light grey. Base coat an off-white in thin coats until there are no brush strokes or see-through edges, even over white primer. You need that paint later for fixes.

Shade only the recesses with a thin brush and a warm brown or light grey wash. Brown keeps the white warm; a blue-grey keeps it cool. If shading all over, thin the grey about half and half and work it round with a soft brush so it does not dry in blotches.
An oil wash or a thinned one-coat grey over gloss varnish lines recesses neatly and wipes off easily, which suits whole armies. Matt varnish once it is dry.
Clean up any wash that strayed onto the panels with the base colour, slimming the lines. Re-shade any that get too thin. Mistakes on white are almost certain, so plan for this step.
Edge highlight every edge in a brighter white, then a smaller final highlight of pure white on the top edges.
Do not fear a fairly dark grey right next to white. Bold contrast keeps white crisp rather than chalky. Too dark a shadow all over, though, makes it read as grey.

By airbrush: base a mid blue-grey over black, then spray paler mixes and pure white with the model angled so only top surfaces are hit. Glaze the mid grey back into shadows. For worn white, paint small chips in white with darker brown inside.

guides.title: Worn and cracked leather
guides.summary: Make leather look old with ragged highlights, fine cracks on worn edges, and a slight sheen left in the creases.
body: Base a dark brown and blend up to a chunky mid brown highlight. Use an earthier highlight than on hard armour so it reads as a different material. For black leather, base matt black and highlight with a pale grey brown in uneven, scratchy strokes.
Stipple a dark brown and black mix into the shadows for a slightly textured surface. Stippling barely shows on thin straps, so keep it for belts, wide straps and larger pieces.

With a lighter tone, paint fine scratches, cracks and nicks round the worn edges, folds and elbows. Let your hand wobble so the edge line is broken, or dot small irregular spots instead of a line. Where a strap bends, run short marks across it from the centre out to the edges.

Place the wear where it happens: belts and straps along their edges, bags at edges and folds, gloves at knuckles and finger bends. Leave one piece cleaner for contrast, and keep straight, neat edges on hard items like shields so only the leather looks scuffed.

Repeat with each lighter highlight, making the marks smaller and fewer, and brighten the very edges with the palest mix. A thin line of the darkest brown just beside a pale scratch makes it look cut in. Keep the brightest marks to a few lit spots; too much and it looks like plastic.

For deeper age, alternate: scratches and dots, then a thin glaze of the base colour to knock them back, then more marks. Make the marks a few steps brighter than you think, as each glaze dulls them. It suits shaky hands well.

Run a dark wash that dries with a sheen into the cracks; old leather stays shinier in the creases and goes dull and pale where it wears. Dot a light beige grey on the most worn spots, and matt varnish the cloth nearby so the leather sheen stands out.

For a batch, coat the leather in a brown one-coat paint and add one deliberately scruffy lighter brown highlight. With an airbrush, spray light then darker tones through a flattened pad of fine wire wool held close, moving it each pass, then pick out trim and stitching by brush.

guides.title: Worn metal edges
guides.summary: Dab a broken line of bright silver along edges, rivets and pits so metal looks nicked and battered.
body: Start dull. Worn metal does not shine much, so use a darkened, thinned metallic for the base and scratchy lines. Run thinned black into the recesses so the bright marks have something dark to stand against.
Use the brightest silver you have for the final edges. The more it contrasts with the dull metal, the better. Used sparingly, it reads as bare metal peeking through.

Instead of a clean line, dab along the edges with the flat of the brush, mixing short strokes, gaps and dots of different sizes so it looks like years of knocks. Keep most marks small; tiny chips look more convincing than big ones. Use the tip for inner detail, and turn the model so each edge is easy to reach.
Pick out rivets, sculpted scratches and the rims of holes and pits, plus the odd dot on top surfaces.

Put the most silver on cutting edges, exposed corners and the parts that stick out furthest, and add a few freehand nicks where the sculpt has none. On painted armour, fine silver lines along dark worn edges read as paint scraped to bare metal.
Keep the light angle the same as on the rest of the model. A thin rusty brown glaze afterwards adds grime. Be patient; this stage takes time.
Alternative: rub a soft, dark graphite pencil, or its powder, onto edges for a dark rubbed sheen. Mistakes dust off with a soft brush, but it can rub off in handling.

guides.title: Wounds and gore
guides.summary: Paint wounds, stumps and guts with deep red darkened in the recesses, raw pink edges and glossy blood.
body: Wash a slightly thinned deep red into cuts, stumps and the inside of mouths and let it settle. When dry, add a little black and wash only the deepest parts.

Highlight the raised flesh with a brighter red, then a pink, and a pale cream on the sharpest corners. On raw muscle, use thin lines along the fibres, mostly in the middle of each muscle, lightening with a warm grey rather than white.
Glaze a thinned purple around wounds and scars, pulling towards the wound, then a stronger pink just round the edges for raw, inflamed skin. Thin red slashes make small cuts.

For guts, base a deep red, wash dark brown so they sit apart from the skin, then finish with a glossy blood effect. For severed chunks, base a pale flesh, flood with clear red mixed with a dark wash, let it dry, then add a thick coat of plain clear red for a wet shine.
Varnish the model matt or satin first, then add glossy blood last so it stays wet-looking. A clear red with a little clear brown over an off-white base glows and varies nicely.

Fresh blood: slightly thinned glossy blood effect round mouths and wounds, with a few trickles running down. Thick, old blood: mix in a little black and dot it where it would collect. Bright red reads better on the table than a realistic brown.
Boils look stronger in a yellow-green against pink skin, with a pale dot in the centre so they look wet.
Treat gore like weathering. Start with the wounds themselves, build slowly and stop early, because it is hard to remove.

guides.title: Painting yellow armour
guides.summary: Paint bright yellow armour over a white or bone primer, shading gently down with warm oranges and browns.
body: Change your water first, as yellow shows every bit of dirt. Prime white or bone and make the base smooth and solid: yellow covers badly and dark spots show straight through. A yellow spray primer also works, but leave it to cure well before handling.

Paint the parts that will be black or dark first: joints, packs, trim and guns. Black bleeding into wet yellow is the usual problem, and yellow is easier to tidy over. Leave arms and shields off if that helps you reach hidden areas.

Base a rich yellow in three or four thin coats, each fully dry. By airbrush, spray white only where the light falls, then thin yellow in light passes. Or spray a warm brown all over, then yellow from above at a low angle: the brown left underneath does the shading.

For speed, put one heavy coat of yellow one-coat paint over clean white, one panel at a time. When dry it will be blotchy on flat plates; drybrush a matching opaque yellow over the raised areas to even it out, then a pass with a little ivory mixed in.

Yellow is pale, so it needs more shading than highlighting. Glaze an orange yellow down the lower part of each panel, then darker warm mixes lower each time. Gloss varnish before any wash so it flows cleanly and does not stain the yellow.
Choose the shade to suit the look: darker yellow keeps it clean, orange warms it, brown makes it duller and grittier. Put a warm mid brown only in the panel lines; a panel liner does this quickly.
Glaze the base yellow back over messy shading or tide marks. Lift excess wash off highlights with a brush loaded with clear medium.
Glaze a bright lemon yellow up the tops of the panels, edge highlight with a very pale yellow, and add white dots on the sharpest corners. Brown chips edged in pale yellow break up big yellow areas.
